title: Packers’ New Practice Squad QB Got Big Endorsement From Greatest of All-Time
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers made a change to the practice squad on Monday by signing quarterback Cam Miller.
Miller was a sixth-round pick by the Raiders last year after completing 69.3 percent of his passes with 81 touchdown passes and 19 interceptions at North Dakota State, which he led to two FCS national championships.
Before the 2025 draft, Miller got a Hall of Fame endorsement.
Tom Brady “liked the way he threw it, his technique, throwing from the ground up and his motion," Raiders GM John Spytek told The Athletic after the draft. “And he thought he had the potential to improve.”
That Miller was a winner mattered in the scouting process.
“I haven't had any interaction with Tom,” Miller said after being drafted , “but from every conversation that I've had with the GM [John Spytek], he has talked to me about how they want to bring in people that are winners, and who have been accustomed and used to winning games. And I think that that was really the x-factor in their choice to take me in the draft.”
He spent his rookie season on the Raiders’ practice squad without playing in a game; the Dolphins signed him to their 53-man roster late in the season.
“Probably his intellect and his accuracy will help him push it down the road,” then-Raiders offensive coordinator Greg Olson said at the time . "He's been a good player and has played in big games. The game's not too big for him, so I think his internal makeup is a real positive for him.”
With the Dolphins this preseason, he completed 42.1 percent of his passes for 170 yards with zero touchdowns and two interceptions and failed to make the roster or earn a spot on the practice squad.
“I think just my knowledge of the game” is what grew the most, he said late in training camp. “I think [offensive coordinator] Bobby Slowik has done such a great job of teaching the quarterbacks defense and running his system.
“I've been such a huge fan of him and the way that he's helped develop quarterbacks in the past, and it's been so great to just learn the game of football from him. I think that's been some of the most improvement, just seeing the field a lot better than I did in the past.”
Miller, a native of Solon, Iowa, was a first-team All-American as a senior in 2024, when he finished second in voting for the Walter Payton Award, which is the FCS equivalent of the Heisman Trophy.
Miller set school records for total yards (11,998), completion percentage (69.4) and passing yards (9.721). He tied Easton Stick’s school record with 129 total touchdowns.
While he played lower-tier competition, he was well-schooled in the factors necessary to be an NFL quarterback.
“I just think coming from a pro-style offense at North Dakota State, I’m accustomed to playing under center, playing in the gun, playing a pro-style offense,” he said after being drafted. “I think NDSU prepared me well, just with the system, doing under center play action, everything that we did in the gun I think is going to translate to the next level. I’m excited to dive into the playbook and start to understand it a little bit more.”
Before the 2025 draft, The Athletic’s Dane Brugler called Miller “an intelligent game manager” who lacked a “power arm” but delivered with anticipation and accuracy.
“The son of a football coach, his mental approach and on-field production showed improvements each season, although he will continue to have his doubters because of the level of competition he faced,” Brugler wrote.
“Overall, Miller won’t wow you right away because the physical traits are average. The more you watch, though, the more you come to appreciate his decision-making and feel for the position. He can be an asset in an NFL quarterback room as a reserve.”
The Packers’ practice squad quarterback had been Kedon Slovis; it’s not immediately clear if that was the corresponding roster move. Slovis competed for a roster spot with the Cardinals during training camp and spent the last two months on Green Bay’s practice squad.
“Just to develop and I think get to the point where coaches trust you to be a guy where they can, whether it’s a backup role or feel like they can bring you in and play in some games,” he told Packers On SI after being signed .
“Obviously, the goal is to be a guy that they want to play but, obviously, there’s some steps to go before that. So, I think that’s the next part is just develop as much as I can and kind of let the chips fall with me.”

title: Packers Sticking With Josh Jacobs; Here Are Jonathan Taylor Next-Team Odds
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are standing by running back Josh Jacobs.
“Obviously, we’re aware of the prior allegations on Josh,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday, a few days after more allegations threw his future with the team in doubt . “We’re going to allow the NFL to do its process, but I would anticipate him being a member of us moving forward. That’s really all I have to speak on.”
With the uncertainty over Jacobs swirling and the NFL trade deadline looming, the Packers are considered one of top contenders to acquire superstar running back Jonathan Taylor.
The Packers are the sixth-most likely team to have Taylor suit up for them after the trade deadline at Hard Rock Bet . Their +1200 odds mean an implied probability of 7.7 percent, which isn’t great but they’re still perceived to be among the front-runners.
Here are the odds from Hard Rock ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline. The Seahawks, who won last year’s Super Bowl, and the Broncos, who reached last year’s AFC Championship Game, are the betting favorites.
New England Patriots: +2000
Green Bay has the sixth-shortest odds; staying in Indianapolis is fifth.
“You know that day always comes,” Taylor told reporters in Indianapolis last week. “For many players, whether you like it or not, the day may come. You may get lucky enough to stay somewhere forever, but you understand the business side of it.”
He added “I'm always proud to wear the horseshoe, proud to be here.”
The Packers are near the top of the board for the odds. However, after the Colts sent All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the 49ers, three NFC teams have shorter odds than Green Bay.
Seattle, which failed to replace Kenneth Walker, are the betting favorites. The Giants, looking for a stud runner to help offset the loss of Jaxson Dart, and the Vikings, who are looking for a premier playmaker to help their defense, all have considerably shorter odds.
The Colts are looking for more than a second-round pick for Taylor. They are under no obligation to trade him and are looking for an offer too good to refuse. The frame of reference is the 49ers giving up picks in the second through fifth rounds in the 2022 trade for running back Christian McCaffrey.
The Packers don’t have a first-round pick following last year’s trade of Micah Parsons. They do have a second-round pick, and they could end up with bonus third- and fourth-round picks after losing Malik Willis and Romeo Doubs in free agency last year.
“You think we’re rebuilding?” Taylor responded to a reporter on Thursday.
“I would say, we’re going out there trying to win. So, for me, being a competitor, and not only for myself but everyone in the locker room, no one goes out there to wave the white flag and surrender. We’re going out there to compete. We’re going out there to get a win. Every time you go on the field, you want to dominate and show that you’re the best.”
The NFL allowed Jacobs to rejoin the Packers a couple weeks ago, and he started in games against the Lions and Panthers.
However, the NFL said it would look into allegations from three women stemming from Jacobs’ time with the Raiders.
Coach Matt LaFleur has had Jacobs’ back ever since he was arrested following a Memorial Day Weekend incident. Has anything changed?
“Like I said, I’m not going to get into that up here right now. We’ll just let the process play out,” LaFleur said.
Jacobs scored three touchdowns in his two games back in the lineup. While it hasn’t been reflected in team rushing success , he is by far the team’s best running back. The former team captain has had the support of the locker room throughout and was welcomed back to the lineup with open arms.
“Yeah, I would anticipate as we go through everything, him being a part of it,” LaFleur said.
Jacobs, who missed the first six games of the season, carried the ball 21 times for just 39 yards in the victory over Carolina.
“I'm sure that's definitely a process for him from that standpoint,” running backs coach Ben Sirmans said on Monday. “We did a lot of work when he wasn't with the team just making sure he was still doing the right type of drills to try to keep him in tune to what he's going to face on a Sunday, like a lot of run simulation drills.
“But I do think he's still getting his footing, especially when it comes to contact and all that.”

title: Winning Isn’t Everything, Truth Is Only Thing for Packers And Josh Jacobs
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – After spending the first six games of the NFL season on the exempt list following an altercation with a female for which he pleaded no contest, the spotlight is back on Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs for all the wrong reasons.
After starting and scoring two touchdowns against Carolina on Thursday, WGBA-TV Channel 26 in Green Bay received records from the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department on Friday following an open-records request. The records show that three additional women contacted the department to allege similar altercations with Jacobs from his time with the Raiders.
Jacobs’ legal team offered a strong rebuttal on Sunday.
From Jacobs’ legal team. pic.twitter.com/ASGAmTLIMX
It concluded with this final statement:
“The three accounts are old, are hearsay, and easily disproven, yet released to the media by police without any investigation to determine whether they were accurate or contradicted by evidence. Josh is answering them in detail because of the character assassination that is occurring, unfairly threatening his career.”
There’s no reason to jump to conclusions and believe the women on face value about the alleged incidents from four or five years ago. That doesn’t mean they are lying – let’s make that abundantly clear – it’s just that in today’s world, really, nobody deserves the benefit of the doubt. Nobody – and that absolutely includes the player, the lawyer, the team and the league.
There’s no reason to believe Jacobs when he (through his lawyers) said that these old allegations are “hearsay” and he’s done nothing wrong.
There’s no reason to believe coach Matt LaFleur when he said, “I know the guy and I know the character of the guy. I’ve said that many times. And, unfortunately, situations occur in life and it’s just an unfortunate situation.”
There’s no reason to believe the team and the league hadn’t stumbled upon this information while doing their own investigations into the May incident. No reason to believe everyone isn’t just kicking the can down the road.
At the same time, contrary to what my colleague, Conor Orr, wrote for SI.com, this should not be about the Packers being “the adult in the room” and releasing Jacobs because the rest of the teams are “sacrificing (their) morals.”
The NFL is a bottom-line business. “Winning isn’t everything, it’s the only thing” is a saying that isn’t too far from reality. Jacobs gives the Packers their best chance of winning games, which is why they stood by him throughout the ordeal. They chose to believe the Memorial Day Weekend incident is a one-off, one horrendous moment for the former team captain.
“I think a lot of times you get in a situation where you might not make the right decision,” LaFleur said when Jacobs returned a couple weeks ago. “I think people learn from their mistakes, and I think he’s extremely remorseful and I do believe that he’s a good person. I’ve been around him quite a bit and I believe in second chances.”
If you’re looking for a hot take on the worthiness of that second chance, I’m sorry. Not today, because none of us know the facts.
We don’t know what happened in May, the incident for which Jacobs pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and damage to a property. There is a video, which both the Jacobs and victim have asked to be sealed for understandable reasons.
Speaking of the video, the NFL removed Jacobs from the exempt list after six games because, without getting to view it, its investigation was at a standstill. It couldn’t keep Jacobs sidelined forever, so it allowed Jacobs to play while saying the investigation was ongoing.
Remember, on the battery charge, the Brown County District Attorney’s Office – which has seen the video – handed down a $1,000 fine. That’s not even a slap on the wrist. That’s like putting your arm around your kid and telling him in a soothing voice, “Don’t do that again.”
Was the penalty so minor because what happened that night was so minor – relatively speaking, obviously – or did Jacobs and the victim agree to a payoff so Jacobs could avoid much harsher discipline legally and from the league?
We all have thoughts and opinions, along with stances on winning games vs. having the moral high ground, but we don’t know the facts behind any of the allegations made by this year’s victim or the other women. There are snippets from those incidents on the police reports and there are rebuttals by his lawyers but, ultimately, the only people who know are the women and Jacobs.
The NFL didn’t suspend Jacobs, so the Packers’ hands are tied a bit in terms of his contract, the collective bargaining agreement and the salary cap.
If the Packers trade for Jonathan Taylor, it means they are moving on from Josh Jacobs. Here's the complexity: Josh Jacobs was never suspended. As such he currently qualifies for 100% termination pay - Meaning if released and he doesn't sign with another team the Packers will…
At the end of the day, Jacobs pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor and not a felony. The old allegations that were made public last week could lead to a suspension, which would open the door for the Packers to release him due to conduct detrimental to the team, but, again, what is the truth? And is there any appetite for actually finding the truth?
Maybe, if the team deems Jacobs misled them about the May incident, but, again, that’s nothing more than speculation based on limited knowledge of what happened.
LaFleur will talk to reporters on Monday afternoon. He will be asked to answer questions that he shouldn’t have to answer. Jacobs’ place on the roster presumably was made by the organization – general manager Brian Gutekunst and team President and CEO Ed Policy. That they aren’t taking the lead on this is absurd. The team hasn’t even offered a wishy-washy statement in the wake of Friday’s news.
What we do know is Jacobs remains on the roster. That’s all we know. Everything else is opinion. It’s up to the NFL and the Packers to sort out the details honestly and to the best of their ability and do what’s right for the organization and the league. Winning isn’t everything. The truth is the only thing.
Whatever the decision, everyone better be damned sure it’s the right one.

title: 3 Yards And Cloud of Dust Would Be Dream for Packers’ Worst-Ever Run Game
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The phrase “3 yards and a cloud of dust” to describe a rushing attack goes back at least 70 years. It’s a fitting sentence to lead off a story about the Green Bay Packers’ rushing attack.
One, the Packers’ rushing attack isn’t just bad. It’s historically bad. And, two, coach Matt LaFleur might let his eyebrows grow out of control for a 3-yard rushing average given how the first half of this season went.
The Packers’ ground game is impossibly horrible. With Week 8 almost complete, they’re the worst in the league with 60.6 rushing yards per game and 2.85 rushing yards per carry. The Raiders are next-to-last in both categories with 77.3 yards per game and 2.99 yards per carry.
Packers are averaging 60.6 yards rushing/game and 2.85 yards/carry. That's lowest per carry thru 8 games since 2016 Vikings at 2.71 and lowest per game since 2019 Bengals were at 59.5 The only team in last 80 seasons to be that low in both thru 8 games was Washington in 1961…
It’s not as if they’ve faced a series of powerhouse defenses. On Thursday night, the Packers rushed for 66 yards and averaged 2.54 yards per carry against the Panthers, who were last in the league against the run at the time. A couple weeks earlier, they rushed for 57 yards and averaged 2.19 yards per carry against the Cowboys, who were last in the league against the run at the time and are again after giving up 202 rushing yards against Arizona on Sunday.
Against Carolina, after 13 of their 26 carries gained 1 yard or less, LaFleur was asked if he’d seen anything to make him optimistic about the rushing attack.
“I mean, if I’m being honest, not a lot right now,” he said, “and that’s our job as coaches. We got to figure it out, because it’s not good enough.”
The Packers have gained a league-worst 485 rushing yards in eight games. That’s 77 yards behind Cincinnati, which has played seven games.
Green Bay’s 60.625-yard average equates to 1,031 yards for the season. Unbelievably, that would be the lowest season-ending number for any team since 1961, when the NFL moved to a 14-game season.
And if that’s not enough, going back to 1947 – the year in which the NFL stopped subtracting sack yardage from rushing totals – Green Bay’s 17-game pace would be the second-lowest season-ending number behind the 1947 Boston Patriots, who rushed for 973 yards in 12 games.
The lowest per-game average since 1947 belongs to the 2000 San Diego Chargers, who went 1-15 while averaging 66.4 yards per game. The Packers would have to average 71.6 rushing yards the rest of the season to not set that dubious record.
The Packers’ best rushing game of the season was 86 yards against Tampa Bay in Week 4. That was the debut of a new offensive line, which led to some optimism. So much for that. They haven’t gotten past 70 yards since. In two games with Josh Jacobs, they rushed for 60 yards with a 3.2-yard average against Detroit and 66 yards with a 2.5-yard average against Carolina.
Their eight-game streak of failing to reach 90 rushing yards in a game ranks as the sixth-longest single-season streak since the historically significant 1947 season. The Falcons in 1994 and the Colts in 1990 hold the record with 10. Only the Cols have a longer streak to start a season.
Since 1947, the Packers’ 485 rushing yards are the seventh-fewest for any team in the first eight games of a season. The Packers have a 5-3 record. Those other teams were a combined 6-42; the 2005 Eagles had four wins and four teams had zero wins.
The Packers’ best rushing game this season in terms of yards per carry was their 3.50-yard average against the Jets in Week 2. If that best game represented their season average, they’d be 30th in the league behind the aforementioned Raiders and Packers.
Those are all big-picture numbers. How about from an individual play perspective?
A “run stuff” is a running play tackled at or behind the line of scrimmage. For Green Bay, 24.7 percent of its running plays have been stuffed; only the Raiders (28.0 percent) have been worse. On the other hand, they also have a league-low 11 runs of 10-plus yards; the league median is 20.
On first-and-10, the league average is 4.27 yards per carry. The Packers are last with a 2.39-yard average – an incredible half-yard worse than any other team and 1.14 yards worse than 29 teams. Green Bay averaged 2.64 yards per carry on first down against Carolina, highlighted by Savion Williams’ 18-yarder on an end-around. Otherwise, the other 13 carries gained 19 yards.
From an EPA standpoint, the Packers are 32nd in expected points per carry and 31st in success rate, according to Sumer Sports.
Would the return of Josh Jacobs help save the running game? His eye for the smallest creases and his pile-pushing history suggested that, yes, he would at least get the running game out of neutral.
That definitely has not been the case.
Jacobs carried the ball 21 times for 39 yards against Carolina with a long run of just 6 yards. During the LaFleur era, which started in 2019, it was the fourth-fewest yards in the league by a back with at least 21 carries. (Also, and semi-related, Jacobs caught six passes for 13 yards, giving him 27 touches for 52 yards. It was the fewest scrimmage yards with 27-plus touches in three decades.)
“It wasn’t a lot out there,” he said after the game.
Still, the Packers are 5-3. Dating to the advent of a 16-game season in 1978, only four of the 36 teams that finished with less than 80 rushing yards per game posted a winning record. So, the Packers have been beating the odds.
“I honestly don't know,” Jacobs said if the team’s success without a running game is sustainable. “I've never been in this situation. But I mean it's a lot of hope. I would say that.
“I see the way that these guys work, the way that they’re intentional. We'll go have meetings without no coaches, just the O-line and the running backs, and we go over what we see and what they're thinking and what I'm thinking and the design of the play and little things like that. So, I think it’s only a matter of time before it gets cleaned up.”
Eight games is a large sample size. The Packers’ run game was terrible in Week 1, it was terrible in Week 8 and it was terrible in every game in between.
It was terrible with MarShawn Lloyd and it’s been terrible with Josh Jacobs. It was terrible with Brian Gutekunst’s hand-picked offensive line and it’s been terrible with his veteran additions. There have been six starting offensive line combinations and 11 individual starters. Nothing has made a difference.
With an opportunity to run out the clock against Carolina, the Packers failed. Against a quality opponent in a do-or-die game late in the season, that could end their season. With a stretch of late-season home games, the elements might dictate that the Packers have to run the ball.
Now, with Jacobs’ future perhaps in limbo again , there are additional questions about the state of the rushing attack.
The trade deadline is set for Nov. 10. Trading for Jonathan Taylor , especially with the new uncertainty surrounding Jacobs, could help, but probably not as much as landing a people-moving offensive lineman.
If it’s not the personnel, it must be the coaching. Fortunately for LaFleur, he had three extra days to sort through all the issues. Then again, he had three extra days after the Atlanta game and it didn’t help a bit.
The legendary Vince Lombardi famously said: "Gentlemen, we are going to relentlessly chase perfection, knowing full well we will not catch it, because nothing is perfect. But we are going to relentlessly chase it, because in the process we will catch excellence. I am not remotely interested in just being good.”
At this point, catching mediocrity would be a huge win.

title: Is It Time for Packers to Smack the Panic Button at Kicker?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers have a kicking problem.
With Trey Smack missing an extra point on Thursday, he is up to a league-high eight missed kicks his season. That includes six over the past four games, which begs this question (and the terrible pun from the headline):
Is it time for the Packers to hit the panic button?
The Packers traded up in the sixth round in this year’s draft to select Smack with the belief that he would upgrade an obvious weakness on the roster.
Everyone expected there would be some growing pains with a rookie kicker, just like there’s growing pains with a rookie at any position. However, those concerns to a large extent are a myth.
Over the last decade, 40 rookie kickers have attempted at least 10 field goals in a season. Will Lutz represents the league median with an 82.4 percent success rate. The overall median is 85.1 percent. For a kicker who attempts 35 field goals in a season, the difference in those percentages is one made kick.
Through eight games, Smack is 11-of-16 on field goals (68.8 percent) and 16-of-19 on extra points (84.2 percent). Among kickers with 10 field-goal attempts, only one kicker has a lower percentage. Among kickers with 10 point-after attempts, only three kickers have a lower percentage.
Just how bad has Smack been? For a team that enjoyed long runs of success by Chris Jacke, Ryan Longwell and Mason Crosby, here’s this nugget from The Associated Press’s Josh Dubow:
Trey Smack now leads NFL with 8 missed kicks (5 FGs, 3 PATs). That's most for a Packers kicker in first 8 games of a season since Max Zendejas had 9 misses in 1988
Against Detroit last Sunday, Smack missed from 26 and 35 yards. Other than a block, Smack’s miss from 26 is the only one from less than 30 yards this season.
Talk about a mental block. He could probably make 100 of those in a row in his sleep but, in the pressure-cooker of a division game at Ford Field, he misfired.
Coaches love to talk about having a next-play mentality. Matthew Golden dropped a touchdown pass against Carolina, only to catch a touchdown on the next play. Jordan Morgan can miss a block on first down but deliver a pancake on the next. Brandon Cisse can be flagged for pass interference on one play and make back-to-back plays in the end zone moments later.
It’s not that easy for a kicker, who might have to stew on a missed kick for an hour or a week.
“We’re better now,” special teams coordinator Cam Achord said on Wednesday, one day before the Carolina game and a few days after Smack in a three-point loss at Detroit became the first kicker since 2019 to miss two kicks of 35 yards or shorter in a game.
“I think for anybody, human nature, myself included, when you don’t go out and execute the way you want, you’re going to be a little bit frustrated, depressed or (feel) like you let people down. But as it goes on, you get back to it, and you can move forward. We’re good now. We’re in a good spot, and it goes back to having all the confidence in him and knowing that he is a confident person. So, I think we’re in a good headspace leading into tomorrow night. And I’m excited to see him kick.”
Smack missed his first extra-point attempt and was booed off the field. He bounced back to make the next three, with the fans celebrating with arguably the loudest cheers of the night. Was that a sign of that next-play mentality and a huge step forward? Or was that merely an NFL-level kicker doing something an NFL-level kicker is expected to do?
General manager Brian Gutekunst has to figure that out. He’s the one who gave up two draft picks to select Smack. He wouldn’t have done it if he didn’t think Smack had the talent and toughness to solve the Packers’ kicking problems. He wouldn’t have paid Brandon McManus’ $1 million roster bonus and then wished him good luck if he didn’t think Smack had what it takes mentally and physically.
Waiting for a young kicker can be a death sentence for a season, though. After a hot start to his rookie season in 2023, sixth-round pick Anders Carlson fell into a slump from which he couldn’t snap. So, it was no surprise at all that he missed a field goal in the Packers’ three-point playoff loss to the 49ers.
But, again, the Packers drafted Smack because they believed in him. He was the consensus best kicker in this year’s draft, so perhaps Gutekunst feels wedded to what Smack can become and inclined to wish away the struggles.
It’s different positions, obviously, so admittedly an absurd comparison, but Jordan Love threw eight interceptions in his first eight games as the starter in 2023. Should the Packers have benched Love at the time? They didn’t, of course, and their patience has been rewarded.
“A lot of people want to talk about the negatives and all that, which is fair. It’s very fair,” Achord said. “There’s no bones about that, but we’ve got to go back to the process that got us here and what we did 90 percent of the time.”
Should Gutekunst have drafted Smack in the first place, when history will tell you that the difference between a drafted kicker (median 85.0 percent on field goals over the last decade and undrafted kicker (85.7 percent over that same span) is negligible? Should Gutekunst have given Smack a free pass onto the roster by releasing McManus and Lucas Havrisik before the first offseason practice?
The answers are probably no and no but, at this point, those questions are irrelevant. What’s done is done. The Packers drafted Smack, they didn’t pressure him with a challenger and now a team with a small margin for error has one of the worst kicking situations in the league.
So, what should they do with him? Do they ride it out, betting that Smack will get “the contact back to where it was and where it can be,” as Achord put it? Or will they bet on whatever unemployed veteran kicker they can find to fix what ails the kicking game, like McManus did in 2024?
There’s no easy answer, especially at a position group in which Havrisik, with a career success rate of 79.2 percent on field goals in 12 games, might be the best option.
Maybe it’s a damned-if-you-do, damned-if-you-don’t proposition. The Vikings drafted Daniel Carlson in the fifth round in 2018 and cut him after two games. He became one of the best kickers in the league with the Raiders, including two All-Pro seasons.
Maybe that will be Smack’s path. Maybe a few extra points will get him out of his funk and he will be a weapon for this year’s playoffs and the next several years’ playoffs. Or maybe he’ll kick the Packers right out of the playoffs and the team’s kicker merry-go-round will keep spinning.

title: Packers Reaching Familiar Trouble Spot With Jordan Love
full_text:
Brett Favre. Aaron Rodgers. Jordan Love.
The Green Bay Packers have been set at the quarterback position essentially since 1992, with those three men having been excellent stewards of the organization.
Quarterback is the most important position in professional sports, so having a great quarterback is the single greatest trump card that any team can possess.
The Packers have essentially had great quarterback play with a few exceptions in every NFL season since 1992. That’s a big reason why they’ve been competitive for as long as they have been, with their 348 regular-season wins being only one less than New England’s 349 during that span.
Love appears to be the latest in that lineage. There is a long way to go before Love matches either of his predecessors. Those two will both be first ballot Hall of Famers. They have seven MVPs, two Super Bowl titles, and three Super Bowl appearances between them.
Favre’s number is retired and Rodgers’ number will be some day, as well.
Favre and Rodgers, however, provide a cautionary tale that appears to be rearing its ugly head in Green Bay this season.
Love has been excellent for most of the season. The Packers have relied on him more than they ever have since he took the reins in 2023.
Love does not have the gaudiest numbers this season, but he is playing incredibly well as he’s helped guide the Packers to a 5-3 record. He’s done so with no help from his running game, an offensive line constantly in flux and pass catchers who lead the league in drops.
As a result, Love has had to play the role of Superman to ensure the Packers are competitive, let alone win.
“Can’t say enough great things about him because he’s carrying the burden of everything right now, just dealing the ball and throwing a lot of great passes,” coach Matt LaFleur said after Thursday’s victory over the Panthers.
Does any of this sound familiar?
If you’ve followed the Packers for any period of time since Favre took over at quarterback, you’ve probably understood that every weekend the team had a chance to win because of who was under center. The concerns you had likely were related to the supporting cast – or lack thereof.
After going to back-to-back Super Bowls in 1996 and 1997, Favre saw the roster around him start to decay. That started at head coach, with Mike Holmgren replaced by Ray Rhodes and Mike Sherman. Neither coach was a savant like Holmgren.
The lack of passing-game weapons surrounding Favre by the end of his tenure, shoddy defenses and inconsistent run games helped prevent the Packers from reaching another Super Bowl. Favre was often asked to play Superman, and inevitably proved to be human.
Rodgers suffered a similar fate when he was the quarterback in Green Bay. His team won the Super Bowl in 2010 before Rodgers won the first of his four MVP awards.
From 2010 onward, however, the Packers never really had a full team surrounding him. He had to carry bad defenses, mediocre run games and catastrophic special teams to the postseason before they inevitably would run into better teams that could exploit those weaknesses.
Like Favre, Rodgers would prove to be human in the postseason, and the team around him was rarely able to save them from defeat if he did not play his best.
Through eight games this season, Love is working through that same fate. Offensively, everything falls on Love’s shoulders. Love is third in the NFL in passing yards per game and the running game is the worst in the league. So, you get this from NFL analyst Dan Orlovsky.
Jordan Love has accounted for 82% of Green Bay's yardage this season.
To be clear, Green Bay’s special teams is not very good, but at least its defense has been good to start the season.
Offensively, however, Love has been asked to carry a significant burden.
Their run game is threatening to compete for the least productive ground game in the modern era . Their offensive line has gotten him obliterated for most of the first eight games. Some of those issues have corrected themselves, but Love has spent most of the season under duress.
The best example of the Packers’ season, and how it could end, came on Thursday night against Carolina.
Love started the game on an absolute heater. He completed 17 of his first 20 passes. The three incompletions? Two drops and one catchable pass. Love’s excellence in the first half and early third quarter helped the Packers build a 27-10 lead.
In a normal setting, that should have been enough. Green Bay’s defense is excellent. A passable run game could help turn the Packers into a boa constrictor and squeeze the life out of the game.
Green Bay’s offense is not normal. Their run game was unreliable, Love cooled off and the Panthers got closer than they ever had any business being.
Can Green Bay survive with a putrid run game? Even Love doesn’t think so.
“Definitely. I think that’s an area we’ve got to keep getting better at, keep finding what’s working, but we’ve got to improve because, especially late in the game, you’ve got to be able to lean on that,” Love said after the game.
“We did some really good things and I think, obviously, late in the game, it wasn’t good enough. We weren’t able to finish the way we wanted so that’s something we’ve got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”
Love is capable of putting on Superman’s cape. He’s done so in Green Bay before. He’s had to do so throughout the season.
Whether it’s Tom Brady, Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, Favre, Rodgers or Love, the best quarterbacks eventually play below their standard.
Asking one man to carry the weight of an entire organization on his shoulders is too much to ask for anyone.
Ask both of the quarterbacks who were great that came before Love. They both should have more than one Super Bowl based on their talent level alone. Ultimately, a lot of factors play into why the Packers’ trophy case is not fully stocked the way that having back-to-back Hall of Fame quarterbacks would indicate it should be.
Moving from Rodgers to Love was supposed to come with the understanding that their quarterback was not going to have to play that role every week.
If the Packers want to win a championship this year, or in the near future, they better figure out a way to win when Jordan Love plays like Clark Kent.

title: Packers Trade for Jonathan Taylor More Likely After Latest Josh Jacobs Update
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are in fact in on a potential trade for Indianapolis Colts superstar running back Jonathan Taylor, a source told Packers On SI on Saturday.
“It’s on the table,” a source said without going any further. Taylor won’t come cheap because other teams are interested and the Colts don’t need to make the deal.
According to Tom Pelissero’s Substack , The Sweep, the Colts already have rejected an offer of a second-round pick plus an additional draft pick.
“The Colts haven’t told other teams exactly what they want for Taylor,” Pelissero wrote, “but it makes sense they’d want something close to deal the Panthers got when they traded Christian McCaffrey to San Francisco in 2022 in exchange for 2023 second-, third-, and fourth-round picks plus a 2024 fifth-rounder.”
The return of Josh Jacobs to the lineup seemed to throw cold water on any interest in acquiring a running back. However, WGBA-TV Channel 26 in Green Bay obtained records from the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department from its investigation of the May incident that led to Jacobs’ no-contest plea for misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property. Those records show additional allegations from before he joined the Packers in 2024.
The Packers would be getting a younger player (Taylor will turn 28 in January and Jacobs will turn 29 in February), a player with less wear and tear (257 fewer touches), a more explosive player (4.8 yards per carry for his career compared to 4.2 for Jacobs) and a player under contract through 2028 (compared to 2027 for Jacobs).
Jacobs is one of the better running backs in the NFL. Taylor is one of the best.
Taylor rushed for 1,431 yards in 2024, 1,585 yards in 2025 and is on pace for 1,426 yards in 2026. His 4.2-yard average this season is the lowest of his career; he averaged 4.9 yards per carry last season.
Taylor has home-run speed. Since the start of the 2025 season, only Derrick Henry and Bijan Robinson have more 20-yard runs than Taylor. Only Henry has more 20-yard touchdowns. His big-play ability would work with Green Bay’s big-play offense.
Like Jacobs, Taylor is an adept receiver. He caught 46 passes last season, when he scored a league-high 20 total touchdowns.
He has 17 fumbles out of 1,691 career rushes. Jacobs has 17 fumbles out of 1,872 career rushes. So, from that perspective, both players are reliable ball-carriers.
As was shown with the return of Jacobs, the problem with the Packers’ running game is the guys doing the blocking and not the guys doing the running.
Green Bay is on pace to finish with the worst rushing average in NFL history. The rushing attack is as bad with Jacobs as it was without him.
On Thursday against Carolina, which entered the game with the worst rushing defense in the NFL, the Packers mustered 66 rushing yards with a 2.5 average. Jacobs carried the ball 21 times with a long gain of a pitiful 6 yards. Half of the team’s 26 rushing attempts gained 1 yard or less.
So, would Taylor actually solve the team’s problems? Or would the team’s limited capital to pull off a trade be better used on a high-quality run-blocking lineman?
Speaking of draft capital, the Packers do not have a first-round pick in 2027 following the Micah Parsons trade. They do have a second-round pick and will have multiple mid-round selections with the compensatory selections coming their way after losing Malik Willis, Romeo Doubs and Quay Walker in free agency.
Still, for a team with holes in the lineup, not having first- or second-round picks to provide young and inexpensive talent would be a challenge.
Taylor is under contract through the 2028 season, so the Packers would have him for two-and-a-half seasons.
If Taylor is traded, the acquiring team would inherit his two-year, $44 million contract, but the $15 million signing bonus would remain on the Colts’ ledger for cap purposes.
Taylor has a base salary of $6.98 million for this season; the acquiring team would only have to pay for the pro-rated portion of what’s left. Taylor has base salaries of $15 million in 2027, which would be guaranteed if on the roster after the Super Bowl, and $9.46 million (with a $7.5 million roster bonus) in 2028.
Taylor would be another expensive player on a roster filled with expensive players. However, the Packers could move on from Jacobs, who has a $12.2 million base salary for the 2027 season, to mostly fund Taylor’s contract.
According to records, three other women came forward with similar allegations. One told Hobart-Lawrence police about an alleged incident from January 2022, when Jacobs was with the Raiders.
From WGBA’s extensive story: “According to the records, the woman alleged Jacobs slapped her across the face and later took her cellphone as she attempted to leave his residence. The woman told investigators that Jacobs grabbed her by the hair, threw her onto a bed, pinned her down and later threw her onto the floor. The woman also alleged Jacobs spit on her and grabbed her by the throat.”
The Packers and the NFL conducted their own investigations; it’s not known if they were allowed to view these records and were aware of the past allegations when the league activated Jacobs and the Packers put him in the lineup. And if they were aware, did they deem them as not credible?
One source recently said that while the NFL classified its investigation as ongoing after removing Jacobs from the exempt list, the case had been closed unless and until it gained access to video of the incident involving Jacobs. Release of the video has been blocked by the victim and Jacobs.
It’s always been the expectation that the league would suspend Jacobs. The question was whether it would be a six-game suspension, with Jacobs’ time on the exempt list covering the punishment, or if he would be suspended for additional games.
The league on Saturday said it would “review these allegations.”
Jacobs’ legal team offered its response on Saturday: “The Brown County District Attorney’s office had these uncorroborated, old, and previously unreported allegations for months. They conducted their own exhaustive investigation, along with the police department, and the D.A. determined that only two misdemeanor charges were warranted. They then entered into a plea agreement with Josh Jacobs. Josh has repeatedly expressed his remorse and is honoring the terms of the agreement.”
Jacobs has played in the last two games.
“I’m excited to be back with the team, with the guys,” he said after his first practice on Oct. 21. “I want to say thank you to the organization really for supporting me throughout this whole process and how everything played out.
“With that being said, I can’t get into a lot of things like specifics of things but, obviously, I’m remorseful and sorry for putting this team in this situation. Sometimes when you go through life, situations occur and a 4-second, 3-second decision can alter your life, honestly. But with that being said, still a human being, man, still trying to learn, still trying to grow from the whole process.”
His touchdown celebration after his first touchdown against Carolina went viral; Jacobs said the Prime Video broadcast didn’t show the “whole celebration.”

title: Finally! Good News on Packers Star Micah Parsons’ Return From Injury
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur this week hinted that Micah Parsons would be back on the practice field following this weekend’s mini-bye.
Indeed, according to multiple national reports , Parsons will make his long-awaited return to the practice field next week with the hope of him making his season debut during the Thanksgiving Eve game at the Los Angeles Rams.
Because the Packers played on Thursday and will get the weekend off, there will be a bonus day on Monday. That’s Nov. 2, though the team probably will hold only a walk-through practice. That would make Wednesday, Nov. 4 – the start of the traditional practice week – the big day.
The Packers will play the Rams on Wednesday, Nov. 25. That means he will get a three-week ramp-up.
As NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport said , the focus for this coming week leading into the New England game will be individual drills, which will help Parsons knock off some rust and gain additional comfort and confidence in the knee. The following week, when the Packers will host the Vikings, Parsons will be incorporated into team drills.
Then comes the Packers’ pseudo-bye week, meaning a few rest days before rolling into Rams Week with practices on that Saturday, Sunday and Monday before flying to Los Angeles on Tuesday to play on Wednesday.
The Packers have persevered without Parsons. They are 5-3, due in large part to a defense that has defied expectations.
The Packers are 11th in points allowed, skewed by an offensive implosion that gift-wrapped the Vikings a bunch of points in Week 1 and one terrible performance against Atlanta in Week 3. The past five games, they have not allowed more than 20 points.
The Packers rank ninth in yards allowed per game and third in yards allowed per play. They have allowed 303 or fewer yards in six of eight games. Rather incredibly, they are a solid 11th in sack percentage without anyone on the roster picking up the slack. Lukas Van Ness has a team-high 4.5 sacks, including one of the team’s six against Carolina.
The team’s four edge players each had a sack against the Panthers but have only a combined total of 9.5 for the season.
That will make Parsons a seismic addition – assuming he returns at anything close to peak form.
While the Seahawks acquired All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and the Bears landed All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, perhaps no move made before the Nov. 10 trade deadline will be more consequential than Parsons’ return.
The Packers were 9-3-1 when Parsons was injured at Denver last season, but they lost their final five games. Despite a myriad of problems this season, they are 5-3 and right in the thick of the playoff chase following the victory over Carolina.
Parsons tore the ACL and suffered meniscus damage against the Broncos, making it a more significant injury than the ACL tears sustained by teammate Tucker Kraft and Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
He had surgery on Dec. 29, meaning his first practice will be a little more than 10 months later and his potential season debut will be a little less than 11 months later.
When Parsons spoke to reporters during training camp, he had this revealing comment. Yes, Parsons has to get the knee back to full strength following the ACL injury. But he also has to get everything back to full strength so one problem doesn’t create another problem.
He believes assorted issues after not practicing for the Cowboys in training camp before last year’s trade might have led to the injury.
“I just think it was just accumulative things within my body – pushing through the no camp, the dealing with injuries throughout the season, and I just think my body just was overloaded, which caused my knee to give out,” he said. “But I don’t really think [about] why the situation happened. I think based off of how I feel at this point, I feel like a much better player in the sense of how I feel.
“I feel more stable. I feel stronger. I probably was blind to a lot of things that I probably should have been working on that I got a chance to correct and get stronger during this process.”
So, Parsons saw the potential upside of how the injury could impact the “longevity” of the 27-year-old’s career.
“I talked to a baseball guy,” Parsons continued. “He’s like, ‘We want a pitcher that kind of go through the Tommy John [surgery] because it’s like he got it out the way,’ you know? So, hopefully, I got my injury out of the way, and I can, based off what others try to say, give me another six to 10 years. So, I’m really excited about that.”
From the team perspective, the Packers don’t want to do anything to jeopardize their enormous investment following a trade that cost them two first-round picks, Kenny Clark and $188 million.
Parsons shares a similar train of thought. In a story this week by ESPN.com Packers beat writer Rob Demovsky, a source pointed to the rise and fall of Parsons’ close friend and former Cowboys teammate Trevon Diggs. He was one of the best cornerbacks in the league in 2021 and 2022 – he led the NFL with 11 interceptions in 2021 – but suffered a torn ACL early in the 2023 season, which ruined his career.
“I think watching one of his best friends go through what he went through, coming back early twice and where his career headed afterward, he already had in his head how to approach this situation,” the source said.
If the target game of the Rams becomes reality, Parsons will have missed the first 10 games of the season. But he’ll be back for the most important games, including a potential playoff run.
“It’s about knowing when to go and it's all about feeling great,” he said during training camp. “Like I don't think Gutey (Brian Gutekunst) or Nate (Weir) or Matt (LaFleur) wants me to go out there if I'm not at 100 percent and risk re-injury and lose me for the year and it's just a waste of a year.
“Everything is about playoffs and winning football games deep in [the season]. Yeah, those games are important, but maybe we don't see Dallas twice, but we see Chicago twice and the games that we have in December or even more playoff games and not to even just look that far ahead, but we got a tough schedule this year and I think for the betterment of everyone, everyone wants me at 100 and wants me in those games so we can make this championship run.”
Matt LaFleur had the perfect six-letter word for his defensive coordinator, Jonathan Gannon, following the Packers' win over Carolina. ⬇️ https://t.co/aCM9sVLN52

title: Packers Midseason Stock Report: Risers and Fallers After 5-3 Start
full_text:
Just like that, we’re at the halfway point of the Green Bay Packers’ 2026 season. They are 5-3 and positioned to make a run at another playoff berth, if not more.
Not everything has been perfect. All three of their losses have come against NFC opponents, and two of which have come against divisional foes. They’ll get a chance to bounce back against Minnesota and Detroit at Lambeau Field later this season.
They have gotten contributions from a wide range of players, and some have seen their value to the team rise during the course of the year. Others have taken a step back. With half a season in the books, who are some guys that are rising and falling? We analyze that here.
Some eyebrows were raised this offseason when the Packers gave Christian Watson a lucrative contract extension to keep him in Green Bay for the foreseeable future. Watson has always carried value in Green Bay’s offense even if he did not have the gaudy box score numbers to show for it.
This year, he has found the box score numbers to match. He is on pace to not just top 1,000 yards for the first time in his career; he’s on pace to reach 1,500 yards. He has grown into a leader in the receiver room, as well, with that leadership on display Thursday night as he was willing to play through significant pain.
Watson’s toughness and ability to fight through a broken rib impressed all of his teammates, and showed why everyone in the organization raves about him whenever they get an opportunity.
Through eight games, Watson leads the team in yards and touchdowns. He has 16 fewer targets than Matthew Golden, but is just one catch behind him. Watson is ascending into a star, which is exactly what Green Bay’s passing game needs him to be.
It’s OK to admit it. You wanted Jim Leonhard, the former Wisconsin Badgers player and coach, to be the team’s defensive coordinator after flirting with the job in the past.
It’s OK to admit that you watched the clips from HBO’s Hard Knocks and were worried that Jonathan Gannon was a strange guy who could not possibly motivate a defense after failing as a head coach.
It’s also OK to admit at this point that if you thought that, you were wrong. Gannon’s defense has been excellent for most of the season. They gave up 39 points in the first game of the year at Minnesota and 35 against Atlanta two weeks later.
Those two performances are really skewing what has otherwise been a really strong showing from Gannon and his defense early in the season.
He has not had his best player for the entirety of the season with Micah Parsons still not practicing. His next-best player, Edgerrin Cooper, played 14 quarters before bowing out with a torn Achilles.
What has Gannon done? He has weaponized his defensive backs and moved them all over the formation.
Gannon’s defense is much more aggressive than any of the men who have preceded him during the Matt LaFleur era. He’s not a loud, boisterous personality like Rex Ryan. He’s not outspoken like some other great defensive coordinators have been.
What he is, is a darn good coach.
The Packers rank fourth in defensive DVOA. They are third in yards allowed per play, including fourth in passing yards allowed per play.
He’s also got collective buy-in from his players. One of the marks of a well-coached team is when the players in the locker room are all saying the same things as the coaches and their fellow players. Green Bay’s defense is constantly repeating the same lines that Gannon states to the media. They’re parroting terminology from each other, as well.
Gannon’s defense looks fast, disciplined and confident in everything it’s doing.
Soon, it will get Parsons back, too.
“I can’t say enough great things about our defense, Jonathan Gannon,” LaFleur said after Thursday’s game. “The job he’s done, just being aggressive the entire game and putting a lot of pressure on the quarterback.”
The potential bad news here is that if Gannon keeps this up, he may get another opportunity to be a head coach somewhere else.
Yes, Golden has had some issues with drops. In fact, he leads the league in drops. You know how you get to the point where you lead the league in drops? You’re always open. Golden is almost always open, and leads the team in receptions with 43 in his second season. He’s second to Watson in touchdowns with four.
Watson and Golden look poised to be the first pair of Packer teammates to break 1,000 yards receiving in the same year since Jordy Nelson and Randall Cobb did that in 2014.
Yes, Golden needs to clean up the drops. He knows that, but he certainly looks the part. If he keeps getting open, the ball will come his way. If the ball keeps coming his way, there’s a good chance he’s going to keep making plays as he has all season.
The Packers are relying on Jordan Love more than they ever have during his time as the starting quarterback.
When Love took over for Aaron Rodgers in 2023, the idea was to keep a team around him that made it so he did not have to play the role of Superman every week. Through eight weeks this season, it’s hard to tell where the Packers might be if Love was not playing as well as he did.
Thursday’s game against Carolina might be a perfect microcosm of the Packers as a team. Love started out the game on fire, completing 17 of his first 20 passes with two touchdowns to get the Packers out to an early lead.
He threw a third touchdown pass in the third quarter to make the score 27-10 and it looked like the Packers were going to coast to victory.
From there, the lack of running game bit the Packers as Love cooled off. He threw a bad interception on a pass he said he wished he had back right after the game ended.
As Love cooled off, the Panthers crept closer. Ultimately, Green Bay was able to escape with a 27-19 victory, but it never should have gotten that close.
Love is operating with an offensive line that has gotten him killed almost every week. His run game is nonexistent. His receivers lead the league in drops. His team leads the league in penalties.
All the while, Love has continued to play as well as he ever has. He’s thrown 16 touchdown passes to just six interceptions. He might work his way into MVP conversations if the Packers can continue to win with him playing well.
Perhaps the two biggest beneficiaries of Jonathan Gannon’s defense coming to Green Bay have been the defensive backfield duo of Evan Williams and Javon Bullard.
Bullard is the team’s nickel defender. He has a tenacity that has been missing from this Packers defense for years. He hunts opposing ball-carriers, and has been asked to hunt opposing quarterbacks more than ever.
“Yes. Not even close,” Bullard said when asked if he was blitzing more this year than last year. “The trust that the coaches have in me, I’m so grateful for that. We come to practice, we work every day, we put things on tape that coaches notice. Some coaches have the guts to dial them. up, some coaches don’t. You respect the ones that do.”
Bullard does not have a bunch of gaudy stats in the box score, but his fingerprints are all over the game whenever Green Bay’s defense is on the field.
Evan Williams has been one of the beneficiaries of Bullard’s willingness to do the dirty work. He does have the box score numbers to match the impact he has made, as well.
Along with the team lead in tackles, Williams has two interceptions, one sack, six PBUs, two tackles for losses and one fumble recovery. Gannon’s willingness to deploy his best defensive players all over the formation makes them unpredictable and more disruptive than they were in recent years.
As a result, the Packers have surpassed their number of takeaways from 2025. Bullard and Williams are big reasons for that.
Far and away the worst part of Green Bay’s team is its run game. Words like historic and generational are often thrown around too loosely, but if you can think of a bad superlative, it fits this Packers team.
The Packers are on pace to break records in a bad way for how putrid they’ve been on the ground…

title: Three Overreactions From Packers’ Win Over Panthers: This Will Ruin Season
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers beat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night. It wasn’t pretty and it wasn’t easy – these Packers are incapable of such things – but a win is a win, and they have five of them in eight games.
Here are our three big takeaways.
Jordan Love’s numbers are mediocre.
His level of play, however, has been worthy of MVP consideration.
Of 29 qualifying quarterbacks, Love is smack dab in the middle with a passer rating of 92.5. He is 22nd in completion percentage. Only five quarterbacks have thrown more interceptions.
But Love has had to carry a heavier load than perhaps any quarterback leading a playoff-caliber team. The pass protection hasn’t been good enough, though it was against Carolina. No quarterback has been saddled with a worse running game. No quarterback has had to overcome more dropped passes or a higher percentage of dropped passes.
Love is not going to win MVP; Buffalo’s Josh Allen, who probably has fewer passing-game targets than Love but at least has a really good running game and reliable pass protection, is in his own tier as the strong favorite at FanDuel Sportsbook .
NFL MVP typically goes to the quarterback with great numbers on a great team. Love won’t finish with great numbers and the Packers aren’t a great team. But they would be absolutely sunk without him. If that’s not valuable, what is?
As coach Matt LaFleur said after a game in which Love threw three touchdown passes: “Can’t say enough great things about him because he’s carrying the burden of everything right now.”
Before the season, I predicted the Packers would finish with an 8-9 record. The reasoning was rather simple. How could the Packers without Micah Parsons find a way to stop quality quarterbacks with an ineffective pass rush and questionable cornerbacks?
It appears I’m going to be “flying the L” on that one because defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has turned lemons into lemonade.
Parsons, one of the NFL’s best pass rushers and defensive players, still hasn’t returned to practice. The team’s next-best defensive player, linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, suffered a torn Achilles in Week 4 against Tampa Bay.
And yet, the Packers emerged from Thursday’s game ranked 11th with 20.5 points allowed per game. They are third in yards allowed per play, fourth in yards allowed per passing play and 12th in yards allowed per rushing attempt. Their 15 takeaways through eight games are one more than they had all of last season. They’ve allowed 20 or fewer points in five consecutive games, their best stretch since 2022.
And it’s not as if it’s Xavier McKinney snagging interceptions left and right or Lukas Van Ness has played up to Parsons’ hype. Six players have at least one interception. Five players have forced at least one fumble. Six players against Carolina had one sack, meaning 11 have at least one this season.
At cornerback, Keisean Nixon is thriving in Gannon’s system and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse is playing beyond his years.  The rookie class of Cisse, defensive tackle Chris McClellan and edge Dani Dennis-Sutton are playing a lot of snaps and all made big plays against Carolina.
With the expectation that Parsons will return to practice next week , a defense that has done more than survive without its All-Pro could really start to thrive for the stretch run.
A couple weeks ago, the Packers faced the Cowboys, who had the worst run defense in the league at the time. Green Bay managed 57 rushing yards with a 2.2-yard average. On Thursday, the Packers faced the Panthers, who took over as the worst run defense in the NFL. The Packers rushed for 66 yards with a 2.5-yard average.
The running game is a disaster. It’s no longer a matter of a small sample size of games or a bad game or two to skew the numbers. The Packers are averaging 60.6 rushing yards per game, which would be the worst in NFL history, and 2.85 yards per carry.
The Packers have 485 rushing yards in eight games. Ten individuals have more rushing yards through six or seven games. Somehow, they’ve gone from bad to worse, with a 2.58-yard average the last three games.
Their best rushing game was 86 yards at Tampa Bay, which leads to this incredible stat from The AP’s Josh Dubow:
The 5-3 Packers are 5th team since 1933 to rush for fewer than 90 yards in each of the first 8 games of a season. Others: 1990 Colts 2-6 1941 Rams 2-6 1940 Eagles 0-8 1935 Pittsburgh Pirates 3-5
Somehow, the Packers are 5-3 despite a running game in which the old “3 yards and a cloud of dust” mantra would be a huge win.
Fewest yards rushing/game for team with winning record thru 8 games of a season: 2026 Packers (5-3) 60.6 2016 Giants (5-3) 68.3 2009 Chargers (5-3) 69.6 2007 Packers (7-1) 72.1 2016 Vikings (5-3) 72.6
Green Bay’s running game, in a word, stinks.
The Packers have had six starting combinations on the offensive line and 11 individuals have started a game. Nothing – nothing! – has mattered. Every team has had at least two 100-yard rushing performances and the league median is four. Green Bay hasn’t even reached 90 yards.
The Packers ran the ball 26 times against the Panthers. Against the worst run defense in the NFL, half of them gained 1 yard or worse. The longest of Josh Jacobs’ 21 carries gained 6 yards.
Green Bay won the game but was fortunate to do so. And here’s where this season will eventually be crushed.
At some point, you have to be able to go into your 4-minute offense and run for two or three first downs to win the game. The Packers were in that situation twice vs. Carolina. On the first, they took over with 5:37 on the clock. Every play on the possession was a pass. On the second, Jacobs rushed for 5 yards and 3 yards to set up Jordan Love’s third-down conversion to Christian Watson. However, Jacobs ran for minus-3, 0 and 1 on the next three plays to give the Panthers the smallest glimmer of hope.
If the Packers can’t run the football successfully against the worst run defenses in the NFL, how are they going to be able to run the football against the best defenses?
Packers are averaging 60.6 yards rushing/game and 2.85 yards/carry. That's lowest per carry thru 8 games since 2016 Vikings at 2.71 and lowest per game since 2019 Bengals were at 59.5 The only team in last 80 seasons to be that low in both thru 8 games was Washington in 1961…
Seattle and San Francisco, two teams who could be standing in Green Bay’s way in the playoffs, rank second and third in yards allowed per carry. Houston and Buffalo, who loom on the late-season schedule, are eighth and ninth. Next week’s opponent, New England, is 11th.
Eight games into the season, there seemingly is no hope.
Don’t take my word for it. Here’s what Matt LaFleur said after the game:
“If I’m being honest, not a lot right now, and that’s our job as coaches. We got to figure it out, because it’s not good enough.”
LaFleur and the coaches had all offseason to figure it out. All of training camp and the preseason to get it started. Eight regular-season games to get things pointed in the right direction.
Jacobs is back in the lineup. Veteran blockers have been signed. New line combinations have been tried, including bat-bleep loony ones such as moving Laken Tomlinson from left guard to right guard – a position he hadn’t played since 2016 and hadn’t practiced since joining the Packers.
Nothing has worked. Not even a little bit. Somehow, it’s actually gotten worse.
“I think that’s an area we’ve got to keep getting better at, keep finding what’s working, but we’ve got to improve because, especially late in the game, you’ve got to be able to lean on that,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “Obviously, late in the game, it wasn’t good enough. We weren’t able to finish the way we wanted so that’s something we’ve got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”
Love’s exactly right. Knowing there’s a problem and actually fixing it, of course, are completely different things.
In 2021, it seemed obvious all along that the special…

title: Texans' Stance on Jadeveon Clowney Trade Rumors Becomes Clear
full_text:
The Houston Texans saw a big name on their defense surface in some trade rumors earlier this weekend as they were in the midst of their Week 8 bye,
And those rumors surrounded veteran edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney, who, according to ESPN' s Adam Schefter, was a name circling around with interest from opposing teams ahead of next week's trade deadline.
Another pass rusher who has generated some interest ahead of next Tuesday’s trade deadline is Houston defensive end Jadeveon Clowney. https://t.co/haFgCAaWA8
Clowney's name popping up in trade rumors did come as a bit of an initial surprise. He was seen as one of the finishing touches to the Texans' defensive line upon his signing earlier this offseason, and has had a slow, yet solid start to his second stint in Houston.
So whether or not the Texans were actually looking to trade Clowney remained a bit in question upon the news first surfacing. However, in the hours following Schefter's report, it seems we now have some more clarity around how the front office actually feels. about a move surrounding Clowney.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson, the Texans are reportedly not actively shopping Jadeveon Clowney as the NFL trade deadline approaches next week. Clowney himself has also not expressed a desire to be traded.
#Texans aren't actively shopping three-time Pro Bowl edge Jadeveon Clowney, per a league source, and he isn't seeking a trade. Simply, the usual process of #NFL teams checking on several proven players' potential availability heading into trade deadline
So instead of the trade interest stemming from the Texans' or Clowney's side, it seems as if that intrigue has simply come from outside of the building from teams that are interested in going and making a move.
And from those teams that have started their season off extremely positively, that interest in Clowney makes sense. He's a productive veteran pass-rusher on a cheap, one-year contract, and could provide depth off the edge that might need some help run-stopping, perhaps with a bit of pass-rushing as well.
Through the first five games of the season that Clowney has been active for, he's put together nine total tackles, two tackles for loss, and 1.5 sacks. He's also been on a much-lower snap share defensively (less than 40%) compared to what he's seen early in the year.
But the Texans don't really have an incentive to trade away Clowney. From Houston's perspective, even while they have started the year off 2-5, this is a group that's still trying to compete in the AFC.
Trading away Clowney may provide some minor draft assets in return, but that might not be of value for a team with its eyes set on clawing into the Wild Card.
So perhaps you can expect the Texans to at least listen to offers surrounding Clowney from other front offices around the league leading up to next week's trade deadline. If Houston winds up dropping to 2-6 after a Week 9 loss vs. the LA Chargers , maybe the logic behind a trade then shifts.
But until then, all signs in Houston are pointing towards Clowney remaining on the roster past the trade deadline, and continuing to fill his role as Houston's third defensive end behind Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter.

title: New Details Emerge on Texans DB Reed Blankenship's Injury
full_text:
The Houston Texans have been without one of their starting safeties in their secondary for the past couple of weeks now.
Not just their versatile nickel, Jalen Pitre, but also starting strong safety Reed Blankenship as well, who's been deemed out since he went down with a concussion during the second quarter of Houston's Week 6 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
However, it was also revealed from the Texans' Week 7 injury report before facing the New York Giants that Blankenship was dealing with a hand injury –– one that wasn't exactly seen when the veteran safety went down against the Jaguars, but an issue that added to his troubles to get back on the field nonetheless.
And it seems like, leading up to the Texans' Week 8 game against the LA Chargers, we now know a bit more about the status of Blankenship.
According to Jonathan M. Alexander of The Houston Chronicle , Blankenship had surgery on his left hand "not long after" the Texans' win over the Jaguars in Week 6.
Alexander also notes that Blankenship is still in concussion protocol heading into the week against the Chargers, and will be a name to monitor as the week progresses.
Texans safety Reed Blankenship, who remains in concussion protocol, also  had surgery on his left hand not long after the Jaguars game, per a source. The Texans will see how he progress through the week.
Blankenship was one of the Texans' biggest offseason additions brought in several months ago one a three-year contract, and was expected to bring an added sense of stability within an already strong Houston secondary.
However, through the first seven games of the season, the Texans' secondary has taken a step back by pretty much all standards. Blankenship has gotten off to a slow start individually, and it certainly doesn't help for him to miss any time in Houston's lineup for any stretch either.
Through the five games that Blankenship has played for the Texans this season, he's collected 45 tackles, three passes defended, a tackle for loss, and managed to claim Houston's first interception of the season back in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts.
We'll know more about Blankenship's status now and moving forward once the Texans are back practicing on Wednesday, and we get an injury report designating the veteran safety as a full, limited, or non-participant.
A concussion absence typically lasts around one to three weeks for most players around the league, but with Blankenship's newly discovered hand surgery, there's a chance that it takes more time for him to return as a starter on the back end of the Texans' defense.
For any time that Blankenship is set to remain out for the Texans' secondary, the name to keep an eye on will be veteran MJ Stewart, who returned from his lengthy absence due to a quad injury earlier this year, and was elevated to a starter last week against the Giants as a plug-and-play replacement.
The Texans will have three practices to take on this week before their Week 9 action against the LA Chargers hits this weekend , but if we don't see Blankenship on the field for any of them, don't expect to see him on the field come Sunday.

title: Why Texans' Jadeveon Clowney Is Drawing Trade Interest
full_text:
The Houston Texans could have a surprise trade candidate on their hands–– and it's their former No. 1 pick Jadeveon Clowney.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, Texans edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney is drawing trade interest around the league leading up to the NFL trade deadline.
Another pass rusher who has generated some interest ahead of next Tuesday’s trade deadline is Houston defensive end Jadeveon Clowney. https://t.co/haFgCAaWA8
It comes as an eye-catching development surrounding one of the bigger names on the Texans’ defense. Clowney, who was a late free agent addition to the team heading into the 2026 season , was viewed as a finishing touch of sorts on an already elite defensive line.
And while the Texans' defensive production to start the 2026 season, or the results of their 2026 season as a whole, haven't been up to expectations, it hasn't been to any fault of Clowney's production–– or lack thereof. So why would he be in trade discussions?
Let's do a little bit of speculation as to why that may be:
Clowney, through the five games that he's played for the Texans this season, hasn't been as productive as he was through the short stint that he played for the Dallas Cowboys in 2025. He's recorded just nine total tackles, 1.5 sacks, and two tackles for loss.
However, Clowney has also played a whole lot less than he ever has throughout his career thus far. Clowney has played in 37% of the Texans' total defensive snaps in the five games he's been healthy for, compared to the 44% he saw with Dallas in 2025. In 2024, he was getting around 64%.
Teams around the league could be seeing a talented pass rusher stuck in a smaller role on a 2-5 Texans team— who's also signed onto a cheap one-year contract with a value of $5.5 million—and want to pounce on him for the cost of a draft pick.
And if the Texans wanted to strike on Clowney's value and expiring contract, while also bringing in some draft capital just a few weeks from their trade to bring in Marvin Harrison Jr., sending him out to another contending team could be a perfect way to do just that.
The Texans sent out a 2027 second-round pick and a future seventh-round pick to the Arizona Cardinals in that deal, and Houston's draft pick collection could continue to change depending on their trade deadline decisions.
The Texans could decide to cash in on Clowney's value, or continue to keep him as a rotational piece of their defensive line , and continue to try and climb out of their 2-5 hole after their Week 8 bye.
Behind Clowney, the Texans' top edge rushers consist of Dominique Robinson and Sebastian Harris. That makes Clowney still a valuable piece of Houston's defense as a third edge rusher behind Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, who's also on a team-friendly, short-term contract.
It remains to be seen which approach the Texans' front office decides to take, but Clowney is at least added to Houston's growing list of trade candidates on the roster heading into the NFL trade deadline that now sits under two weeks away.
