title: Raiders Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: Mixed Bag From Road Win
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' plan all along was to lean on their collection of talent, specifically their young talent. That became even more true during Sunday's win over the New York Jets. Las Vegas made enough plays in all three phases to pull out the win.
The Raiders' roster is filled with rookies and second-year players who become significant contributors. Several have already done so, as can be seen in the inevitable growing pains Las Vegas has faced early under Klint Kubiak. Yet the group played well.
Below are the power rankings of the Raiders' rookies and second-year players who made an impact in Sunday's win over the Jets.
Las Vegas turned to Washington to lead them out of the backfield on Sunday, allowing running back Ashton Jeanty some time off. Washington was key to Las Vegas' win, as his productive day on the ground helped open up opportunities for success for the unit overall.
The Raiders may continue doing some version of this until Jeanty returns to full strength. However, another solid week of production on the ground for Washington, especially against a much better San Francisco 49ers team, may be something the Raiders consider long-term.
The Raiders drafted Zuhn partly because he can play all five offensive line positions. With most of their offensive line solidified, the Raiders' offensive guard position has doomed several of Kubiak's game plans this season. Sunday, the Raiders mixed things up.
Las Vegas spent the entire offseason developing Zuhn at several different positions. After doing just about all they could to try to fix their right guard position, the Raiders finally leaned on their offseason preparation by starting Zuhn at right guard.
Aside from the results, Las Vegas is already seeing a return on investment from yet another one of John Spytek's draft picks. Zuhn could be what they need at guard for the rest of this season. Even if he were only better than the other guards on the roster this season, it would be a steal for Las Vegas.
“I thought Trey [Zuhn III] was calm in there. I thought he was well prepared. That was not a surprise, but I thought he played well. I think there’s things that he’s going to want to improve on. But I was pleased, along with the coaching staff, with the effort that he put on the field and what his future looks like for us,” Kubiak said Monday afternoon.
At the end of the first half, Jeanty had one carry, one target, and one catch. It was a noticeably light workload for the talented running back. Yet he made one of the game's biggest plays in the second half, as his 45-yard reception proved vital down the stretch.
The reception was a reminder that Jeanty is far from healthy, while also showing what he can do when he is. Among running backs, Jeanty ranks near the top of the league in receiving yards. Kubiak noted on Monday that he plans to use Las Vegas' running backs.
“I stand by what I said, that we’re going to need Mike [Washington Jr.], we’re going to need Ashton [Jeanty], we’re going to need Dylan [Laube]. They’re all part of our success, run and pass, and Ashton made huge plays for us in the game yesterday in the pass game, in protection,” Kubiak said.
“Phenomenal in protection like he’s always been, and just the way the game went yesterday, Mike got more carries, and going forward, we’re going to be counting on all three of those guys.”
The entire defensive backfield struggled on Sunday. Overall, Stukes did not play badly. Even on the big play he allowed, he was in a solid position to make a play. Stukes' continued development is critical for him and Las Vegas' defense.
McCoy is beginning to get more playing time as Las Vegas needs all the help it can get in its defensive backfield. McCoy spent all of last season away from football. Halfway through the season, he still looks a step behind at times. He never had a chance on a touchdown he allowed.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Report Card: The Good, Bad, and Ugly
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.--The Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) head to Santa Clara, California, this weekend to take on the team that, at this point, has to be one of the favorites to represent the NFC in the Super Bowl: the San Francisco 49ers (6-1).
But before we turn our full attention to the 49ers, let’s go back to the 38-33 win on the road this past weekend at the New York Jets and put it under the lights of the microscope and off you, my final report card from that enormous win.
I gave specific details about this win and what everyone is overlooking , but this article is different.
It isn’t even a winners-and-losers perspective; it is a report card at five levels, so let’s take a look.
The Raiders weren’t perfect, but they scored 38 points, ran the ball effectively, and, when watching the film, the OL was better than I initially thought.
Mike Washington Jr. didn’t reach the century mark, but he did run the ball 25 times; QB Kirk Cousins threw 26 times, keeping the Kubiak offense balanced, which is what it is built on.
He ran unafraid, attacked defenders when necessary, and created separation when possible. Kubiak was very pleased with the rookie.
“I think it comes back to proving it in practice, having solid practice days, and being on point with his assignments. He’s continued to improve, and coming in as a young player, like all young players, there’s a lot to learn, and early, there are things you don’t want to expose them to. You want them to learn the meeting room."
"You want them to learn the hard way in practice, so that you’re not learning the hard way on Sunday. Everyone learns hard on Sunday, coaches and players. But it’s been a development process to get him to this point.”
Not only did the Raiders put up 38 points, but they also saw Kirk Cousins throw for three touchdowns and run for another. They were 64% efficient on third down and had 333 yards of offense.
Were there things that weren’t pretty? For sure, but the other team has a lot of talented players, and they were game-planning as well.
It was a great day for the Raiders.
Additionally, while no one in this league is perfect, Trey Zuhn III gave the Raiders their best RG play of the season. Kubiak was pleased with him and wasn’t afraid to say so.
“I thought Trey [Zuhn III] was calm in there. I thought he was well prepared. That was not a surprise, but I thought he played well. I think there’s things that he’s going to want to improve on. But I was pleased, along with the coaching staff, with the effort that he put on the field and what his future looks like for us.”
The defense wasn't bad all-around, but as a unit, it was. They allowed 33 points and 439 yards of total offense. They struggled to get pressure from the defensive end position outside of Maxx Crosby, and they got run at, around, and over.
That said, we need to address one big elephant in the room.
Eric Stokes is a very good CB in this league, and I was a major proponent of GM John Spytek resigning him. I still am. On Sunday, he was tasked with covering two elite WRs with essentially no pass rush. Any CB would struggle in that situation.
I am not saying he was perfect, but especially watching the film, I can tell you he was left on an island with a pass rush from the DE spot that looked like they stayed in Las Vegas unless their jersey said, “Crosby.”
Stopping the run was brutal.
Make no mistake: the Raiders offense, with very little help from the defense, won the game, and Kubiak addressed the ugly rushing defense head-on.
“It’s not going to happen overnight. Something that is going to take practices, it’s going to take experience, it’s going to take us putting our heads together and having a better product so that we’re not giving up those many yards on the ground. But the people that we have doing it together, our players and coaches, I believe in, and that’s a really important piece of it.”
Kubiak elaborated, “We have each other’s back, and the thing I love about our defense is that when things didn’t go well, we kept playing. We got key stops. Made a huge play at the end with [Jeremy] Chinn, and in the NFL, it’s not always going to be pretty. It’s not always going to be how you wanted it to happen. But at the end of the game, it’s who won the game, and I think as a team we found a way to win.”
We know the DBs are young; we know the Raiders are thin on the DL, and some well-paid veterans signed to free-agent deals aren't producing. That is factual. The Raiders need young players to grow up fast, another year of free agency and the NFL Draft to address some thin areas, and guys paid to do a job to do it.
There are some terrific players on the Raiders' D, but the sum of their parts is exactly why I told you all offseason that this was a rebuild, and why it will remain that all year, even with an overachieving offense.
Joe DeCamillis, the Raiders STC, is a superstar, and joining forces with an aggressive young coach like Kubiak is a marriage made in heaven.
The analytics and the critics said he shouldn’t have taken Matt Gay out of a field goal attempt toward the end of the game. Kubiak couldn't care less about the critics or the analytics; he did what he's done all year, showed faith in his guys, and secured the win.
Some coaches fear losing; Kubiak loves to win. His players love it, and so do I. He talked about ignoring the critics and the analytics, and his answer was pure Kubiak.
“I just see him kick in practice. I’ve seen the clutch kicks that he’s made. We were at the line that we had confidence in on that yard line, and we’ve got to get the ball closer for him offensively. But we had confidence in that.”
Dylan Laube may be the size of a jockey at the Kentucky Derby, but he played like a rabid dog who won't back down on multiple plays, and it was the best collective effort of any Las Vegas Raiders team I have covered in a single game since they have been in the desert.
Let’s start with the defense, where I am sure the same fans who attack Dylan Laube on social media after an early-season fumble are the same ones calling for Rob Leonard to be fired.
This is a rebuild; he doesn’t have nearly the weapons offense or the special teams do. That doesn’t mean the defense is void of talent, by any stretch of the imagination, but the Raiders knew the defense would be the proverbial Achilles' heel this season, and it is.
When the D looked good early in the preseason, I took heat for telling people to relax.
Leonard, like OC Andrew Janocko and Kubiak, is a first-time coach in their current position, and they've made mistakes and must learn. But he hasn’t forgotten how to coach; the young players are getting better, and he will be fine.
If some of these issues are going on next year, then he has a problem, but not now.
Kubiak was outstanding, and DeCamillis was his usual rock star.
Rick Dennison’s calming elite leadership of the OL showed as Spencer Burford looked exceptionally well, and his tutelage of Zuhn had the rookie making an immediate impact.
Miller and Glaze were both good considering the Jets' scheme, and Tyler Linderbaum, while satisfactory, is an elite C and didn’t play like one.
As impressive as the road games have been, and I go to them all, not one Raiders road game in the entire seven years I have covered this team impressed me as much as Sunday.
This wasn’t the first time in the Northeast, but the Raiders took over MetLife and made life miserable for the Jets.
I may not be a Raiders fan per se, but I am a fan of the Raider Nation, and once again you made my dear friend Matt Millen look smart. He told me once, “There are 31 teams in the NFL who have a fan base that thinks they are part of the team, but there is one team, the Raiders, where the players and organization think the fans are part of the team.”
The fans deserve a game ball; my hat is off, and you were simply outstanding.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College…

title: How Raiders' Week 8 Win Proves What's Possible in 2026
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 8 matchup was just what they needed after facing four of the league's best teams. It was far from pretty, but the Raiders won a game on Sunday that they likely would have lost last season. Ironically, the win came against the quarterback who helped them land the No. 1 pick.
Sunday was a poetic day in many ways: veteran quarterback Geno Smith showed that his lone season with the Raiders was not all his fault, and that he took more responsibility for the Raiders' 3-14 2025 campaign than he probably should have. That is usually what comes with playing quarterback.
Sunday was a battle between the past and the present, as Smith and Kirk Cousins both had excellent outings. Las Vegas' win over the Jets shed more light on what the Raiders are and what they can be when they play sound football. A win is a win, regardless of who it is against.
After a sluggish first half in which Las Vegas' offense registered 97 total yards and its defense gave up 140 rushing yards, the Raiders turned things around on both sides of the ball in the second half. Las Vegas entered the second half down by nine points, but possessed the ball first.
After four long weeks, the Raiders notched another win to reach .500 for the season. In less than half the season, Las Vegas has surpassed last season's win total. The Raiders used a second half full of complementary football to finally pull away from the Jets in the final moments of the fourth quarter.
Entering Week 8, the Raiders scored a total of three points across their previous four third quarters combined. Against the Jets, the Raiders offense exploded for its best third quarter of the season, scoring more points than in any other third quarter.
Veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins led the Raiders downfield on their very first offensive drive after halftime for a score. It was the first time Las Vegas scored on their first offensive drive after halftime. It was far from pretty, but the win confirms that Las Vegas played one of their best games of the season.
The Raiders have plenty to fix, as the first half was another example of Las Vegas getting off to a slow start. However, unlike the past four weeks, the Raiders played well enough in all three phases, albeit at different times in the game, to finally break their losing streak.
Las Vegas' ability to win a game despite things not going their way for much of it. That in itself is progress for Kubiak's young Raiders. The Raiders of the past two or three seasons would have folded in similar situations. They do not have much time to celebrate, with a tough Week 9 slate ahead.
For now, the Raiders will enjoy being back on the winning side. It is a long season, and Las Vegas is still working its way through one of the league's toughest schedules. Still, progress shows in various areas, as the Raiders' .500 record shows.
Las Vegas' win against the Jets was far from their best performance, especially for a defensive backfield that has been the team's biggest weakness for multiple seasons.
However, the Raiders invested heavily in the offense this offseason. Kubiak was hired largely because of his ability to draw up and call high-level offensive plays. Offense has been the missing component over the past four weeks,
Tyler Linderbaum was signed to a record-breaking contract that completely reset the market. The Raiders' front office added Jalen Nailor and Spencer Burford. They recently signed Michael Mayer to a new contract and still have a massive one in line for Brock Bowers.
This was all in addition to using the No. 1 overall pick on a quarterback. Offense has been the focus since Pete Carroll was fired. Moving forward, they need the unit to play as it did on Sunday, and not like it did during their losing streak.
Las Vegas invested far more in its offense than in its defense, even with both sides adding impactful players to sizeable contracts. This offseason, the Raiders' front office focused heavily on its offense. Sunday, the offense woke up before it was too late and saved its struggling defense.
Sunday proved that the Raiders can win games when playing complementary football while the game is still within reach.
Sunday proved the Raiders' defense can play horribly—and Las Vegas can win —if their offense shows up before the fourth quarter.
The next step will be to see if the defense can vastly improve and how quickly they can do so.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: The Biggest 2026 Raiders Story Everyone Is Overlooking
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) went into the largest media market in the United States, New York, over the weekend and did something that isn’t getting the attention it deserves.
It is the single largest tangible evidence of the Raiders' rebuild, and the flabbergasting fact is that even the legendary fans missed it.
For over twenty years, the storied franchise continued to sell a fan base unlike any other, one that sees their fandom as a way of life: Raider Nation, the old edict of Al Davis, “Just Win, Baby.”
While they consistently lost, when they had brief success, it was celebrated more out of shock than embraced as a sustainable and tangible reality of a new direction.
I have documented the collapse of 2025 in detail, and won’t redo that here, but since Mark Davis, Tom Brady, and John Spytek got on the same page about the future, everything has worked.
The patience shown throughout Klint Kubiak's interview and hiring process was admirable; so was the patience in free agency and the thorough deployment of the 2026 NFL Draft, with no panic or turning from the plan.
Entering the season, the Raiders knew they had positions with no players (WR1), multiple spots that were thin (DL & OL), and places where they were very young (DB, WR).
Fans screamed for Spytek to hire someone other than Kubiak, fearing Kubiak would leave the Raiders at the altar. Spytek ignored them.
Some fans clamored for a trade for a WR1 like Marvin Harrison Jr., and Spytek wisely said no.
Some fans and media bemoaned the playing of Kirk Cousins, wanting the No. 1 overall pick, which NFL executives ranked as the best QB prospect in the last four NFL Drafts: Fernando Mendoza; Kubiak ignored them.
Today, they still don’t have a WR1; they are still woefully thin at DL and OL, and very young at WR and DB.
Every week, young players are making young-player mistakes. Now, however, the Raiders rookies are being lauded for their contributions.
Today, Cousins ranks second in the NFL in touchdown passes and ranks among the top in passing yards. Fernando Mendoza, every week, looks even more like a star as the spotlight on Cousins has allowed him to blossom and learn what being an NFL QB is, not just playing it.
The Raiders' rookie head coach, offensive coordinator, and defensive coordinator have all made rookie mistakes, and all have bright, promising futures.
I said every rookie and young player gets a pass in 2025; that disastrous year was on ownership, and that includes GM John Spytek.
This is truly Spytek’s first year.
The wise knew the Raiders' defense was a concern before the year. It still is. So is the run game. This is a rebuilding year; no one is panicked.
Everything we pointed out before the season is true.
Kubiak’s commitment is quickly demonstrated in an unlikely emerging bright spot. After an early-season fumble and a social media attack, Klint Kubiak doubled down, and Dylan Laube is developing into a special-teams superstar, bringing true fear to opponents who must game plan for the unlikely star every week.
The Raiders aren’t making dumb salary cap decisions, trades, or signings, trying to shortcut the process and wager away the last 11 months of real progress.
In a city known for gambling, Tom Brady, Mark Davis, John Spytek, and Klint Kubiak have been as far from that as humanly possible.
Instead, they are acting like insider traders on Wall Street, using their experience to play the odds when they are in their favor.
They have trusted their football acumen. Not afraid to make big moves, they don’t do it to pacify the media or the fans; it has to make sense.
Knowing they couldn’t build a champion in one year, they are playing long-ball and attempting to rebuild the Raiders into a dynasty.
At Newark Airport today, a man said to me, “Ten years from now no one will give a (excrement) that Kirk Cousins was the QB; we aren’t winning a Super Bowl this year. Just throw Mendoza in.”
In the past, sentiments like that would have moved this franchise. I know of things they didn’t want to do, but did.
Now the noise is ignored. Now the only thing that matters at the team’s headquarters is the process and the plan.
The people in charge, Brady, Spytek, and Kubiak, all have Super Bowls.
While I can assure you they all respect Raider Nation, they know another Lombardi Trophy for this franchise is what guides every decision. Does this get us closer to winning another title? Not what will the fans say on Twitter?
If all of this goes as planned, like the last 11 months, that man in the airport is right. No one will remember what Cousins did in comparison to Mendoza. But Mendoza will. The Raiders will, because what he became went back to a seed planted in 2026.
No one is talking about the fact that, in just eight games, the Raiders won their fourth game of the season yesterday. Last year, at rock bottom, they barely won three times in seventeen games.
In a rebuilding year, the Raiders are better. Not only better this year, but also in the long term. In the past, decisions were made for short-term gain, and now Raider Nation is learning that long-term decisions can pay off, too.
Thanks to ownership's patience in trusting football over emotion, a GM who trusted his football acumen and thorough planning, and a head coach who, while understanding the rebuild, forgot he wasn’t supposed to win this year.
The Raiders' fuel right now isn’t a dominant OL or DL, or having the most talent. They are beating the teams they are supposed to beat, and somehow restoring hope in a franchise that, while it has weaknesses everywhere, is still a team.
Down nine points in the third quarter, Kubiak’s infused Silver and Black forgot this is where they implode. They forgot that the DL and OL are thin. They forgot that they didn’t have a WR1, and the WR and DB spots are young.
Dylan Laube forgot the memo that he would never make it, and Klint Kubiak, Andrew Janocko, and Rob Leonard forgot they were first-time coaches in their respective positions, destined to fail. Rookies forgot they were supposed to screw up.
A noise rose from the shadows of East Rutherford; a fan base had bought in. Thousands of people took over MetLife Stadium; the all-familiar "RRRAAAIIIDDDEEERRRSSS" chant roared across the world on TV.
Lying on the canvas, this fan base, this coaching staff, this front office, these owners, and the roster of players just kept getting up. Kept punching and kept fighting.
The Silver and Black channeled something that would have made Al Davis proud; they kept fighting.
When the game ended, the ghost of 2025 was exercised.
All wins count as one; each week is a one-game season, according to Kubiak.
Kubiak is wrong. This one was special. This one was different.
I expect the Raiders to lose the next two, but that won’t be the story. A page was turned on Sunday. They tore off the rearview mirror.
The rookie coaches and players are still rookies; there will be more learning moments, more mistakes, losses, and failures in 2026. They are still thin at multiple spots; they still don’t have a WR1. All of that is true.
But they have a team, a vision, and in just eight games, tangible proof that the people in charge know what they are doing.
If trades happen, it is because they make football sense. If players are playing, it is because they see value, and with nine games left, you know the light at the end of the tunnel isn’t a screaming locomotive coming to kill tomorrow's dreams.
Somewhere ahead are the bright lights of meaningful postseason football.
The plan is working. You saw that on Sunday. Ten years from now, many won’t remember this, but those who are open will.
2026 will tell a lot of stories. Some will be hard and frustrating because growth has pain, but future success has a cost, and the Raiders are paying it now.
They all count one, but not yesterday. The Raiders left the baggage of 2025 in Gotham and picked up the roadmap for the future.
The Raiders are already far better than last year, and not…

title: Encouraging, Discouraging Signs for Raiders in Week 8 Win
full_text:
For the first time since Sept. 27, the Las Vegas Raiders have won a game.
In Week 8, the Raiders defeated the New York Jets, 38-33, ending their four-game losing streak. With the trade deadline on Nov. 10, Las Vegas was in danger of being forced into tough conversations about considering selling off pieces. However, this result puts those concerns to rest, for the time being. That said, here are encouraging and discouraging narratives emerging from Sunday's win.
No one has claimed Las Vegas' offense has been the issue during the four-game skid, but there were certainly discussions about swapping Kirk Cousins for Fernando Mendoza. The 38-year-old quarterback quieted those doubts, completing 19-of-26 passes for 247 yards and three touchdowns in the barnburner win.
The rushing attack continues to slog along, as the Raiders took 33 carries for 95 yards (2.9 yards per attempt) and one touchdown. We'll talk about that department in a second.
The second-year running back was usurped by Mike Washington Jr. in Week 8. Washington Jr. outcarried Jeanty 25-2, demoting the former No. 6 overall pick to solely a receiving-down back.
While it's good that Kubiak can rely on the rookie running back, nobody foresaw this situation unfolding the way it has. For the Raiders' offense to reach its potential, Jeanty has to be much better as a runner.
Las Vegas' defense has been an issue all season, failing to contain opposing offenses. That was apparent on Sunday, as the Jets scored 33 points while tallying 290 passing yards and 166 rushing yards.
Right now, the Raiders' only path to victory is to outscore their opponents in shootout environments. As much as Cousins has impressed, this probably isn't how Kubiak wanted this team to operate. Additionally, the front office invested a surplus of resources into the defense through free agency and the draft, and it clearly hasn't paid off yet.
While the offense has been a well-oiled machine, the wide receiver corps has left much to be desired, and the Raiders still lack a true WR1. On Sunday, Jalen Nailor was the only wideout with a single reception, catching four passes for 38 yards and one touchdown.
Las Vegas' passing attack has been heavily dependent on Brock Bowers, Michael Mayer, and Jeanty. Other than them, it's been a revolving door of which wide receiver will produce. Tre Tucker has had a few explosive games, but he failed to record a single reception this week. Assuming Las Vegas doesn't acquire a wideout at the deadline, that position will be one of the top needs this upcoming offseason.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Grading Each Raiders Position Group Following Week 8 Win
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders snapped their four-game losing streak with a road win over the New York Jets in Week 8.
Below are the grades for each position group.
Kirk Cousins played a masterful second half against the Jets on Sunday. Cousins finished the first half with 79 passing yards, while completing six of his seven passes. The Raiders entered the half down 23-14.
Then, Cousins and the Raiders' offense rode their best third quarter of the season to victory. In the second half, Cousins completed 13 of his 19 passes for 168 yards and two touchdowns.
That is the type of impactful stats the Raiders need from Cousins while they are still truly competitive in games, not when they are down two or three possessions entering the fourth quarter. Sunday proved that not all stats are the same— timing and context matter greatly.
The Raiders needed more from their ground game, since it had contributed little over the previous four weeks. Starting Mike Washington at running back threw a curveball for the Jets that they could not figure out for four quarters, as Washington paced Las Vegas' offense.
The Raiders leaned on the ground in the second half, running the ball 22 times for 68 yards, compared with 19 passes. Washington's strong second half took a decent part of the workload off of Cousins, allowing him to manage the game properly.
Ashton Jeanty finished the first half with one run and one reception on one target.
However, the burst he displayed on his 45-yard reception in the fourth quarter, which was mostly yards after the catch, showed that giving Jeanty some time off, as they did in the first half, was probably a move worth trying before Week 8 .
Connor Heyward is a chess piece.
Jalen Nailor was the only receiver to catch a pass against the Jets. Nailor and Tre Tucker combined for four catches on five targets. One of those receptions was a touchdown.
It would be a mistake to judge the unit's impact by stats, since Nailor did not have stats when the Raiders signed him this offseason. Instead, notice that Nailor and Tucker open up the offense, especially for the team's tight ends.
Las Vegas' first offensive drive displayed what the Raiders' brass has in mind for the unit long term.
Las Vegas' offensive line only allowed one sack on the day. Through Week 8, the unit has allowed the third-fewest sacks per game in the league. Last season, the unit allowed the most sacks in the league.
The unit also paved the way for a productive day running the ball.
Best group of tight ends in the league.
It was far from pretty, but Las Vegas' defensive line quietly proved it can be effective enough against the run when the team is actually competitive enough in games that opposing offenses cannot run the ball an inflated number of times. In the first half, Las Vegas' defense allowed 140 rushing yards.
Las Vegas entered halftime down 23-14. Then, the Raiders' offense woke up early in the second half, instead of at the start of the fourth quarter, and produced its best third quarter of the season. Las Vegas scored points on its first offensive drive of the second half for the first time this season.
The Raiders' offense also scored more points in the third quarter than it had this season. After scoring three points in the past four third quarters combined, Las Vegas' offense scored 14 points in the third quarter on Sunday.
After allowing an eye-popping 140 rushing yards in the first half, Las Vegas' defense held the Jets to an equally eye-popping 26 rushing yards total in the second half. The Raiders' defense showed what it can do when its offense does its part.
It's almost as if the Raiders' offense scoring points helps the defense, mentally and physically.
Las Vegas' defensive line's improvement against the run allowed Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker to be used properly in ways that fit their respective skill sets.
Sunday's win over the Jets clarified the specific issues plaguing the Raiders' defense. Stopping the run has been an issue, but they've struggled because of the running backs and quarterbacks they have faced in the weeks leading up to Week 8.
With Geno Smith not being nearly as much of a running threat as Patrick Mahomes, Drake Maye, or Josh Allen, Las Vegas' defense eventually focused on stopping running backs out of the backfield rather than a mobile quarterback who is accurate and a talented runner.
Holding the Jets to 26 rushing yards in the second half forced Smith to throw the ball even more. Still, Las Vegas' defensive backfield also tightened up in the second half. Smith finished the first half with a 131 rating. His rating dropped to 64.3 in the second half.
It was far from pretty, but the Raiders' young defensive backfield figured it out just in time. They even sealed the win with an interception.
Dylan Laube's kickoff return for a touchdown was the Raiders' first in 15 years. It was the first time a kickoff had been returned for a touchdown this season in the entire league. That should explain how big of a deal it was. At halftime, Laube had as many points as the Raiders' offense.
Throughout this season, Laube's success, or lack thereof, has directly impacted the Raiders' offense. When he has a productive day returning the ball, Las Vegas' offense generally does well. When he does not have a good day returning kicks, the Raiders' offense struggles.
Kicker Matt Gay also had another strong outing, converting all five extra-point attempts and converting a 53-yard field goal with 31 seconds left, with Las Vegas up by only two points. His field goal forced the Jets' hand, as they needed a touchdown to win.
Without Gay's field goal, the Jets would have been in field-goal range with less than 30 seconds left, only down by two. Gay's eight points were the difference in Las Vegas' five-point win.
Punter AJ Cole continued to prove himself as one of the league's best at his position. Cole averaged over 50 yards per punt against the Jets.
Las Vegas' special teams unit accounted for a chunk of the Raiders' 38 points on Sunday. Hats off to special teams coordinator Joe DeCamillis' unit on a stellar outing.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Overreactions to Raiders Ending Winless Skid vs. Jets
full_text:
It wasn't pretty, but the Las Vegas Raiders are back in the win column for the first time since September, ending a streak of 11 consecutive losses in November and a four-game losing streak that lasted all of October.
For the last four weeks, it looked like this week would be the week the Raiders could get back into the win column. Now, they sit at 4-4, still in the thick of things, and may have to win in high-scoring games to have a chance this season. With that in mind, here are some overreactions to Sunday's win against the New York Jets.
Kubiak effectively made rookie Mike Washington Jr. the early-down running back, carrying the ball 25 times for 83 yards, while Ashton Jeanty got most of his work done on third down in pass protection and the receiving game. Instead of Caleb Rogers or Jackson Powers-Johnson, the Raiders started rookie Trey Zuhn III at right guard for the first time.
These moves have made Washington the effective No. 1 running back for the Raiders' offense, regardless of the talent that Jeanty possesses. It's unclear whether Jeanty will get going at any point this season, but for now, Washington is the one to carry the load.
This is the reality of a team committing to a rebuild. If the Raiders were 6-2 fighting for the AFC West lead, I'd be on board with them making a move for a defensive tackle, edge rusher, or defensive back. Yet I don't see this happening, and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard will have to make do with what he has.
There is too much inconsistency in the secondary; the linebackers can find a clear lane to the ball carrier because the defensive tackles are being pushed off the ball and combo-blocked; and the edge rushers opposite Maxx Crosby remain ineffective. No one is saving this defense anytime soon, and Raiders fans will have to deal with it.
This isn't a question for me, no matter how good Trey McBride is in Arizona; Brock Bowers is the best tight end in the game and easily one of the most ridiculous receiving threats in the NFL.
This is a player who missed two games to start the year and is continuing to dominate any linebacker or defensive back covering him, as he added seven catches for 92 yards and two touchdowns against the Jets.
He is impossible to beat at the catch point and is a dangerous threat in the open field. With the way Kubiak deploys Bowers in the passing game, he is a force multiplier on offense.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Winners & Losers: Resilient Raiders Refuse To Lose vs. Jets
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) came to Gotham and tamed the New York Jets (2-6) 38-33. 2026 has been nothing short of an overachieving season.
When I made my final regular-season record prediction , I had the Silver and Black pegged at 3-5.
To say this franchise is ahead of schedule under the leadership of Klint Kubiak would be an understatement.
As I sit here in the press box, a lot from this game is percolating in my head, and like I do each night after the game, I'll offer you my winners and losers beyond the score.
Coming into the game, Cousins led the NFL in touchdown passes and ranked third in passing yards.
He was nothing short of sensational today with three more touchdown passes, 247 yards through the air, no interceptions, and, oh, by the way, he ran for another. His QB rating was 141, and he was sensational.
The NFL world so desperately wants to see the No. 1 overall pick that NFL executives ranked as the best QB prospect in the last four drafts, Fernando Mendoza, but Cousins' play won’t allow it.
Kubiak praised his play: “That's who he's been all year. He's been a leader, he's been a playmaker for us, and that's been the story of the season so far. We have a lot of season to go, so we need to clean up the mistakes.”
For Cousins, it wasn’t about his stats; he only wanted to talk about the team snapping a four-game losing skid.
“It’s tough to lose in this league. I think only one other time was I a part of losing four games in a row. It’s hard. It happens, but it’s hard. We’ve played some good football teams, and it took everything we had today. It’s great to get a win, to be .500 in November now and to be playing meaningful football is important. It doesn’t get any easier from here, and we understand the challenge ahead.”
Every week, the rookie Arkansas Razorback Mike Washington Jr. (MWJ) continues to reward the staff for their trust, and he does more and more.
With Ashton Jeanty and the running game struggling lately, he took the lead and didn’t disappoint.
He ran 25 times for 83 difficult yards and looked comfortable and in command, pounding the ball when there was no way to go. Like Steph Curry of the Golden State Warriors, famous for creating his own shot, MWJ created something out of nothing when there wasn’t a hole.
Kubiak was happy for him, but he wasn’t satisfied. “I thought Mike did a good job. He ran hard. I think we took a step forward in that aspect of our game, but it's something that's not a finished product.“
Cousins waxed a little more loquacious for his teammate, and his joy for him was tangible.
“He’s from New York, so he had a ton of family here and friends, and I was really happy for him. He did today what he’s shown us in practice and through camp with the way he ran. We’re going to have to lean on him moving forward a lot, and Ashton as well. Mike did a great job for us today.”
Dylan Laube, the Raiders “Dog,” went wild in front of his family and friends with a kickoff return for a touchdown, an incredible play on a kick out of bounds, a superb special-teams play, and nearly blocking a kick. He may not be that large, but the way he played today makes me wonder if he is the Raiders equivalent of Clark Kent, with a big S under his uniform.
Laube said of his performance, “He’s from New York, so he had a ton of family here and friends, and I was really happy for him. He did today what he’s shown us in practice and through camp with the way he ran. We’re going to have to lean on him moving forward a lot, and Ashton as well. Mike did a great job for us today.”
I asked Kubiak about his special teams weapon, and he was more than willing to praise his performance.
“He's back home, you know, a lot of family here, so it was cool for him to have that moment. Dylan is a stud player for us. He continues to make plays, and as you continue to make plays the expectations continue to rise and he's earned that.”
Cousins was even more verbose. This team loves Laube, and you can count their QB as a fan.
“It’s complementary football. Especially when you go on the road, to be able to have that seven-point gift given to your offense and get the wind at your back makes a big difference. It’s what winning football teams do. There are so many different ways to win in this league. I was really happy for Dylan, like you mentioned, coming back to where he grew up. He had so many people here as well, like Mike, and that had to be a special moment for his family, too.”
The Georgia Bulldog and the best TE in the NFL had seven catches for 92 yards and two touchdowns. He made catches that defied gravity and looked like the superstar that the NFL already knows he is.
Cousins' description of how he played was almost comical, because it sounds so absurd and it is 100% true.
“I think what’s hard is when you play with Pierre Garçon, DeSean Jackson or Justin Jefferson, you’re used to throwing to guys who are really open. There were times, even when they would get doubled and I would progress off of them, and Kevin O’Connell would say to me, ’Still throw it to Justin when he’s covered.' I was like, 'I don’t like throwing to covered guys. I like throwing to open guys.'"
"The coaching point with Brock has been like it was with Justin, where it’s like, when he’s covered, you still need to throw it. That kind of breaks my instincts.”
Cousins continued to explain, “My instincts are to progress and throw to open guys. I think you can see there are moments this year where I can be better, and then there are moments where I’m starting to figure that out. He’s made me right, if you will.”
Even Kubiak, who isn’t usually funny, was in awe. “It surprises me when he doesn't catch it (laughter). That's the truth.”
The Raiders are 4-4. The defense struggled, and we will dissect that and dig into it this week before they head to San Francisco this weekend, but for now, we focus on these four winners.
I will get into some tough discussion on the defense with my report card later in the week, but this team, behind the iron jaw of their first-year coach, didn’t quit. That defense is under the microscope for what is sure to be a less-than-stellar prognosis, but one fact stands out: when it had to, it got key stops. No quit. They may not be great, but they got grit.
Al Davis would have been proud of this win, and that is saying a lot.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Raiders Stock Report: Risers & Fallers After Thrilling Win Over Jets
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 8 matchup against the New York Jets desperately needing a win. After four straight games against the league's top teams, the Jets were, on paper, the team Las Vegas needed to get back on track after a tough few weeks.
Week 8 was supposed to be a manageable game for a Raiders team that has one of the league's toughest schedules. Las Vegas' road slate against the Jets is sandwiched between games against multiple teams with Super Bowl aspirations.
Las Vegas' offense woke up just in time to pull out a thrilling victory against the Jets on Sunday. Their defense played a solid second half, holding New York to 10 second-half points.
Falling behind early and trying their hardest to come back in the second half is becoming the Raiders' identity. Below are the players who are rising and falling after the Raiders' Week 8 loss to the Jets, their fifth straight loss.
Despite many narratives, Las Vegas' offensive line entered Week 8 in the top 10-15 in several statistical categories. The unit excelled significantly more in pass-blocking than in run-blocking. On Sunday, the unit excelled in both, helping Las Vegas jump out to an early lead.
The unit has its deficiencies, but when it comes to giving the quarterback enough time to throw the ball or escape the pocket and make a play, Las Vegas' offensive line plays well. Las Vegas' ground game was its most efficient in weeks because the line played well overall on Sunday.
Nailor's numbers have not shown the true impact he has on the Raiders' offense. However, Nailor's absence noticeably strained the unit in Week 6. His return made a subtle but significant difference for Las Vegas' offense in Week 7, opening things up, despite his lack of stats.
His impact was even more noticeable on Las Vegas' opening drive, as he registered two catches for 24 yards, which were pivotal in the Raiders' 10-play, 60-yard touchdown drive.
Bowers continues to prove he is the best tight end in the league. The price keeps rising weekly, as Bowers shows he is arguably just as much of a wide receiver as a tight end.
Laube entered Week 8 among the league leaders in kickoff return yards. This forced the Jets into a mistake. On the kickoff following their opening-drive field goal, the Jets kicked the ball out of bounds. This gave Las Vegas the ball at their own 40-yard line. This is the type of starting position the unit needs.
Las Vegas' offense capitalized on the good field position, scoring a touchdown on their first drive. Laube's solid kickoff returns this season immediately impacted the game. Laube helped the Raiders score their first touchdown without even touching the ball.
Then, Laube directly impacted the game by returning a kickoff 95 yards for a touchdown. It was the Raiders' first kickoff return for a touchdown in 248 games. Laube's is a valuable weapon for Las Vegas. The Raiders would not have snapped their losing streak without Laube.
Stokes made two big third-down plays to hold the Jets to a field goal, including on a drive when the Jets had a first-and-goal on the Raiders' five-yard line. Aside from those two plays, the Jets repeatedly targeted Stokes, especially on third-and-short situations.
The Raiders focused first on stopping that aspect of the Jets' offense. However, that left several of Las Vegas' questionable defensive backs in one-on-one situations. Instead of letting their opponent choose, the Raiders picked their poison. It was the passing game.
This was still better than struggling against both the run and the pass, as Las Vegas' defense had done in the previous four games. However, the improvement against the run cost the Raiders through the air, especially Stokes. It simply was not a good outing for the Raiders' best cornerback.
Still, it made more sense for the Raiders to depend on Stokes to figure it out than to switch their defense back into a schematically unfavorable situation.
The rookie looked lost on the Jets' first touchdown. He also could have played better against the run on the Jets' first touchdown after halftime.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 4 Instant Observations From Raiders' Comeback Win vs. Jets
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders snapped their four-game losing streak with an impressive comeback win against the New York Jets on Sunday. After falling behind early, as has been the case, Las Vegas used an uncharacteristically productive third quarter on offense to beat the Jets.
Below are my instant observations from the Raiders' outing on Sunday.
Starting rookie running back Mike Washington and making him the team's primary back gave Las Vegas' offense more of a presence on the ground than it had in recent weeks. However, even that was minimal statistically early on, as Washington finished the first half with seven carries for 24 yards.
Las Vegas' offense scored one touchdown in the first half. The Raiders had 97 total yards in the first half.
Still, using Washington as the team's primary back threw the Jets off, as there was no way to prepare. Las Vegas has barely used Washington this season. In the second half, he effectively put the unit on his back, allowing Cousins to stay within his wheelhouse of completing short-to-medium passes.
The depth chart and schematic changes the Raiders made on offense had a direct impact on the game, especially in the second half. The second half against the Jets was arguably the most productive second half Las Vegas' offense has had this season.
The Raiders should have rested Jeanty against the New England Patriots, as it was clear early on that Jeanty had not fully recovered from the injury he suffered shortly before the start of the regular season. However, removing Jeanty completely, regardless of health, significantly hurts Las Vegas.
Las Vegas cannot sit Jeanty for a game, as it puts them at a competitive disadvantage of significant proportions, since Washington is not as effective at catching the ball out of the backfield as Jeanty is. However, the Raiders' coaching staff could effectively rest Jeanty while keeping him active.
At halftime, Jeanty had one rush, one target, and one reception. That is more of a resting than a benching. It may be framed differently by the coaching staff, but they did the right thing by giving Jeanty's body as much of a rest as possible while not hurting the team by sitting him.
Entering the season, the Raiders' defensive backfield vulnerability was well known. Las Vegas' defensive backfield has been an issue for several seasons, long before most of the players currently on the unit arrived. However, the unit itself is also subpar.
Las Vegas entered the season knowing they would need the unit to overachieve in order for the defense as a whole to be productive. Sunday was an ugly day for the unit, one week after an ugly performance against the Los Angeles Rams.
The Raiders lost Darien Porter after only one play. Yet the unit struggled so badly that the issues clearly stem from the group as a whole. The Raiders must aggressively address the unit with additional moves this offseason.
Entering Sunday, the Raiders had scored three points in their past four third quarters combined. Washington accounted for half of the unit's yards on the drive, as Las Vegas rode the young running back into the red zone, where the Raiders capitalized with a touchdown.
It was the first time Las Vegas' offense had scored on its first offensive drive after halftime this season. In seven games, the Raiders scored 26 points in the third quarter. They scored 14 points in the third quarter against the Jets.
It was the most points Las Vegas has scored in the third quarter this season. Their third-quarter success against the Jets confirmed that their third-quarter offensive woes entering Week 8 were a significant issue for the team.
Las Vegas' solid third quarter was just what the team needed, as the Jets' offense kept Las Vegas' defense on its heels for most of the game. Sunday, the Raiders' offense saved its defense. They did so largely with a productive third quarter.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Examining the Mistakes that Cost the Dolphins in Week 8 ... And How to Fix Them
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins gave themselves a chance to pull off an upset against the New England Patriots in Week 8, but ultimately came up short at Hard Rock Stadium.
Maybe the simplest explanation is that New England is a better team that rose to the occasion in the second half when the Dolphins failed to do so, with a dubious replay overturn clearly not helping matters, but Miami also did it to itself.
As young teams are prone to doing, the Dolphins hurt themselves with mistakes that had little to do with the Patriots.
They are the type of mistakes the team will have to eliminate to continue the progress they've already shown in the early stages of this massive rebuilding project.
This is the one that stands out as the biggest self-inflicted wound because it was so unnecessary, and it turned a third-and-5 situation into a third-and-20 on the Dolphins' second drive of the third quarter after New England had scored to cut their lead to 13-3.
The Dolphins needed to at least get a first down or two to stop the Patriots momentum, but Gordon gave them no shot.
Gordon got an earful from quarterback Malik Willis on the sideline after the drive after head coach Jeff Hafley also talked to him, but beyond Gordon having to hear it from his teammates, this is one mistake with no easy fix beyond Gordon learning how to control his emotions.
And that's the tricky part, right? Because we want Dolphins players to play hard and with passion, but also control their emotions once they reach a certain point.
The fix here isn't benching Gordon because he's become so important to the offense with De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
Of course, if this happens a couple more times this season, then there'll be a major problem, but for now let's just hope he's learned his lesson.
Look, missed field goals happen, it's just that Zane Gonzalez badly going wide left on a 43-yard attempt down 24-13 midway through the fourth quarter basically sealed the Dolphins' fate.
It's not like the Dolphins are operating with a great margin for error, so they basically need their kicker to be near-perfect — like Riley Patterson was in 2025 when he went 27-for-29.
Gonzalez missing (again, badly) on his third attempt during his second practice squad elevation should make the Dolphins think long and hard about devoting a roster spot to him after he's elevated for a third time next Sunday against Detroit.
Sure, Drake Maye deserves maybe a small degree of credit for shaking off Johnson's tackle attempt when he came in free from the blind side on a fourth-down blitz, but that was way more about Johnson and what he did wrong.
The day after the game, why Johnson dove at Maye's legs instead of running through his back remains a mystery. Even more so because Johnson has been a good tackler — maybe ever a great tackler for a cornerback — so far in his rookie season.
Maybe he got too excited about the possibility of a big play, maybe he was going too fast and lost some body control. Regardless, this is a teaching moment for the Dolphins' defensive coaches because, again, it's not like Johnson isn't physical or a good tackler.
The Dolphins should have started their drive after New England took the lead at 17-13 at their own 40, but instead began at their 12 after Jaylen Wright fielded the kickoff near the sideline and Julius Wood was flagged for holding.
All Wright had to do was put himself out of bounds before touching the ball — it wasn't difficult — and that would have resulted in a penalty on the Patriots.
Yes, that drive ended with the Malik Willis interception off the helmet of a Patriots defensive lineman, but the yardage difference off the kickoff based on the same sequence of events would have given them the ball after the pick at their own 19-yard line instead of their 47. Maybe they call plays differently from back there and don't score the touchdown that made it 24-13.
In any event, this should be Kick Returning 101 and we've seen player after player in the NFL do that move and invariably earn praise from TV analysts for their great awareness.
Here's the thing, though: This is something special teams coordinator Chris Tabor already should have drilled into every one of his kickoff returners, whether it be Wright, Malik Washington or anybody else who's gotten practice reps back there.
And now he should remind his returners before every kickoff about the rule.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 8 Loss
full_text:
Some things are too good to be true, including the Miami Dolphins winning two games in a row, as they fall to New England by a painfully close score of 24-19.
To many fans, the idea of "tanking" and not messing up their draft stock went out the window as soon as they saw that a win over the Patriots was possible, and it certainly looked that way at halftime. However, the offense, defense, and special teams all seemed to regress in the second half.
In the end, the Dolphins lost their third straight game by a touchdown or less. A competitive game for sure against the defending AFC champions, but it's the Patriots. Any loss against them is guaranteed to sting.
To see Savaiinaea on this list is frustrating because this performance came out of nowhere. He's been having a stellar resurgence for the Dolphins this season, but if everyone is guaranteed at least one stinker per season, this was certainly it for him.
The first half was especially difficult for Savaiinaea. Mainly matched up against Christian Barmore and Corey Durden, he struggled to give Malik Willis time in the pocket and was a non-factor in blocking for Ollie Gordon and Miami's run game.
Barmore breezed by Savaiinaea for a sack on Willis on their second drive of the game on third down, forcing a punt despite being near midfield. And while it didn't end up mattering because Miami scored four plays later, he was called for a holding penalty that wiped a 15-yard touchdown for Gordon off the board.
This performance by Savaiinaea really came out of left field. He hadn't allowed a sack or committed a penalty through the first seven weeks of the season. The o-line obviously took a hit with Kadyn Proctor not playing, but the Dolphins will hope this was a one-time slip-up and nothing more.
The jokes about Robinson appearing on milk cartons should thankfully be over after his performance against the Patriots. After the shaky start to the season he had, he's only gotten better, and he blew up against the Patriots with three solo tackles and two sacks.
In the first half, the Dolphins sent the house on Drake Maye play after play, usually to resounding success. His second sack came after getting past a trio of New England linemen, literally brute-forcing his way to the quarterback and forcing a punt.
That said, New England eventually cracked the code in the second half, and Miami's pass rush began to sputter. But for Chop specifically, this was the game he needed to start proving to Miami that he deserves to stay a member of the Dolphins. Consistency is key, however, and it won't get any easier against Jared Goff and Detroit's offense.
OK, there's really not much that Johnson did wrong in this game. He actually provided much-needed durability to the secondary, being one of four players to play all 60 defensive snaps alongside Jacob Rodriguez, Jordyn Brooks and Michael Taaffe.
Really, there's only one major thing he did wrong, but he likely won't hear the end of it for a while. On fourth-and-2 with five minutes to go in the second quarter, Johnson had Maye dead to rights, breezing by Eli Raridon and facing the back of Maye, who never saw him coming. It looked like a surefire sack.
Instead, Johnson dove low and to the left of Maye, who then completed a 12-yard pass to extend the drive. Thankfully for Johnson, New England would go on to miss an ensuing field goal, but it's an awful look for the rookie. If he's given 100 chances to tackle Maye in the same situation, he would likely take him down 99 times, but unfortunately not 100.
How do you, as an underdog, wish to upset a team that has aspirations of making it back to the Super Bowl? You need a spark, and Rodriguez delivered that in the second drive of the game.
Down by three, Rodriguez performed his signature peanut punch on Efton Chism III, knocking the ball free. It was ultimately recovered by JuJu Brents and led to the Dolphins tying the game with a field goal of their own. That fumble proved to both Miami and New England that the Dolphins' defense could hang with the Patriots.
The list of winners and losers for Week 8 is filled with players who earned their spots mainly based on a single play. But every play matters more in a game that was won or lost by seven points or less.
That said, this was a disappointing game for Gordon, who was held to 69 yards on 19 carries. Is it too surprising? Not really, as the Patriots have one of the best run defenses in the NFL. As we mentioned earlier, his best run of the day was wiped off the board due to a holding penalty.
But in Miami's second drive out of halftime, Gordon committed an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that resulted in a third-and-20. Not surprisingly, it forced a Dolphins punt, and the Patriots drove 73 yards in 13 plays to score a touchdown and take their first lead since early in the first quarter.
Gordon was irate on the sidelines, having to be cooled down by his quarterback. His emotions have been tested multiple times this season, including their loss to Cincinnati, but at least that tantrum was limited to the sidelines and, to some, justified given their struggles. But costing the team 15 yards and indirectly leading to a Patriots' lead that they wouldn't give up is unacceptable in a game like this.
Coleman was only targeted three times in this game, but he was a guaranteed target in all three of them, recording 46 yards. However, his final reception is an early highlight for the fifth-round pick.
It's not just that he scored a 35-yard touchdown that gave the Dolphins a sliver of hope with just about two minutes to go. It was the way he did it, absolutely shredding Charles Woods' ankles. His draft profile, which highlighted his speed and effectiveness after the catch, checks out.
Between Coleman, Douglas, and Bell, the group of rookies contributed almost equally in this game in terms of receptions and yards. It's a nice sight to see, but if anyone had doubts about what Coleman can contribute from the trio, he shut them down with that touchdown.
Miami's offense looked promising in the first half, taking a 13-3 lead to the break. But everything unraveled for the unit after halftime, and the play-calling on offense was a major contributor.
Even looking away from the back-to-back punts in the third quarter, the tempo of the offense in the fourth was off. They were at a deficit but handled the situation like they were ahead, draining 10 minutes and 23 seconds off the clock in their final three drives. Had they picked up the pace, there may not have been a need to go for an onside kick after the Coleman touchdown.
It didn't feel like there was a sense of urgency you would expect for an offense down by double digits with not much time remaining.
Pinion was asked to punt four times in this game - an unfortunate number, but he was at least consistent - with his kicks going 50, 40, 45, and 48 yards, respectively. His best work was his second attempt, pinning the Patriots deep at their 15-yard line.
Was it anything too special? Not really, but factoring in the not-so-optimal weather conditions and how sloppy the field can get, it was refreshing to see a mistake-free game for him. Pinion also handled a pair of kickoffs, resulting in a touchback on both occasions.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 8 Snap Counts Stories: Rookie Revelations, Top Guys Emerge
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 24-19 loss against the New England Patriots on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by guard Kadyn Proctor missing the game because of a concussion.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord and offensive lineman Andrew Meyer.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to six rookies with Proctor being out. The six starters were fullback DJ Herman, Will Kacmarek at tight end, wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- There two things that stand out about the offensive snap counts, both of them involving rookies.
-- While Malik Washington missed a few plays after taking a big hit to the head on a play that resulted in a personal foul flag against New England, Caleb Douglas still looked like he emerged as the No. 1 wide receiver in this game. He played 56 of the 65 offensive snaps, compared to 48 for Washington and Chris Bell also got an elevated role with 45 snaps. That was a big jump from Bell's 31 snaps against the New York Jets in Week 7.
-- Then there was rookie tight end Will Kacmarek, who played only 20 snaps on offense, his lowest total since the season opener after he had dealt with injury issues in training camp. Kacmarek has been on the injury report in recent weeks with a hamstring problem, and if that's the reason his snap count was limited, then maybe the Dolphins need to sit him for a game to get him completely healed. If not, we'd question using him so little when the running game could have used extra blocking help against the Patriots.
-- Kacmarek's usage on offense ended up being the same as Herman, and we just don't understand that — again, barring injury complications.
-- It again was the Ollie Gordon II show at running back, as he played 53 snaps (82 percent) and Jaylen Wright got only eight offensive snaps. Given Wright's lack of production — he's averaging 1.9 yards per rushing attempt this season — it's difficult to argue against the snap distribution here, though the Dolphins might eventually want to take a look at recent waiver wire pick-up Kaytron Allen.
-- Veteran Jalen Tolbert was active but got only six offensive snaps, by far the fewest of any of the wide receivers.
-- Four players were on the field for all the team's 60 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe and CB Chris Johnson. Those were the same four with 100 percent participation against the Jets in Week 7.
-- Josh Uche again led all edge defenders with 48 snaps, with Chop Robinson second with 33. Rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn got only two defensive snaps and didn't play on special teams, and one can't help but wonder why the Dolphins wasted his third and final practice squad elevation for that amount of work. The Dolphins now won't be able to use in another game this season unless they sign him to the 53-man roster.
-- Also note that Llewellyn's low snap count happened even though fellow edge Malik Herring missed some game time because of an injury before returning.
-- The Dolphins went big on about a third of their defensive snaps with at least three of their interior defensive linemen. The snap counts behind Zach Sieler were pretty even between Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers and Kenneth Grant, with all of them getting between 27 and 37 snaps.
-- In his second game back after being on IR with a knee injury, rookie Kyle Louis played a season-high 11 snaps on defense in a nickel role.
-- Linebacker Willie Gay Jr., back after missing the Jets game because of illness, played 27 defensive snaps alongside Rodriguez and Brooks.
-- Tackle Chukwuebuka Godrick, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Kansas City Chiefs after the cuts to 53, made his season debut and it consisted of four snaps on special teams.
-- Godrick and Kaytron Allen were among the six non-specialists who saw action only on special teams, along with LB Shaka Heyward, LB Jackson Woodard, CB Reese Taylor and G/T Caedan Wallace.
-- Finally with special teams, rookie Seydou Traore again led the way with 22 snaps, followed by 17 for Julius Wood, followed by 16 each for Louis, Heyward, Woodard and Allen.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 8 Instant Takeaways: Second-Half Collapse Costs Potential Signature Win
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins really had a shot at getting their first signature win of the Jeff Hafley era, they really did.
But if it hadn't already been established, the game served as a reminder this is a team that's operating with a very small margin for error, and there were a few too many of those in the second half, along with a controversial officiating reversal that changed the momentum.
Truth to be told, this was an encouraging performance by the Dolphins in the big picture, even if they did let one slip away after leading 13-3 at halftime after completely shutting down an injury-riddled New England offense.
The Dolphins are making progress, that's what's important here. And, yes, they did make progress and still look much improved from the team they were in the early weeks of the regular season.
Dolphins fans no doubt will lament the replay official overturning the Dolphins' fourth-down stop when they were leading 13-10 in the third quarter, instead giving New England a first down that kept alive what became the touchdown drive that gave them the lead for good.
But it wasn't the only play that swung the tide.
Ollie Gordon II got flagged for an unnecessary and, frankly, stupid unsportsmanlike conduct for yapping at an opponent to turn a third-and-5 into a third-and-20 in that forgettable third quarter. Then Zane Gonzalez, elevated from the practice squad for a second consecutive week, badly missed a 43-yard field goal attempt to basically put the Dolphins in a position where there only shot was to recover an onside kick, which basically never happens in the NFL anymore.
Beyond that, New England simply was the better team in the second half when they outscored the Dolphins 21-6, though the Dolphins again were plucky and fought to the end, as we figure they'll do all season even if the wins aren't that frequent.
-- It figured that Gordon would have a tougher time against the Patriots, particularly with Kadyn Proctor missing the game with his concussion, and that's how it played out. And we wouldn't fret over his ability to have other big games.
-- While we don't necessarily complain about play-calling, there was a pretty obvious lack of urgency in the fourth quarter when the Dolphins were down two scores and still running the ball, and often letting the play clock run down.
-- This isn't their identity, but this was a game where the Dolphins needed to air it out in the fourth quarter, not be calling running plays on second-and-12.
-- Malik Willis was fine, even though his performance wasn't as good as it was against the New York Jets. He certainly wasn't the reason the Dolphins lost.
-- Guard Jonah Savaiinaea has no doubt made significant improvement in his second season, but there's still some lapses that show up in his game.
-- Jarrett Kingston did a respectable job in place of rookie Kadyn Proctor, though he had to overcome a shaky start.
-- On the flip side, Austin Jackson had one of his best performances of the season.
-- The defense hardly could have played better in the first half and it seemed as though everybody chipped in.
-- What hurt more than anything in the second half were the two big plays, the two long touchdown passes that accounted for almost half of Drake Maye's passing yardage.
-- Props to Jacob Rodriguez for creating a turnover with a perfect Peanut punch, though he overall had a pretty quiet game.
-- The pass defense continues to get shredded, with Maye completing 80 percent of his passes. The coverage on DeMario Douglas' 43-yard touchdown was particularly depressing as he caught a pass wide open between defenders and had so much space that he could zigzag the rest of the way to the end zone.
-- Chris Johnson is normally a very good tackler, which is why it was so baffling to see whatever that was that he attempted against Maye when he came in free from behind for what should have been a sack. He should have had redemption later on that drive with a fourth-down stop, but of course there came the overrule from the replay assistant when television replays didn't suggest anything obvious enough to overturn the original ruling.
-- That play was just yet another example why instant replay stinks.
-- Yes, Willie Gay Jr. looked kind of bad on Maye's rushing touchdown off an option play, but the reality is he was one defender against two offensive players. There didn't appear to be anybody outside to handle the pitch had he zeroed in on Maye, so he was kind of in an impossible position there.
-- The special teams again had a rough outing, but missed field goals will happen and long punt returns allowed unfortunately have become commonplace. What's unforgivable is Jaylen Wright fielding a kickoff near the sideline instead of putting himself out of bounds before touching the ball, which would have created a penalty on the Patriots and given Miami the ball at its 40. Those are fundamentals the Dolphins simply have to recognize.
-- Guess we could blame it, like everything else, on Miami being a young team. But those are the kind of mistakes we want to see disappear sooner rather than later.
-- In the final analysis, though, this was a frustrating loss because the Dolphins put themselves in position for the big upset and weren't able to deliver. The first part alone, though, was a sign of progress.

title: Examining the Outside Factors That Could Impact the Dolphins' Week 8 Game Against New England
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' Week 8 matchup against the New England Patriots won't be lacking for storylines, including Miami's quest for a second consecutive victory, but there are some that go beyond X's and O's.
The Dolphins will go into the game following their breakthrough 28-25 victory against the New York Jets to face the defending AFC champion Patriots, who have a 4-3 record following a Thursday night loss against the Chicago Bears in Week 7.
The Patriots will go into the game missing star wide receiver A.J. Brown and backup running back TreVeyon Henderson, while the Dolphins will be without rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor with star running back De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
New England will enter the game as a 7.5-point favorite, according to the FanDuel Sportsbook, but if you believe in the idea that weather can be an equalizing factor, then the weather in Miami Gardens on Sunday should be considered.
It was raining in Miami Gardens on Sunday night, but the forecast called for the weather to actually get worse — if not much worse — throughout the afternoon and into the night.
The outlook as of 10 a.m., according to Weather.com, read as follows: "Storms likely for the next several hours. Potential for heavy rainfall."
There also is a flood watch in several areas of the northern parts of Dade County, where Miami Gardens is located.
With the expectations of thunderstorms, we also can't help but look back to the Dolphins' 2018 season opener against the Tennessee Titans when two lightning delays lasting more than an hour each made the game last more than seven hours.
And obviously the field conditions could become a factor at some point with the ball getting slippery and footing also potentially becoming an issue.
The other outside factor in the Dolphins-Patriots game that needs to be watched, even though it hopefully won't affect the outcome one way or the other, was the officiating crew switch late in the week.
The officiating around the NFL has come under a lot of scrutiny this season, but it may have reached a high point (or low point maybe?) in the Green Bay Packers game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field last week, leading to Packers safety Xavier McKinney lashing out publicly after the game.
McKinney drew a fine from the NFL for using the term for bovine excrement in talking about the officiating, but he wasn't the only one complaining.
Ton Brady openly criticized at least one call for roughing the passer during the game, but the most egregious call came for an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty when Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown got up after catching a pass, a Packers defender tackled him thinking the play wasn't over but knocked down an official in the process, with the official responding by throwing a flag while on his back.
Likely as the result of not wanting the spotlight on the officiating crew of Alex Moore, the NFL took them off their scheduled assignment for the Sunday night game between Philadelphia and Washington and moved them to the Dolphins-Patriots game, which will be shown to a ridiculously small portion of the country as the "other" 4:25 p.m. on CBS opposite Kansas City at Denver.
Moore's crew, for the record, officiated the Dolphins' home opener against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3, calling eight penalties on each team. Moore also worked the Dolphins-Patriots game at Hard Rock Stadium in Week 2 of 2025.
