title: 4 Winners, 2 Losers from Patriots' Comeback Win over Dolphins
full_text:
While it may not have been the prettiest win in the world, the New England Patriots took down the Miami Dolphins 24-19 at Hard Rock Stadium on Sunday afternoon.
New England improved to 3-0 against AFC East opponents, thanks in-part to the majority of the players listed below.
Here are the four biggest winners, and two biggest losers, from the Patriots' victory over the Dolphins.
While he has had plenty of ups and downs throughout this season, Maye's performance on Sunday was one of his most impressive as a Patriot, all things considered.
On the surface, Maye's stat sheets looks impressive, but nothing to write home about. The third-year gunslinger completed 16 of his 20 passes for 199 yards and a pair of touchdowns, plus punched in another score on the ground. More impressively, however, he did so without many of the New England offense's key pieces.
Running back TreVeyon Henderson, wide receivers A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins, plus offensive guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu were all unable to play on Sunday. Plus, starting tight end Hunter Henry left the game early.
"That's what being a great quarterback in the National Football League is," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said when asked about Maye's success despite the offense's injuries. "Not a whole lot of excuses. You go out there and you find ways to win for your football team...being one of the best quarterbacks in the league, that's what the job description requires."
Although Durden was on the field for just 26 of New England's defensive snaps (40%), he made them count. The 27-year-old was a game wrecker on Sunday, especially in the first half.
Durden finished the day with 1.5 sacks and four total tackles. He also tallied three pressures on just 13 pass rushes. Plus, one of his highlights of the day came on a run stuff where he moved an offensive lineman nearly five yards backwards.
It's time that teams get familiar with Cory Durden (unless I'm just way behind).  I'm not sure how he looks on a down by down basis - but he absolutely has some big time flashes. https://t.co/1XKEoh9R9S pic.twitter.com/HvQxnh1Hw9
"I felt great," Durden told reporters after the game. "I had a great week of preparation. You know, it's been ups and downs. That's what comes with it during the week. So, just trying to get better and keep going. And I feel like it showed up today."
Back in the same stadium he played his home games at while with the University of Miami, Borregales faltered on Sunday. While weather conditions were far from ideal, the second-year kicker missed a 40-yard field goal attempt in the second quarter, which would have tied the game up.
Fortunately for New England, Borregales has been relatively stable this season. That was just his second missed field goal of the year, in addition to one missed point-after attempt.
With New England's top-three receivers out due to injuries, the Patriots needed somebody to step up in the room. That man-up was Douglas. The 25-year-old hauled in all three of his targets, tallying 76 yards and a score.
He also may have had the play of the day, a shifty 48-yard catch-and-run for a touchdown.
TOUCHDOWN, POP!!! 📺  CBS pic.twitter.com/TVjfofNOIu
"Man, we've been preaching opportunity," Douglas said on Sunday. "I think our coaches do a great job of having everybody prepared as a starter. I feel like, man, when somebody gets hurt,it's somebody that steps up and know what they're doing."
New England headed into Miami without its three best wide receivers, its second running back and its starters at both offensive guard positions. However, what was already bad somehow got worse.
Tight end Hunter Henry, who has been one of Maye's top targets throughout the signal caller's entire NFL career, left the game in the second quarter with a foot injury and did not return. Plus, rookie edge rusher Gabe Jacas left the game late and also did not come back in. An already depleted Patriots roster has somehow gotten thinner by the week.
Consistency was key for Stevenson on Sunday. The 28-year-old led New England with 19 carries for 82 yards. Plus, he added an extra three receptions through the air. Despite taking a top-end workload while missing two starting offensive linemen, Stevenson did not have any of his rushes go for negative yards.
Plus, he recovered the onside kick toward the end of the game to put the Patriots in position to win it.
"He loves the football team," Vrabel said when asked about Stevenson. "You can see it by the way that he prepares, the way he plays, the way he protects the guys that don't have the ball or how he plays when he doesn't have the ball.His ability to protect the quarterback when they blitz.You know, he does a lot of things for us."

title: DeMario Douglas Comes Up Big in Patriots' Rejuvenating Victory
full_text:
With three receivers out, the New England Patriots needed someone to step up in the passing game. They got that production out of DeMario Douglas, who had himself a fantastic game in the 24-19 win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday afternoon .
Douglas finished with three receptions on three targets, 76 receiving yards and a 48-yard touchdown that came on the back of a Kevin Byard interception just a few moments before.
Without A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins, it was one of Douglas' best performances as a pro — and can help show the Patriots truly what they have in the 25-year-old.
"It shows the team grit," he told reporters postgame. "We didn't start off well in the beginning, but I love how we played in the second half. Came out there heads up, heads high. We started playing complimentary football."
Both Douglas and Kyle Williams (1 reception, 43 receiving yards, one touchdown) helped catapult the Patriots into the lead in the second half. Douglas' touchdown, which was his fourth of the season, came because he relied on his pure speed to outrace Miami's secondary. In games past, like against the New York Jets in Week 6, he fumbled the ball after trying to do too much. He said he wanted to avoid that today.
So what was going through Douglas' mind when he was sprinting his way to the end zone?
"I said I get this ball, I'm finna score," Douglas laughed. "I had it in my head like, I'm finna get this in the chicken box. That's what I said. I'm finna get this in the chicken box, and thank you God. He blessed me. He blessed me for sure."
Douglas also had a first down conversion on fourth down that appeared short, and was called short, before replay assist helped overturn the call on the field.
It was a gutsy outing for the Patriots offense as a whole, who also lost Hunter Henry in the game with a foot injury. Still, the receivers were able to make things happen in a game that didn't look like it would be positive in any which way. At halftime, the Patriots trailed 13-3 and looked lost in their own way.
"We just stopped hurting ourselves," Douglas said. "We were killing ourselves, you know, in that forst half, man. Felt like when we got in this locker room, we knew it, we knew it.
"And we told ourselves, 'let's settle down and take a breath and go out here and play our football, play our type of football game.'"
The Patriots had just four receivers active for the game , with Efton Chism III and Ryan Miller rounding out the group. Hollins is eligible to be activated off of IR this week, so his return will be a much-needed one. But ultimately, the mindset of Douglas and the rest of the receivers have helped them during this stretch.
"Man, I love the preparation that we have," Douglas said. "We have big guys go down and how we prepare and we don’t skip a beat. I applaud Chiz (Chism) and Dub (Williams). They come, stepping in, and they’re playing their role. Third down, touchdowns. Chiz making big plays to move that rock, man. Man, I’m proud of our group."

title: The Good, Bad, and Ugly from Patriots' Week 8 Victory over Dolphins
full_text:
The New England Patriots surged in the second half against the Miami Dolphins to improve their record to 5-3, marking their third in-division win of the season. Let's break down the good, the bad, and the ugly from Week 8.
New England's defensive line feasted against a Miami offense missing first-round rookie guard Kadyn Proctor (concussion). The Patriots' pass rush got home against Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis five times, a season-high sack total. Gabe Jacas (1.5 sacks), Corey Durden (1.5 sacks), Elijah Ponder (0.5 sack), Christian Barmore (0.5 sack), Christian Elliss (0.5 sack) and Jaylen Reed (0.5 sack) kept Willis under pressure throughout the afternoon. The run defense was a similar story. After rushing 25 times for 103 yards and a touchdown in Week 7, Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon was held to just 69 yards on 19 carries (3.6 yards per carry). As a team, Miami was held to just 74 yards on 23 attempts, largely thanks to a dominant performance from Durden , who added two tackles for loss to his 1.5 sacks.
Cory Durden gets to the QB 😤 NEvsMIA on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/T6ty0eGyh7
OK, It wasn't all bad. Safety Kevin Byard recorded his first interception as a Patriot after a pass deflected off the helmet of defensive lineman DaQuan Jones, leading to a 4th-quarter scoring drive for the offense. That is objectively a good result. However, beyond that one play, the secondary continually allowed big gains to Chris Bell, Caleb Douglas, Greg Dulcich, Kevin Coleman Jr, and Malik Washington. According to Pro Football Focus, Carlton Davis allowed six catches on seven targets for 42 yards, Christian Gonzalez gave up four catches on six targets for 52 yards, and Charles Woods allowed a 35-yard score on his only target of the game. With an explosive Green Bay offense on the horizon, New England will need a much stronger performance from its defensive backs.
After a first half in which the Patriots managed just three points, Drake Maye found his rhythm coming out of the break. Without A.J. Brown (knee/ankle) and TreVeyon Henderson (illness) , and still awaiting the returns of Romeo Doubs (shoulder) and Mack Hollins (calf) from injured reserve, Maye was working with a depleted group of pass catchers. The wide receiver room consisted of Efton Chism III, Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas and Ryan Miller, who was elevated from the practice squad for this matchup. Despite the limited options, Maye delivered an efficient performance, completing 16 of 20 passes for 199 yards and two touchdowns. He also added five rushing yards and a score on the ground. All three of Maye's touchdowns came in the second half, marking his fifth consecutive game with at least three total touchdowns.
Drake Maye fakes the pitch and scores! NEvsMIA on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/AnYFWNgzRv
New England saw tight end Hunter Henry (foot) and outside linebacker Gabe Jacas (knee) leave this matchup. It'd be impossible to tell the story of the 2026 Patriots without injuries. We'll have to wait until the team hits the practice field Wednesday for a clearer picture of the severity of both injuries, but there's no denying how important Henry and Jacas are to their respective units. Losing either for an extended period would be a significant blow.
As mentioned, New England entered this matchup shorthanded at wide receiver, creating an opportunity for someone to step up. Williams and Douglas absolutely capitalized on their increased opportunities. Douglas finished the day catching all three of his targets for 76 yards, including a 48-yard catch-and-run for a score. Williams had only one catch on the day, but it was a pivotal 43-yard bomb that kicked off their second-half comeback.
Down 6-3 with 2:24 remaining in the first half, Borregales pushed a 40-yard field goal attempt wide right. Miami followed with a scoring drive, making the missed opportunity even more costly. Borregales finished the day 1-for-2 on field goals, converting from 34 yards while going 3-for-3 on extra-point attempts. This season, Borregales is 10-for-13 (76.9%) on field goals as he looks to build consistency down the stretch.

title: 6 Instant Takeaways From Patriots' Soaking-Wet 24-19 Win Over Dolphins
full_text:
After a thrilling loss to the Chicago Bears in Week 7, the football pendulum swung back in the other direction for the New England Patriots. It was an extremely wet and sloppy game for the Patriots, but a strong second half (led by three touchdown drives) turned what didn't look good at all into a 24-19 win over the Miami Dolphins.
It wasn't pretty, and it was clear that the Patriots were down some big names offensively (A.J. Brown and TreVeyon Henderson were both inactives). Still, the Patriots flipped a switch and proved that they were the far dominant team in what was their fifth victory of the season — and third over a division rival.
Drake Maye, slow in the first half, had another sparking stat line in totality. He finished 16-for-20 with 207 total yards (before kneel downs) and three touchdowns in the win, settling into the soaked conditions to earn his second career win in Miami.
Here's what happened, and what it means going forward.
Already without Brown, Henderson, Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs, the Patriots couldn't afford to lose anybody else on the offense. In the first half, after he grabbed a catch to open up the drive, tight end Hunter Henry would head to the locker room. He'd later be ruled questionable to return with a foot injury.
Henry, one of four tight ends active for the game, would come back onto the sideline to test out his foot before halftime. He didn't end up getting back in the offensive huddle and he retreated back into the locker room. Henry would not return.
Without the vet on the field, the Patriots didn't consistently move the ball. Yes, that changed once the second half began, but it was an ugly start to the afternoon. Receivers couldn't break out of coverage and the pocket couldn't hold up for long.
Maye was also sacked three times, but it ultimately didn't matter. The second half offense exploded and showed why this team remains in Super Bowl conversations.
On a Patriots defensive line where Milton Williams and Christian Barmore get most of the headlines, it was Cory Durden who made the biggest mark in the game. The 27-year-old had a career-high 1.5 sacks in the loss, both of them coming on the first two drives of the game.
Durden also had two tackles for loss against the run in a game where the Patriots held the Dolphins' rushing attack to just 63 total yards. Ollie Gordon, who came into the game on a little bit of a header, had just 58 of those yards and they weren't able to move the ball consistently in between the tackles .
But it wasn't just him. The Patriots sent the house a number of times, getting good plays out of Williams, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas. They finished the game with five sacks, including the first one in the career of safety Jaylen Reed.
The Patriots came into the game with 14 turnovers — the second-most in the entire NFL — and have turned it over at least once in every game. At some point, the Patriots were bound for a perfect game, right?
It didn't happen in Miami. Backed up deep in their own territory, Maye hit Efton Chism III for a short pass. Chism tried to make something happen, and Dolphins rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez punched it out. The Dolphins would take over at the Patriots' 19-yard line and would be forced to settle for a game-tying field goal.
Alijah Vera-Tucker's hamstring injury and subsequent placement on IR opened up a hole at left guard. Walter Rouse, the converted tackle who the Patriots traded for in August , was the first player to step up and he was named the starter in back-to-back weeks.
But that didn't last long. After a really tough first half where he got beat a number of times, Rouse was replaced by veteran Ben Brown at left guard. Brown didn't play in the Week 7 loss to the Bears because of a knee injury, but didn't come into this week with an injury designation. After Brown came in, the Patriots offense started to click.
With the offense sputtering, the Patriots needed something to happen. That first came by way of Kyle Williams and a long catch. Stop me if you've heard that before.
In the third quarter and trailing by 10, Maye launched it to Williams deep down the middle of the field. Williams, who came into the game with one touchdown this season, beat rookie safety Michael Taaffe for a 43-yard touchdown. It was originally ruled as incomplete after the ball bounced off of Williams' knee, but was overturned after a passionate challenge by Mike Vrabel.
Elite flag throw from Vrabel pic.twitter.com/RPgjdwmpGo
On their next drive, after a fourth-down pickup by DeMario Douglas, the Patriots rolled out the speed option play call for Maye at the right time. The quarterback kept it himself and he powered his way in for his third rushing touchdown of the season. That score gave the Patriots the 17-13 lead, their first since it was 3-0 in the first.
With the Patriots leading by four, the Dolphins offense trotted back onto the field to try and reclaim the lead. That didn't end up happening, and the Patriots — who had been preached for weeks that they needed to start forcing more turnovers — finally got their wish.
Willis tried to push the ball deep down the middle of the field, but his throw hit off the front of DaQuan Jones' helmet. The ball fluttered into the air and fell right into the awaiting arms of Kevin Byard, who led the NFL in interceptions a season ago. That pick eventually led to a DeMario Douglas touchdown, ballooning the lead to 11, and gave Byard his first pick as a Patriot .
Miami would add six points on a long touchdown from Kevin Coleman Jr. (in which Charles Woods slipped in coverage, leaving the Dolphins wideout wide open) with 2:04 left in the fourth quarter. The ensuing onside kick attempt would fall into the hands of Stevenson, and after a Stevenson first down carry, the win was finally set in stone.

title: Patriots Week 8 Inactives vs. Dolphins: With A.J. Brown, TreVeyon Henderson Out, Who Steps Up?
full_text:
The New England Patriots , like most games this season, won't be at full strength for their Week 8 game against the Miami Dolphins. Injuries continue to pile up for the 4-3 Pats, and while they were relatively healthy during practice this week, two big names won't end up suiting up.
Wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson were both ruled out Saturday, so the Patriots will need to find ways to fill the roles left by those two offensive stars. It hasn't been the greatest of seasons for Brown and Henderson to this point, but their explosiveness will be missed.
Here's a look at the inactives for both the Patriots and Dolphins, including several members of the New England offense that could leave big holes.
QB Behren Morton (emergency third QB)
RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness)
WR A.J. Brown (knee/ankle)
OG Kadyn Proctor (concussion)
One big return for the Patriots is Carlton Davis, who'll suit up after missing three-straight games with a neck injury. His return forces the young trio of Karon Prunty, Channing Canada and Elliott Davison to the sideline. Offensive guard Ben Brown also returns after missing last week's loss with a knee injury.
Behren Morton will remain the emergency third quarterback and can only enter the game if Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito both get hurt. If the Patriots were to put in Morton, that means Maye and DeVito wouldn't be able to re-enter the game unless they're medically cleared to return.
The Patriots got Brown back into the lineup a few weeks ago, but he hasn't been as advertised. He's caught just six passes since being activated to the 53-man roster and is now dealing with a knee injury that's plagued him for several years.
Without Brown, the Patriots are down to just four receivers for the game — DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III, Kyle Williams and Ryan Miller, who was temporarily elevated to the roster from the practice squad this weekend. That group will be tasked to help pick up the slack left from Brown, Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs.
"We want our best players to play, and I would consider him one of those," head coach Mike Vrabel said Friday about if the team had considered scaling back Brown's playing time after a lot of snaps in the last two games. "Again, we're really here focused on trying to get a win on the road in the division."
Because the Patriots are slim at wideout, all four tight ends on the active roster (Hunter Henry, Eli Raridon, Cameron Latu, Tanner Arkin) will dress.
Henderson hasn't been that dynamic this year, often rotating into the game with third-string Corey Kiner. Against the Bears in Week 7, he only carried the ball three times and spent most of the first half on the sideline. The Patriots signed Lan Larison off of the practice squad to help fill an open roster spot and try to add some insurance in a thinner running back room.
The Dolphins will be without their starting left guard in Kadyn Proctor, who sat out all three of the team's practices this week with a concussion. The first round rookie had been playing well to start his NFL career, but will now miss his first game. He'll be replaced by Jarrett Kingston, who was claimed off of waivers ahead of the regular season.
Without Proctor, the Patriots' defensive line trio of Milton Williams, Christian Barmore and Cory Durden have a shot to impact the game from the interior. The Dolphins' offense is powered by their ground game, led by quarterback Malik Willis and running back Ollie Gordon.
"Ollie's a big back. He's taken advantage of his opportunities, just like we always talk about in the National Football League. He's got, whatever, the last four games, four touchdowns, he's averaging 4.8 yards a carry," Vrabel said. "So, he's doing exactly what we talk about and getting opportunities and making the most of them. Whether they pull guys, it's gap scheme or zone or toss crack, you basically just have to be able to get guys over there. When they move and they add gaps somewhere else, you're going to have to either take linemen over there, or you're going to have to get linebackers to fit and secondary players to be able to make tackles."
If the Patriots are able to make life tough in the trenches and stop the Dolphins' ground attack, this could be the easiest way for the visitors to come out of South Florida with a win.

title: Saints Make Coaching Staff Changes, but Mickey Loomis Shouldn't Escape Blame
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have fired run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti following their Week 8 bye, according to Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football.
The decision comes as head coach Kellen Moore attempts to fix one of the NFL's least productive rushing attacks, with New Orleans sitting at 2-5 through seven games.
The Saints have parted ways with run game coordinator TJ Paganetti, according to sources. Paganetti came from Philadelphia, where he helped architect the run game and was part of developing one of the league’s best offensive lines
The Saints are averaging just 86 rushing yards per game and 3.5 yards per carry, with their struggles reaching a low point in a 16-10 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris on Oct. 25.
New Orleans had one of the most embarrassing rushing performances in franchise history, managing only 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts and averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Paganetti joined Moore's staff in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles , where he helped develop one of the NFL's most dominant rushing attacks.
During Philadelphia's Super Bowl-winning 2024 season, the Eagles rushed for a franchise-record 3,048 yards and averaged 179.3 yards per game, ranking second in the NFL.
However, that success never consistently translated to New Orleans.
While Paganetti deserves some responsibility, the Saints' problems extend beyond coaching.
While Moore is getting heat for the Saints’ offensive struggles, ultimately the biggest issue with the New Orleans Saints is the person who hired him: general manager Mickey Loomis .
Loomis is responsible for building the roster, including the backfield and the offensive line, the two weakest links on the Saints.
The running back room, featuring Alvin Kamara , Travis Etienne , Kendre Miller and CJ Donaldson , hasn't delivered consistent production.
Etienne's placement on injured reserve has further complicated matters, especially when the Saints signed him on a four-year, $52 million deal.  Kamara, by contrast, hasn't shown the same explosiveness that made him one of the NFL's most dynamic playmakers.
The offensive line also remains a concern despite significant investments, including first-round selections Kelvin Banks Jr. , Taliese Fuaga and Cesar Ruiz along with the free agent signing of David Edwards for $76 million
New Orleans has struggled to consistently create running lanes, particularly along the interior, leaving its running backs with limited opportunities.
Paganetti arrived in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with Philadelphia, where he helped develop one of the NFL's most productive rushing attacks. However, the Eagles also had considerably better offensive line personnel.
Moore and Loomis must now share responsibility for determining whether the Saints' struggles stem from their offensive philosophy, player development or questionable roster construction.
Firing Paganetti sends a message that the current production is unacceptable, but changing coordinators won't automatically solve personnel deficiencies.

title: Saints Midseason Stock Report: 4 Bright Spots Amid a Disappointing Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter their bye week with a disappointing 2-5 record despite the hype around the Saints being contenders to possibly win the NFC South.
While the season has been anything but positive, the team still has bright spots on both offense and defense.
Here's a look at four players who have performed above and beyond as we reach the midseason point.
Tyler Shough hasn't been perfect, but the second-year quarterback continues to show encouraging signs of development under coach Kellen Moore .
Through seven games, Shough has completed 67% of his passes for 1,721 yards, 13 touchdowns and six interceptions. He's also contributed 111 rushing yards and two touchdowns.
His pass yardage and touchdown totals are both in the top 10 as he is tied for seventh in passing touchdowns and ninth in passing yards, but for a majority of the season he was either No. 1 or No. 2 in passing yards.
Those numbers are impressive considering New Orleans' struggles establishing a consistent rushing attack and protecting its quarterback.
Despite occasional mistakes, Shough has demonstrated improved accuracy, pocket presence and command of Moore's offense.
If he continues developing and limits turnovers, the Saints should feel increasingly confident about their quarterback situation.
Wide receiver Chris Olave has shown why the Saints gave him a 4-year, $132 million extension.
Through seven games, the former first-round pick has caught 49 passes (fourth in the NFL) for 636 yards (third in the NFL) and two touchdowns, averaging 90.9 receiving yards per game.
He opened the season with four 100-yard performances in his first four games, including a dominant 182-yard outing against Detroit .
Chase Young has arguably been New Orleans' most impressive player on defense through seven games.
The former No. 2 overall pick has recorded seven sacks, establishing himself as one of the NFL's most productive pass rushers.
Out of 50 edge rushers with at least 125 pass rushes, Young ranked second with a 90.0 Pro Football Focus pass-rush grade.
Young is on pace to record over 15 sacks, potentially putting him in the conversation for Pro Bowl recognition.
Though Young draws much of the spotlight, Carl Granderson is quietly putting together a standout year as well.
Across seven contests, the experienced defensive end has registered 25 tackles alongside 5.5 sacks, highlighted by a 1.5-sack effort versus Pittsburgh .
Granderson's current trajectory puts him on track for roughly 13 sacks, setting up a potential career mark.
Combined, Granderson and Young have racked up 12.5 sacks, forming one of the few reliable highlights for New Orleans' defense.
Even with the unit's broader difficulties, his growth paired with Young gives the Saints a high-caliber pass-rush duo for the future.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Harbaugh Says Giants Are “Open for Any Call”
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is on a nonstop mission to keep the roster competitive as the team chases the NFC East title.
To that end, he confirmed he’s not afraid to call people around the league who might be in a position to do business with the Giants, even if that person is a team owner, as he did with Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk.
“I left a message because you’re turning over every stone, going to try everything,” he said on Monday after the team went through a light practice. “I’ll put it out there: We’re open for any call. Anybody who wants to call us or call anybody, call.”
Harbaugh drew criticism from national talking heads for reaching out to Strunk, adding that he didn’t speak with her but left her a message.
He insisted there are no rules specifying who can talk to whom in the league, noting that he knows all the owners. Giants general manager Joe Schoen, meanwhile, knows the general managers.
Together, they aim to find talent that fits the team in both the short and long term.
“We’re not part of any secret society oath that says you can only talk to somebody,” he said.
“We’re not in that. We didn’t get memoed on that. We’re not in that agreement. So, as I said, anybody can call us. We won’t be adhering to that particular agreement.”
There’s no telling at this point if the Giants’ aggressiveness in searching for roster upgrades will pay off, but Harbaugh said the plan is to stay proactive.
But that comes with a caveat: The goal is not only to find good players but to find players who fit what the Giants have been building under Harbaugh.
“That’s always the goal. Easier said than done. And it’s hard to find players that can make you better, because we have good players,” he said.
“So, it’s got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag. I mean, it’s not like we have a bunch of draft picks either. We’re not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks, so we don’t have draft capital to burn. We don’t. So, we have to be smart shoppers that way.”
With the Giants’ 2027 draft picks dwindling, Harbaugh did not rule out dipping into the team’s 2028 draft capital to make a deal that, again, would have to meet certain criteria.
“For me, it wouldn’t want to be a one-on-one kind of thing. You want to have a short-term and a long-term win if you’re going to do it with draft capital,” he said.

title: Giants Add Familiar Face at Running Back as Skattebo’s Injury Status Raises Questions
full_text:
The New York Giants were back to work on Monday after their Week 8 bye, but one key offensive player worked with trainers on the sideline during the media portion of practice.
Running back Cam Skattebo, who said he felt something in his hamstring after his 42-yard run against the Houston Texans in overtime two weeks ago, was spotted working to the side with trainers.
It’s unclear whether Skattebo is simply trying to buy a couple more days to let his hamstring fully heal before the team begins its prep for Sunday’s road game at Philadelphia, or whether the injury could limit him in practice and, potentially, the upcoming game.
Head coach John Harbaugh characterized Skattebo's status as "day to day."
Either way, the Giants, who last week placed running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. on IR with a hamstring injury, are not taking any chances of going into the critical division matchup with just Devin Singletary and newcomer Gregory Desrosiers, whom they signed last week off the Chargers’ practice squad.
To that end, New York has signed running back Eric Gray, its fifth-round pick in the 2023 draft, to its practice squad.
Gray, who was with the team this summer, appeared in 34 games over three seasons, including just four in 2025 after landing on PUP due to a knee injury. He has 31 career rushing attempts for 79 yards and caught 16 of 18 targets for 104 yards, with no rushing or receiving touchdowns.
Gray struggled with ball security during his time with the Giants, fumbling six times in 2023 and 2024. He also returned 27 kickoffs for 653 yards in a bid to carve out a role as a return specialist.
This past summer he led the team in receptions with eight catches for 54 yards. He also led the Giants in rushing with 90 yrds on 30 carries.
Gray was with the Cleveland Browns practice squad in September but was released in early October.
In other practice news, outside linebacker Abdul Carter was not spotted at practice during the media viewing portion. Harbaugh said the outside linebacker was held out of practice because he was sick.
The Giants do not have to put out an injury report until Wednesday. The players are off on Tuesday.

title: Why the Giants Should, and Shouldn’t, Make the Trade for RB Jonathan Taylor
full_text:
The New York Giants have apparently been looking for a workhorse running back even before the start of the 2026 season, if reports of their interest in Kenneth Walker during free agency and Jeremiyah Love during the draft are true.
Recently, head coach John Harbaugh, before the team’s Week 7 win against the Houston Texans, who at the time came into that game with the league’s third-best run defense, seemed to long for a Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley type of situation while also challenging those running backs already on the team to step up and grab the bellcow spot.
And despite the Giants’ running game having had one of its best showings this year, there is still plenty of talk that the Giants are interested in acquiring Colts running back Jonathan Taylor via trade.
But is that the right move? Taylor is certainly a fine running back, but Indianapolis reportedly wants a haul similar to what the Carolina Panthers received when they traded Christian McCaffrey to the 49ers. With reports that the Broncos, Packers, and Vikings are also interested in Taylor, the Colts appear to be in the driver’s seat to wait out the best possible offer in a trade that, if it happens, could go down to the wire.
For the Giants, there are reasons why they should definitely make the trade and reasons why they shouldn’t. Let’s look at both sides.
Critics of the trade argue the Giants aren’t one running back away from a Super Bowl run, and they have a point. In our view, New York needs a defensive tackle more, given the inconsistency of its defensive line depth, particularly against the run.
But those viewing Taylor as a short-term acquisition aren’t looking at the full picture. Taylor is under contract through the 2028 season, when he’d turn 29.
That means Taylor wouldn’t be a half-season rental. And beyond the draft pick package the Giants would have to give up, Taylor would cost the Giants $410,588 for every week he’d be on the Giants roster, plus an additional $60,000 for every game in which he’s active, which isn’t back-breaking.
Looking ahead, his 2027 salary swells to $15 million, which becomes fully guaranteed on the fifth day of the waiver period according to Over the Cap . But he’d only cost the Giants $16.020 million in 2027 and $17.980 million in 2028 if he plays out his contract.
That might seem like a hefty amount to have to pay beyond the draft assets to acquire him, but if Taylor, who played over 80% of the offensive snaps in 2024 and 2025 and is at 77% this season, can keep up that production, it might be worth it.
But as far as the draft compensation goes, what people aren’t talking about is the Giants’ quarterback situation.
If J.J. McCarthy continues to play well, that could set the Giants up to trade one of their young quarterbacks on a rookie contract to recoup some of the assets they would have to surrender to get Taylor, especially considering how the college quarterback class, which at the start of the season was thought to be so promising, has thus far been a disappointment between injuries and performance.
There are more reasons for the Giants not to make this trade than there are to do it, and for fairness’ sake, we’ll set aside our continued, strong belief that the Giants need a defensive tackle more than they do a running back.
Let’s go back to what Harbaugh said when he longed for a bellcow running back, a la Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley. The Giants had just come off one of their worst games of the season, and Harbaugh had challenged his running backs to step up and take over.
Cam Skattebo did just that in the team’s Week 7 overtime win against the Texans. His 180 rushing yards brought him to 360 for the year and boosted his average yards per carry to 4.5, ahead of Taylor’s current 4.1 average .
This isn’t to say Skattebo is a better running back than Taylor. That comparison really can’t be made, given that one player has a far more impressive career résumé than the other.
This also isn’t to say what Skattebo did in that game is sustainable. On the flip side, it’s not fair to say it isn’t sustainable either.
If we’re looking at this season’s production, Skattebo, behind an offensive line whose effectiveness in run blocking some have questioned, is averaging 1.35 yards before contact compared with Taylor’s 1.20, and 3.15 yards after contact compared with Taylor’s 2.92 (per PFF advanced data).
Another reason the Giants may pause on parting with a large haul for Taylor is McCarthy, who has affected the running game.
Per Next Gen Stats, the Giants faced only 11 loaded boxes of 8+ defenders in their Week 7 win over Houston. They averaged 6.0 yards per carry (third-highest) against loaded boxes in that game.
Before Week 7, the Giants faced 77 loaded boxes (sixth most) and averaged 3.0 yards per carry.
Coincidence? Perhaps. Or perhaps, with a mobile quarterback back in the lineup, that has not only forced opposing defenses to account for the quarterback as a runner, but also reduced their willingness to load the box for fear of being burned by a deep throw.
And that theory could have merit. In Weeks 1-5, the Giants completed 37% of their deep pass attempts of 20+ air yards. In Weeks 6 and 7, with McCarthy in the lineup, that percentage jumped to 60%.
We have made no secret that we believe a defensive tackle is the greater need.
Despite their strong showing against the Texans in Week 7, the Giants still have the league’s 26th-ranked run defense, allowing 128.1 yards per game and 4.82 yards per rushing attempt (27th in the league).
Several factors are behind that, the biggest issue seems to be a drop-off in depth behind starters D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris that, despite the resources the Giants have devoted to the position since the offseason, has not consistently produced the desired results.

title: Harbaugh’s Giants Face a Defining Week After the Bye
full_text:
The New York Giants enjoyed a nearly week-long break from what has been a physically and mentally demanding, yet rewarding (so far) season, and they return to work on Monday with what should be a relatively light practice.
Ahead of them are two key division games: one on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles, whom Big Blue hasn’t beaten since 2013, and then a quick turnaround at home against the Washington Commanders, who beat the Eagles on Sunday.
The Giants? Since 2008, John Harbaugh’s first season as a head coach (then with Baltimore), they are 11-7 coming out of a bye, which ties them for eighth in the league over that span.
Harbaugh holds a 15-3 record after the bye, tied with Pittsburgh for the best post-bye record.
And if you want yet another reason to be optimistic, consider that Harbaugh’s Ravens teams, after coming back fully rested from the bye, have outscored opponents by 181 points, the largest margin in the league over that period.
While history paints a rosy outlook for the Giants in 2026 under Harbaugh, there is still a matter of getting through the week and preparing for a wounded Eagles team at a place where some funky things have befallen the Giants in recent years (the most recent being the devastating season-ending ankle injury suffered by running back Cam Skattebo).
That said, here are some of the key storylines still to unfold.
Say what you will about the quality of the NFC East, but Harbaugh and the players are not taking these next two pivotal games against the Eagles on Sunday and the Commanders on the ensuing Thursday lightly.
Nor should they. Division games carry extra weight because of tiebreakers. The Giants not only have a chance to put further distance between themselves and the Eagles (motivation in itself), but they’ll also need to come out on top against the Commanders to win the head-to-head tiebreaker after tying them in the first meeting.
There’s another reason these two games are paramount for the Giants. After the Commanders game, New York faces a murderers’ row of opponents, starting in Week 11 with a home game against the Jaguars, followed by a reprieve against a struggling Colts team, and then games against the 49ers, Seahawks, Browns and Lions, all teams with winning records who are jockeying for a postseason berth.
How the Giants come out of their two division games starting this weekend will tell a lot about whether they’re for real or have benefited from playing lesser opponents.
Will they or won’t they? Harbaugh has shown he’s not afraid to keep churning the roster, and with the team having an opportunity to win its first division title since 2011, don’t expect Harbaugh and the Giants to let the grass grow under their feet now.
The question, though, is whether the team will be buyers, sellers, or both. We think it will be both; we proposed trading center John Michael Schmitz to the Packers for a draft pick. But if anything, the Giants are more likely to be buyers.
If so, will it be Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, or will the Giants look to add depth to their defensive line?
If they do make a move, will it be of the blockbuster type, such as what the Colts reportedly want for Taylor, or will the Giants play it a bit more conservatively with another running back option like Tony Pollard of the Titans, or a defensive tackle like Dalvin Tomlinson of the Chargers, Zach Sieler of the Dolphins, or A’Shawn Robinson of the Panthers?
The trade deadline is November 10, so the next eight days should be very interesting to follow.
So far, the Giants and quarterback J.J. McCarthy look like a match made in heaven, so much so that some members of Skol Nation have expressed regret over Minnesota’s decision to send McCarthy packing.
With good reason. In Weeks 6 and 7 (we don’t count Week 8 since the Giants had a bye), McCarthy had a respectable 63.3% pass completion rate, 14th among 26 quarterbacks with at least 40 dropbacks over that span.
His 495 passing yards rank eighth among that same group, and he’s averaging 10.1 yards per attempt, which is first.
Granted, it’s a small sample size, but it’s also encouraging moving forward, starting against the Eagles, whose pass defense has allowed 235.4 yards per game, 24th in the league.
When we last left the Giants, they had several players looking to heal up nagging injuries.
The most significant is left tackle Andrew Thomas, who has been laboring through a painful groin injury. The Giants will likely continue managing his workload the rest of the season, but if the time off helped enough that Thomas doesn’t look like he’s moving in slow motion after every snap, that’s a plus for the Giants.
The time off also hopefully helped right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor’s ailing calf. Eluemunor was questionable for the Week 7 game at Houston, but he pushed through after missing the previous week with the same injury.
And let’s not forget punter Jordan Stout, who pushed through a right knee injury in Week 7. Stout, our pick for special teams MVP through the first half of the season, posted his lowest net yard average (38.5) in Week 7 and saw his gross punting yard average fall below 50 after two straight weeks well above that mark.
Others expected back this week include starting cornerback Greg Newsome II, who missed Week 7 with a concussion, tight end Theo Johnson (neck), and safety Tyler Nubin (neck).

title: Giants Midseason Awards: Best Players, Biggest Surprises and the Turning Point
full_text:
As their Week 8 bye comes to a close, the New York Giants continue to take stock of their performance through the first seven games.
For the first time since 2015, Big Blue sits atop the NFC East with a 4-2-1 record . By adopting a structured yet proactive approach across all three phases of the game, veteran coach John Harbaugh has the Giants in contention for a playoff spot in just his first season at the helm.
Despite losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart and outside linebacker Brian Burns to season-ending injuries, several team members have stepped up to help the Giants become one of the NFL’s best comeback stories to date.
With that in mind, here are the Giants players (and one moment) most deserving of accolades so far in 2026.
Heading into the Giants’ Week 1 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys, Nabers had not seen regular-season action since suffering an ACL tear in Week 4 of the 2025 season. As such, both fans and media alike questioned whether he would be healthy enough to be productive in 2026.
Yet, just one year after his season-ending injury, Nabers leads all Giants pass-catchers with 605 receiving yards on 48 catches with two touchdowns.
Not only has the sixth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft logged receptions of 46, 42, and 39 yards this season, but he has also compiled 158 yards after the catch. Whether he is catching passes from Dart, 12-year veteran Jameis Winston, or newly installed starter J.J. McCarthy, Nabers has routinely proven himself to be New York’s most dangerous receiving threat.
As a result, Nabers edges out tight end Isaiah Likely by a hair as the Giants’ top offensive player in the first half of the season.
Though strong cases could be made for safety Jevon Holland and rookie linebacker Arvell Reese, Carter has been the most consistent presence in coordinator Dennard Wilson’s defense.
The third overall selection in the 2025 NFL Draft has played 88% (288) of the team’s defensive snaps.
At the start of Week 8, Carter was tied with Miami Dolphins defensive end Chop Robinson for the NFL lead in pass-rush win rate (35%) by an edge rusher, per ESPN. This year, he has compiled 18 total tackles, seven quarterback hits, and two sacks.
Few pass rushers in the NFL can offer speed-to-power techniques the way Carter can. His athleticism and instincts give him the chance to be a consistent, disruptive force in the pocket against opposing quarterbacks, only increasing his already high value to New York’s defense.
While some may understandably consider New York’s fifth overall selection in April’s draft their best defensive player to date, Reese has left little doubt about his status as their top rookie.
Through the Giants’ first seven games this season, Reese leads the team with 56 total tackles, along with 1.5 sacks, five tackles for loss, and two quarterback hits.
The 6-foot-4, 243-pounder has been New York’s top triple threat, demonstrating high-level prowess in stopping the run, dropping into coverage, and rushing the passer.
As a result, Reese has found comfort playing all over the field. Though he is unquestionably at his best when aligned inside, he has also been a factor on the edge when called upon to help in the pass rush.
Should he continue his success into this season’s second act, Reese will help the Giants earn a playoff berth.
Unlike Nabers or Carter, Stout rarely makes the highlight reels. Still, it is hard to imagine the Giants having the type of success they’ve had this season without their veteran punter.
Entering Week 8, Stout led the NFL in yards per punt, averaging 51.6. In fact, 12 of his punts have landed inside the opponents’ 20-yard line.
When the offense has struggled to move the ball, the 28-year-old routinely flips the field beyond 50 yards. His longest punt of the season traveled 78 yards during New York’s Week 3 loss to the Los Angeles Rams.
Named a first-team All-Pro in 2025, Stout is once again poised to earn the honor this season, provided he continues to be the Giants’ standout specialist through the remaining 10 games of 2026.
Once considered a liability by several preseason pundits, the Giants’ secondary has been one of the team’s strengths in 2026. New York ranks among the league’s best in total takeaways (9) and interceptions (6), five of which came from Giants defensive backs.
Cornerback Deonte Banks has been one of the club’s most-improved players. With Wilson utilizing him as a true matchup cornerback, Banks has compiled 20 total tackles, 10 passes defensed, and a 98-yard pick-six against the Arizona Cardinals.
Just one week ago, he remarkably limited Houston Texans star receiver Nico Collins to one catch for four yards, solidifying his status as one of New York’s top defenders.
Safety Jevon Holland has been equally impressive. Despite struggling through much of the 2025 campaign, Holland has bounced back to lead the team with three interceptions, fortifying the back end of the Giants’ secondary in the process.
If cornerback Paulson Adebo and safety Tyler Nubin can overcome their first-half struggles, the Giants’ defensive backfield will keep the defense strong throughout the push for the playoffs.
Notwithstanding the early-season struggles of their running backs, the timing of New York’s need to bench Schmitz in favor of Bryan Hudson makes the center the team’s biggest disappointment.
In the wake of Dart’s injury, the offensive line was counting on its centerpiece to solidify its run blocking and pass protection. Unfortunately, Schmitz struggled to protect the pocket and prevent pressure up the middle.
The Giants’ second-round pick (No. 57 overall) has earned a 45.7 overall PFF grade this season, ranking him 33rd among 35 qualified centers.
On only 191 offensive snaps this season, his PFF pass-blocking grade of 42.3 and run-blocking grade of 49.7 place him near the bottom of players at his position.
With just over 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter of the Giants’ Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, McCarthy stepped onto the field to relieve beleaguered starter Jameis Winston.
The former Michigan Wolverine orchestrated three late-game scoring drives and helped the Giants nearly complete an improbable comeback in the eventual 34-27 loss at MetLife Stadium.
His 243 passing yards in the fourth quarter were the most by any player in 11 minutes of play in NFL history.
Fortunately for the Giants, McCarthy was just getting warmed up.
In his first start for Big Blue since being acquired via trade with the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 28, the 10th overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft led the Giants on four scoring drives in a 27-21 Week 7 overtime win over the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium.
McCarthy completed 20 of 28 passes (71.4%) for 252 yards, earning a passer rating of 99.1. Across four quarters and overtime, the 23-year-old showcased his multifaceted skill set while staying calm, cool, and collected.
After the loss of Dart for the season, and with Winston’s inconsistent play, McCarthy appears poised to provide stability and leadership to the Giants offense, traits that will serve him well as he leads the club to the postseason for the first time since 2022.
With all due respect to outside linebacker Brian Burns or any other player who suffered a season-ending injury, we’d have to go with quarterback Jaxson Dart.
While the Giants have survived the loss of their starting quarterback, if Dart had not been knocked out for the rest of the season, they would not have had to spend a fifth-round pick to acquire J.J. McCarthy to run the playbook as originally designed.

title: Harbaugh’s Tough Love Has the Giants in First Place Entering November
full_text:
It’s November 1, and the New York Giants are in first place in the division, playing like a team that is going places.
Let that sink in, Giants fans. This season, the Giants sit atop the NFC East with a winning record despite season-ending losses to starting quarterback Jaxson Dart, outside linebacker Brian Burns, and inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds.
This hasn’t been smoke and mirrors either. Head coach John Harbaugh and his staff have swooped into East Rutherford not only with an eye for talent and a focus on getting the most out of it, but also with an understanding of how and when to push the right buttons to get even more from their players.
The best example came after an embarrassing Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson openly called out those players who weren’t giving their full effort.
Harbaugh cut running back Najee Harris for underperforming in his role as the lead back in that game, then passive-aggressively complained about the rotation. The head coach then challenged the remaining running backs to step up and show they wanted the RB1 job.
Harbaugh also sent defensive lineman Jihad Ward, who was thought to be one of the guys not running hard to the ball on defense, packing despite the team being thin on the defensive line.
The result? Message received by the players. The Giants came out swinging against a Houston Texans team in Week 7, which came into that game with the third-best run defense and whose offense was starting to heat up, and they took the Texans to the mat, beating them 27-21 in overtime.
“ I don't know if it's so much philosophy. It's just a week-to-week feel thing with your guys,” Harbaugh said when asked about when to challenge players openly.
“Our guys understand that we have to confront everything that has to do with our football, and if we do that, that comes from a place of love because we care enough, we all care enough, and we need to hear it too, as coaches, and we did from our players.”
“There were some things about game planning in terms of how much was on our plate in different kinds of ways that we had to know, and I think first time through, we're trying to build in a lot of football that over time kind of adds up,” he said when asked for an example of some feedback the players offered the coaches that the coaches acted upon.
“We were probably getting in front of ourselves, getting over our skis a little bit, I would say maybe, in terms of just being on point with execution. We talked a lot about that; we did, we did talk a lot about that. Our coaches tried to do a good job of responding, and I thought the coaches did a good job too.”
It’s all part of the big picture quest, which is to win the division, which of course would mean a postseason berth and playoff game at home, which, if they accomplish that objective, would incredibly mark just the second time since MetLife Stadium opened in 2010 that the Giants have had a postseason game in their own building.
If Harbaugh has his way, the Giants will have a lot of those late January games at home. But for now, it’s one step at a time.
“We have a long way to go, we have a lot of work to do, we're going to be playing some really tough games coming up here in the next few weeks, really physical, violent, tough games that are going to require our best football, our best execution,” he said.
“We're going to have to be at our best. November football is in front of us, and that's what we've got to be pointing towards.

title: Is the Grass Greener? Checking In on the Giants’ Biggest Free Agent Losses
full_text:
There’s an old saying that the grass isn’t always greener on the other side.
So as the New York Giants finish their Week 8 bye, we thought it would be interesting to check in on some of the Giants’ biggest free agent losses (players who signed significant contracts with other teams) and see how they’re doing with their new teams compared with the players who replaced them for the Giants.
The Tennessee Titans predictably went after many of the Giants’ unrestricted free agents after hiring former Giants head coach Brian Daboll as their offensive coordinator.
Leading the pack was receiver Wan’Dale Robinson, who received a four-year, $70 million deal, the richest contract of any of the Giants’ unrestricted free agents.
So far, you have to wonder if the Titans are questioning the move. Robinson, who was targeted more than 130 times in each of the past two seasons (2024 and 2025) and had his first 1,000-yard receiving season in 2025, has been targeted just 42 times this year.
He has caught 29 passes for 205 yards, a career-low 7.1 yards per reception, and two touchdowns in seven games.
Extrapolated over the full season, Robinson is on pace for 102 targets, 70 receptions and 498 yards, hardly numbers worthy of the contract he received as a free agent.
The Giants have taken a committee approach at slot, with tight end Isaiah Likely and receiver Malik Nabers as the primary options and additional snaps going to Darnell Mooney and Charlie Jones.
Likely (11th) and Nabers (fifth) rank in the top 11 among receivers and tight ends in receptions, with 41 and 48, respectively, despite sharing slot snaps.
The Giants were said to have wanted Flott back, but at the last minute, the Titans came in with an offer that convinced him to leave.
That was a good thing for the Giants, as one might have wondered what Flott’s return to Big Blue would have meant for Deonte Banks, whom Flott beat out for the starting job in 2025.
Flott, as is usually the case throughout his career, has missed one game due to injury: Week 2. He has 14 tackles and three stops and has allowed a 63.2% reception rate , up from the career-low 53.0% he allowed last year as a Giants starter.
In cornerback coverage rating (minimum 150 coverage snaps), he ranks 24th out of 50 , behind Banks (T-17th).
If that’s not enough for the Giants to consider Flott’s departure a blessing, Flott’s reception rate ranks 40th out of 50, while Banks has allowed 50% of the pass targets against him to be completed (T-7th) in the same 50-man sample.
Daniel Bellinger was never really intended to be a TE1 on the Giants, so comparing his stats to Isaiah Likely’s wouldn’t be fair. However, we can compare Bellinger , the Titans’ TE2 behind Gunnar Helm, to the Giants’ TE2, Theo Johnson.
Bellinger has caught 60% of his pass targets, while Johnson has caught 44.4% of his. Among the 53 tight ends with at least nine pass targets, Johnson’s 44.4% catch rate is dead last .
Schlottmann was one of the Giants’ more underrated players in 2024 and 2025.
Although he missed his first season with Big Blue because of a broken leg suffered just before the season began, he played well enough in relief of John Michael Schmitz when the second-round pick was injured.
In 2025, Schlottmann finished with PFF grades of 70.9 overall, 70.0 in run blocking and 77.0 in pass blocking, all career bests. In 363 offensive snaps in 2025, he allowed just three pressures.
This year, he has played 398 snaps as the Titans’ starting center and has allowed 10 pressures, with PFF grades nowhere near his 2025 output.
Bryan Hudson has played 299 offensive snaps since taking over for Schmitz as the Giants’ starting center. Among the 32 centers with at least 250 snaps this season , Hudson ranks fifth in pass blocking, while Schlottmann ranks 15th.
Hudson is also tied with Chiefs center Creed Humphrey for the fewest quarterback pressures allowed (three) among the 32 qualifying centers. He is also one of 14 centers in that group who have not surrendered a sack .
During his time with the Giants, Belton excelled on special teams, leading the Giants’ units with 20 tackles last season (seven solo).
This year, former Jets linebacker Zaire Barnes has taken over that production, leading the Giants with 11 special teams tackles (six solo) and a forced fumble.
In the secondary, Belton is ranked the 14th most productive safety among the 38 qualifying safeties who have played at least 350 defensive snaps.
That’s nowhere near what Jevon Holland has accomplished, however. Holland is currently the second-highest-ranked safety in the qualifying group and the fifth-best coverage safety (Belton is ranked 30th).
Holland also leads the group with a 45.5% reception rate allowed , giving him a career-best 18.2 coverage rating . Belton has a 75% reception rate allowed (19th) and a 128.6 coverage rating, which ranks 35th among the 38 safeties.
