title: How Alontae Taylor Bought Himself Time With Titans After Comeback Showing in Week 8
full_text:
Entering Week 8, I tabbed CB Alontae Taylor as the next guy that the Tennessee Titans would trade. His pending move to nickel appeared clouded by fellow defender Marcus Harris, and Taylor's inability to make an impact on the outside seemed to make him an outlier.
Taylor's performance against the Cincinnati Bengals yesterday completely quieted that notion, at least for now. Not only did Harris unfortunately exit the contest with an ankle injury, but in his wake at nickel, Taylor played his best game of the season for Tennessee.
On top of forcing a pivotal fumble in the second half, Taylor finished second on the team in QB pressures, with five. The only player ahead of him was DE Jacob Martin (6), who had three sacks by himself. That's elite company, especially for a corner.
Taylor would finish the contest with five total tackles. All 47 of his snaps came at nickel. Harris' status is unclear, but regardless of how that situation pans out, Taylor more than made the case for his process to be trusted in Robert Saleh's defense.
That’s exactly why you want Alontae Taylor in the nickel. He’s an awesome blitzer and run defender.
He's facing the perfect storm to work his way back into a primary role, and Tennessee should be thrilled to take him off of potential trade boards.
After all, spending $58 million on a free agent only to bench him in Week 6 isn't something you can push under the rug. It appears that one of Tennessee's premier offseason pickups is beginning to make good on the investment that was made for him.
Taken with CB Cor'Dale Flott's own stready improvement over the past few weeks, the new faces Tennessee paid to lay down as the basis of Saleh's defense are beginning to fully look the part. Trading away Jeffery Simmons guaranteed that the defense would need a rest of some kind, but the fewer long-term assets the Titans have to move, the better.
Taylor quieting some of the noise around his play in Week 8 opens the door for more obvious moves for the Titans at the deadline. Tony Pollard, in the last year of his contract, may have played his way into some solid draft capital in the last few games.
Elsewhere on defense, S Amani Hooker and DE Jacob Martin are alluring veteran candidates whose value peaked with their own team-leading performances vs. the Bengals. Nothing has to be forced. If Taylor keeps climbing, he'll be just what Tennessee expected him to be entering this year.
That is, a starting, playmaking contributor at the center of a rebuild that's looking better by the game.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Mill: Cam Ward's Best NFL Game Takes Trade Deadline Pressure Off Tennessee
full_text:
Going into Week 8, the November 10 trade deadline was beginning to look make-or-break for the Tennessee Titans. Little to nothing has been clicking on a consistent basis in Robert Saleh's first season, and little to nothing appeared off the table as far as the market goes.
Against the Cincinnati Bengals, the final result wasn't out of the ordinary. The Titans are 1-7 after yet another loss. However, Cam Ward having his best game as a professional throws all other worries to the wayside for a moment. Ward looked like a franchise QB.
All the sudden, who the Titans must move and the sort of capital they need to acquire in return feels slightly less important. Don't get us wrong, there are still trades Tennessee could very well make within the next eight days.
However, they're simply not as critical if Ward is playing at this level. Previously rising conversations about drafting a QB in 2027 have taken a backseat to one encouraging sentiment. That sentiment is the basis of today's Titans Mill.
If Cam Ward keeps playing like this, the Titans can keep building around him. That would mean the world to Saleh's tenure, as well as the franchise's rebuild.
In yesterday's loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, Ward threw for a career-high 304 yards, and rushed for a career-high 41. He passed 26/40 on the day, threw two touchdowns, and broke a five-game INT streak. Ward's 81.0 QBR was the second highest of any signal caller on Sunday.
The Titans' 36 points was the most the team had scored in five years. Ward made a questionable decision or two down the line (taking a sack at the end of regulation), but he looked improved in every other facet. He looked every bit of the franchise guy Tennessee drafted him to be.
In the case that the Titans had to draft or sign another QB next season, the Jeffery Simmons trade appeared to only be scratching the surface of in-season moves. Executing the football equivalent of a heart transplant right before a coach's second season is no easy feat.
Every pick is a little more important, and you have to hope the next guy doesn't disappoint in the same way. Saleh and his staff scrambling to fast track this rebuild around a different signal caller isn't off the table, but Ward could not have responded at a better time.
Now, when it comes to making deadline moves, the Titans have a defining performance from Ward in their back pocket. The pressure is temporarily off to have all the pieces together and ready by next season for a new guy.
Again, this isn't to say that Tennessee won't move pieces, or that Ward is safe. But the QB's career game removed the pressure for a full-on fire sale by November 10. It bought general manager Mike Borgonzi and Coach Saleh a little more time to see what the group they've got right now has.
The Titans may be 1-7 heading into the bye, but their trajectory is brighter right now than it has been since Week 1. Another game like this from Ward, and offseason projections may shift entirely. His pull is that serious.

title: Titans’ Veteran DE Emerging as a Blue Chip Trade Candidate With Deadline Looming Large
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans fell to 1-7 in the 2026 NFL season on Sunday after a 43-36 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals on the road in overtime.
Despite not doing enough to pull off a victory in overtime , the Titans showed promise on both sides of the ball and received standout performances from multiple players, including edge rusher Jacob Martin. The 30-year-old signed a two-year deal with Tennessee in March and has established himself as one of the franchise's best offseason additions.
Martin had his best game of the season against the Bengals, posting three sacks and nine quarterback pressures with four defensive stops, and it couldn't have come at a better time.
Though Martin has exceeded expectations so far in 2026 and is under contract for another year, it would make sense for the Titans to move him before the 4 p.m. ET deadline on November 10 . The Temple product is tied for fifth in the NFL in sacks (6.5) and should attract interest from contenders in need of pass-rushing support.
Trading Martin would allow Tennessee to take a closer look at the younger talent in the edge rusher group, especially Femi Oladejo and rookie first-round pick Keldric Faulk. Additionally, the Titans are still in a rebuild, so acquiring picks for a veteran piece like Martin would be a savvy move by general manager Mike Borgonzi.
Contenders such as the Detroit Lions, San Francisco 49ers, Cleveland Browns, and Buffalo Bills could be interested in Martin's services. The veteran journeyman is on an affordable deal and is providing quality pass-rushing production this season, so plenty of other teams should be in the running.
As for what Tennessee could get back for Martin, a fourth-round pick seems like a realistic return. A third-round pick is possible, but unlikely, given that Martin will turn 31 in December and isn't a consistent game-wrecker.
By trading All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears last week, the Titans signaled that they are willing to discuss trades for their veteran contributors and are looking ahead to the future. It would be a surprise if the team doesn't make another move by November 10, and dealing Martin would be a logical course of action.
The Titans will enjoy a bye in Week 9 before hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium in Week 10. We'll see whether Martin is still on the roster by then or instead playing valuable snaps for a playoff contender.

title: Titans' Trade Stock Hits a New High With Multiple Players After Loss to Bengals in Week 8
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans dropped another close game, losing 43-36 to the Cincinnati Bengals in an overtime thriller.
The Titans are now 1-5 in one-score games this season, and 1-7 on the year. Despite the loss, the Titans played arguably their best game of the year on a day where QB Cam Ward overcame not having WR Carnell Tate to produce the first 300-yard game of his career.
That development is gonna make the upcoming trade deadline more interesting. Ward obviously needs all the help he can get, but we’ve also reached a point where the stock of some of the Titans’ likeliest trade candidates has never been higher.
It creates an internal dilemma where the team has to weigh the pros and cons of trading a key piece, especially offensively. Is the capital being offered more valuable than having someone who can help Ward develop?
That’s the answer Tennessee will have to answer when teams inevitably come calling ahead of next Tuesday’s deadline. I don’t believe the Titans will just give players away for the sake of getting something in return, but as we saw last week, everyone has a price.
With that said, let’s dive into which players we should be keeping our eyes on as the trade deadline draws near.
The Titans’ veteran running back is one of the more complicated trade candidates. Pollard has undoubtedly increased his value over the last two weeks, totaling 246 rushing yards and five touchdowns while averaging over five yards per carry.
That type of consistency out of the ground game makes life easier on the Titans’ young quarterback. Trading away someone like Pollard could make the Titans incredibly one-dimensional, especially with RB Tyjae Spears’ inability to stay on the field.
However, if the Titans can get an early day-three pick (round four or five) in return for a running back on an expiring contract, they absolutely have to consider it.
Before the recent breakout, I thought maybe Tennessee could get a late day-three pick (sixth or seventh round) in return. But with how the Memphis product is playing, it wouldn’t shock me if someone offered a fifth-round pick to secure a consistent ball carrier for an offense with championship aspirations.
I personally don’t think someone would realistically go to a fourth-round pick for a rental, but if someone does offer that, then that’s something that Tennessee should take without hesitation. Even if it requires sending something like a future sixth or seventh-round pick in return to seal the deal.
But considering how important Pollard is for Ward, I think it’ll take at least a fifth round pick to lure him away.
Few have increased their stock as much as Hooker has of late. The veteran safety has already tied his career high of five interceptions through eight games ( most in NFL ), including three on Sunday against the Bengals. Hooker has also had a couple of close calls that could’ve increased that total even further.
Most INT this season Amani Hooker         5 10 players tied        3 pic.twitter.com/JHq91I4PXm
The former Iowa standout still has two years left on his contract and could be someone teams consider a real investment rather than a rental.
At this rate, Hooker would likely fetch a fourth-round pick in return, and if it turns into a bidding war between multiple teams, you could even see a team possibly go as far as offering a conditional third-rounder to secure his services.
If that’s the case, again, Tennessee should jump all over it.
CB Alontae Taylor is one of the Titans’ prized offseason additions that hasn’t panned out the way anybody hoped it would. But with CB Marcus Harris’ status unknown going forward after exiting with an ankle injury in Week 8, I believe Taylor ends up becoming more likely to stay than not.
Staying on defense, Titans' veteran pass rusher Jacob Martin has already set a new career high with 6.5 sacks through the team’s first eight games, including three against the Bengals today.
Pass rushers are a premium come playoff time, so with his value being as high as it is, it wouldn’t shock me to see a team offer a mid-to-late day three pick to try to take him away.
Lastly, WR Calvin Ridley makes sense for everyone involved. Ridley has fallen down the depth chart in Tennessee, so he may be better suited trying to help a playoff-caliber team that needs a veteran receiver to help stabilize their room.
I don’t think this one would take much; a late day-three pick could probably get it done. If someone does offer that, Tennessee would be wise to take it.

title: Robert Saleh Postgame: 1 Offensive Tendency That Fueled Cam Ward's Career Game Despite Loss to Bengals
full_text:
No Tennessee Titans fan is going to feel "good" after a loss. At the same time, at a certain point in the middle of a 1-7 campaign, you have to be happy about signs of progress that are geared toward a team's future. The Titans got a sign like that today from Cam Ward.
In spite of a 43-36 loss - with plenty to complain about therein - Ward answered the call and kept Tennessee in the game in the second half. His 304 passing yards were a career high. Ward also threw two touchdowns and avoided a pick for the first time in five weeks, passing 26-40 on the day.
The second-year QB is still 4-21 as a starter. He took a brutal sack at the end of regulation, and sailed a pass past Elic Ayomanor that ended overtime. But something clicked for Ward today, and a performance like this one could be seen as a turning point if he keeps it up.
What clicked, exactly? Well, in his expectedly dejected postgame-presser, head coach Robert Saleh noted one aspect of the offense in passing. When the Titans went tempo, Ward balled out.
"He looked awesome today," Saleh said of Ward after the game. "I thought the offense was outstanding today... the tempo really does help Cam."
Brian Daboll has been continuously criticized for calling inconsistent plays and not trusting Ward to get into a rhythm under center. Ward has had plenty of his own issues, but his OC not even trying to move the ball downfield at times hasn't helped the QB's case.
Today, however, Daboll and Ward worked together to generate numerous chunk plays. This was particularly impressive in the absence of premier WR Carnell Tate; when Tennessee sped things up in Cincinnati, Ward's often-questioned decision-making faded into the background.
Entering today ( per TeamRankings ), Tennessee had by far and away the lowest time of possession in the NFL with an average of 24:41, as well as the second highest no-huddle rate at 16.1%, according to Sharp Football Analysis. The Titans finished just one second shy of the Bengals' TOP today, with 32:11.
Their predictable, short-field passing game had a lot to do with the low TOP prior to Week 8. Retaining and even upping the tempo, combined with giving Ward looks downfield in Cincy, fully opened the game up for the second-year QB.
A loss is a loss, absolutely. Ward won't be excused for all of his mistakes either. But the Titans' passer didn't achieve the first 300-yard game of his career by any accident. Daboll's faster, more aggressive play-calling fueled Ward's improvement.
In what looks like a trial run for the Titans the rest of this season, Tennessee should fully commit to seeing what Ward has as a game-changer, rather than hoping he fits the mold of game manager in week after losing week. That starts and ends with trusting him beyond the sticks.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans Fall to Bengals in Overtime Thriller: 3 Major Takeaways From the Painful Defeat
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans entered today coming off a heartbreaking, last-second defeat at the hands of the Cleveland Browns last week. The Titans blew that game after jumping out to a dominant 14-0 start, fueled by a breakout run from Tony Pollard.
Today, Tennessee got out to a 13-0 lead in the first quarter fueled by - you guessed it - a breakout run from Pollard. What followed was an overtime thriller that nobody expected between 1-6 and 4-2 teams; one that ended in the same old way for Tennessee.
The Titans ultimately lost 43-36, failing to make good on a golden opportunity late to win this thing. Here are three takeaways from a game that should've cast a positive shadow over this franchise.
Tennessee trading away DT Jeffery Simmons earlier this week called the defense into question in a huge way. Today's game both helped and hurt their overall case.
That unit showed flashes today. Amani Hooker led the way with a mind-boggling three interceptions, doubling QB Joe Burrow's season-long INT total prior to today. On top of Hooker's leading efforts, Alontae Taylor forced a second-half fumble.
Taylor's move to nickel has clearly benefitted the CB, and may even save his role in this defense. But you can't allow 462 yards passing to the opposing team and expect to win. The takeaways are brilliant, but this incomplete defense still can't do enough to be commended consistently.
Cam Ward deserves a tip of the hat today. On the heels of a wave of doubts landing on Ward's shoulders following his showing last week and the Simmons trade, the QB had arguably the best game of his career.
Ward's 304 yards represent a new career high. He finally broke his five-game INT streak and, even considering a lost fumble in the third quarter, played a solid game. Taking a sack that led to an overtime loss is a serious negative mark, though. Ward would finish passing 26/40.
The QB still isn't entirely out of the woods at this point, especially with that aforementioned sack signaling Ward's decision-making issues remain (see also a crucial fourth-down ball that didn't come close to Elic Ayomanor in OT), but this is still a net positive performance that turns the dial in the right direction for him.
Coming off a career, three-touchdown game in last week's loss to the Browns, Pollard continues to build on his value as a veteran out of the backfield today.
The 29-year old RB posted 117 yards on 21 carries today, including two more touchdowns to add to his tally. Pollard is at six scores on the year now.
These past two weeks have been huge not only for Tennessee's offense, but for the trade value that Pollard could have ahead of the looming November 10 deadline. He's effectively the best player in this offense right now (sans Carnell Tate) and poses as either a reliable back or rising trade asset.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: How New-Look Titans Can Build on Promising First Half and Upset Bengals
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are in a competitive game with the Cincinnati Bengals through one half, as the team trails the Bengals 14-13, but has shown plenty of promise on both sides of the ball.
Despite facing heavy scrutiny on a weekly basis this season, the Titans' offense has come to play on Sunday. Quarterback Cam Ward has been solid, completing 14 of 22 passes for 166 yards with a 86.6 passer rating. Ward has completed passes to seven different receivers and is keeping the ball out of harm's way.
Running back Tony Pollard has been one of the most productive players at his position in recent weeks, and that has continued into Week 8. Pollard currently has 67 rushing yards on nine carries, and scored a 40-yard touchdown in the first quarter .
As for the defense, head coach Robert Saleh's unit has struggled at times to contain the Bengals' dynamic passing attack, but the group forced a turnover in the first quarter, an interception by safety Amani Hooker off quarterback Joe Burrow. A sack by edge rusher Jacob Martin also led to a key goal-line stand for the defense in the second quarter on fourth down inside the 5-yard line.
The Titans arguably played their best half of football all year against the Bengals, and if Saleh's squad can keep it up, an upset could be on the way.
Tennessee must continue to play clean football. A turnover by the offense or a surplus of penalties will kill the Titans' chances of winning, as they don't have enough talent to enter a shootout with the Bengals.
However, Tennessee also won't be able to tally its second win of the year if they play scared, conservative football. The offense must keep its foot on the gas, and the defense should continue to make Burrow uncomfortable, while also stepping up against the run. Bengals running back Chase Brown is averaging 6.8 yards per carry, which isn't going to cut it for the Titans' defense.
Despite trading defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on Thursday and signaling that the rebuild is still ongoing, Tennessee is showing signs of life, and an upset over a playoff-contending team like the Bengals is just what the Titans need right now to get back on track as a franchise.

title: Titans' Road Duel vs. Bengals: 2 Ways Tennessee Can Spark Hope... Even in a Loss
full_text:
We'll say it over and over again: Moral victories don't count for much. At the same time, the Tennessee Titans have counted few actual victories this season. At 1-6, and now having traded away their best player, it's about taking what you can if you're Tennessee at this point.
What's exciting about the guys that remain? What can Robert Saleh and Mike Borgonzi build on alongside their newly-acquired draft assets? Are the young players still developing as needed? These are the questions Tennessee should be asking right now.
Of course, an actual win is the ultimate positive - but without the shorthanded Titans surprising a 4-2 playoff team on the road, here are two ways Tennessee can generate some positivity even if they do fall short today.
In the absence of Simmons, the Titans desperately need other members of the defensive line to step up. This is a unit that looked weak enough with Simmons as-was; without him, the outlook is bleak for the forseeable future.
Still, with Jonah Laulu being picked up off waivers and Nazir Stackhouse seeing a recent uptick in snaps ( and production ), there are pieces here that have the opportunity to prove themselves.
Between now and the offseason, guys on the d-line are essentially auditioning to keep their spots post-draft and however else Saleh decides to shake things up prior to his second year. Few players are safe (outside of veterans like John Franklin-Myers and Jermaine Johnson II).
That makes for shifting sands in the future, but a massive window for multiple players right now. Seeing Laulu, Stackhouse, or someone else produce would be a solid sign of progress in Week 8.
To say that the stove is boiling under Cam Ward right now would be an understatement. Not only has his recent play caused doubt about his future as the team's leader, but the Simmons trade opened the door to worry about how this franchise actually feels about him.
It's no longer unfair to say that Ward could soon be short on time as the undisputed starter in Nashville. He's thrown for 200+ yards only one time this season. His 4-5 touchdown-to-interception ratio is the simplest way to show he's fallen behind in year two.
But with a solid showing at Paycor Stadium fresh off a roster-shaking move? Ward could buy himself a bit of faith amidst a sea of unanswered questions for Tennessee.
The climb is tough with his favorite target, rookie WR Carnell Tate, confirmed to sit for the contest. All the same, the gate remains open for Ward to re-earn the hope that he gave this franchise when he was taken first overall last year. That hope would go a long way for the Titans right now.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Predicting Titans' Starters vs. Bengals: Who replaces Jeffery Simmons at DT?
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have had a tumultuous week that included shipping off the face of the franchise for some much needed future draft picks. And despite that gut punch, the team somehow has to turn around just a few days later and try to beat one of the best teams in the NFL.
To say the Titans have their work cut out for them on Sunday would be an understatement. The Bengals enter this game looking like a like legitimate Super Bowl contender in all three phases. As for the Titans, well, let’s just say they do not.
With all of that said, let’s take a look at who the projected starters are for the Titans ahead of their Week 8 matchup with the Bengals.
With RB Tyjae Spears out once again, look for another heavy dose of Pollard with possibly some Nick Singleton carries sprinkled in for the first time in a few weeks.
With rookie WR Carnell Tate out, this passing attack could be in for a long afternoon unless one of these guys steps up.
This would be a great time for one of Tennessee’s prized free agent signings to make his presence felt, but considering the current trajectory offensively, It’s probably best not to get your hopes up.
The loss of DT Jeffery Simmons will be palpable at least for the rest of the season. The Titans will have to hope that Franklin-Myers is capable of becoming a dominant three-tech once again to help fill the massive void left by Simmons. While Thomas is the likeliest candidate to start in the short term, don’t be surprised to see rookie DL Keldric Faulk get some playing time inside now that Simmons is gone.
Robert Saleh has expressed his continued confidence in Faulk, and I’d imagine we start to see more packages with the rookie kicked inside as the season unfolds.
Faulk definitely needs another offseason in an NFL program to add the necessary size and strength to be successful, especially along the interior, but these inevitable reps will be critical for Faulk as he tries to figure out where he’s most comfortable heading into next season.
Williams and Flott have sneakily been a solid tandem along the boundary, but they have a massive test waiting for them this week. If the Titans are gonna have any shot of pulling off the upset, they’ll need this group to limit the impact made by Bengals star WRs Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
Unfortunately, that’s much easier said than done.
With P Tommy Townsend also sitting, the Titans will have to rely on the newly acquired Thomas Morstead to flip the field for them.

title: Commanders Daily: How Washington Set Up Treylon Burks’ 53-Yard Catch Against the Eagles
full_text:
While the Washington Commanders have struggled to stop opponents from getting explosive plays, they haven't been very successful at getting them either. That changed Sunday night. With 2:51 left in the third quarter, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels found receiver Treylon Burks for 53 yards, moving Washington from its own 40 to Philadelphia’s 7. It came exactly one play after Dorance Armstrong forced Tanner McKee’s fumble, which Charles Omenihu recovered, and it was the longest reception this season by a Commanders player.
Former Arkansas Razorback Treylon Burks with a nice move on Quinyon Mitchell #NFL #SNF pic.twitter.com/0sKPUugAfF
Commanders head coach Dan Quinn pointed to Burks’ earlier second-quarter comeback route when discussing how one route can create an opportunity for a double-move later. "There was a deep comeback by Trey Burks. He ran it at about 24, 25 yards," Quinn said. "And it was a good throw, good rip on the comeback. And that is kind of the setup for a double move later that can go for a big pass. And so that’s kind of the back-and-forth that you work with in the passing game."
#Commanders Jayden Daniels was lethally accurate pushing the ball downfield, going 3/3 for 104 yards on passes that traveled 20+ yards in the air Treylon Burks came down with two and Antonio Williams had the other. Check it out #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/t8xphqD1SM
The play Quinn is referencing was a 21-yard pass from Daniels to Burks on second-and-6 that moved Washington from its own 15 to its 36. The comeback route (first play above) shows Burks pushing upfield before breaking back toward the sideline. A defender expecting that comeback can get caught moving forward when the receiver sells the same break and takes off downfield. That catch helped Washington’s 89-yard touchdown drive , which ended with Stefon Diggs’ eight-yard reception to tie the game at 10. Quinn also made it clear that Washington has to pick its spots. “If you get the specific looks that say, hey, here’s the chance to go put the ball up. Oftentimes, if you chase too much, you can get yourself into trouble. But when the moments are there, are you able to go nail them?” Quinn said. Burks finished with three catches for a team-high 81 yards, which Washington certainly needs with Terry McLaurin out for the season . The Commanders could have gotten more out of his biggest catch, though. After reaching Philadelphia’s 7, they gained nothing on their next three plays and settled for Drew Stevens’ 25-yard field goal to stretch the lead to 16-10. Getting Burks open downfield gave Washington a chance to put that game further out of reach. Against the Rams, the offense needs to finish more of those chances in the end zone.

title: Dan Quinn Fears Serious Injury as Commanders Weigh Running Back Options
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are still sorting through injuries following Sunday's win over the Philadelphia Eagles , and one name could throw a monkey wrench into their running back rotation. Jeremy McNichols suffered a foot injury during the third quarter of Washington's 27-10 win over the visiting Eagles and did not return. Head coach Dan Quinn identified the issue today: "He does have a midfoot injury, JP. I'm concerned it's serious." Quinn's acknowledgment that Washington may need to examine additional running back options speaks volumes. For now, the team has no confirmed recovery timetable or diagnosis as they brace for additional scans on McNichols' injured foot. "I'll give you an update as it goes to Wednesday, but it's something that the team for sure is concerned with," Quinn said. McNichols recently returned from injured reserve after missing the first five games with a quadriceps injury. He had five carries for 21 yards and one catch for seven as he was starting to settle back into his role in Washington's three-man rotation.
Here are #Commanders RB Jeremy McNichols’ final two plays before he left the game with a mid foot injury The team is concerned that it is a significant injury pic.twitter.com/sbFGN0u9hQ
As we hit the midpoint of the season in Week 9, the running back rotation has taken some hits along the way. Jacory Croskey-Merritt is currently on injured reserve with a groin injury for at least two more games. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler are the remaining healthy backs on the active roster. White did well against Philly with 55 yards on 11 carries and a touchdown; Ekeler added 36 yards on eight carries and scored on a two-point conversion. Devin Neal and Craig Reynolds are the team's current practice-squad options. Washington hosts the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. Quinn expects to provide another update Wednesday, when the Commanders should have a better idea whether they need to bring in another running back. title: Commanders Snap Judgment: Why Antonio Williams Should Stay Ahead of Diggs and Burks
full_text:
Stefon Diggs caught the touchdown, and Treylon Burks supplied the biggest gain. But neither veteran was the receiver the Washington Commanders used most in Sunday night's 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles . That was Antonio Williams. The rookie led Washington with seven targets and five catches for 54 yards, and his snap count showed how much work he's getting with Terry McLaurin out for the season. Now the question is whether Washington keeps putting that much of its passing game in his hands. Snap Judgment : Williams ( 50 snaps - 83% ) led the receivers in playing time, ahead of Burks (40 snaps - 67%) and Diggs (39 snaps - 65%). I'd keep him at the front of this rotation. Williams caught three passes for 20 yards on Washington’s 89-yard touchdown drive. His five-yard catch on third-and-4 kept the possession alive, and a 10-yard reception on second-and-10 moved the chains again. In the fourth quarter, his 30-yard catch was the biggest gain on the drive that pushed Washington’s lead to 19-10.
Antonio Williams was sensational Sunday night. Unguardable pic.twitter.com/uh06r9UegT
Tone's got hands 🫴 @a_williams2022 | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/PFB5qF2kQQ
Charles Omenihu returned with Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw inactive , finishing with a sack, three quarterback hits, and a fumble recovery. Snap Judgment : Omenihu played 46 defensive snaps (67%), compared with 49 for K’Lavon Chaisson, 45 for Odafe Oweh and 40 for Dorance Armstrong. I'd keep him involved when the front gets healthier. Omenihu was also credited with a quarterback hit on the fourth-down pass Rasul Douglas intercepted late in the fourth quarter. Douglas returned it to Philadelphia’s 37, and Washington scored on its next possession.
Austin Ekeler finished with eight carries for 36 yards and scored on the two-point conversion. Snap Judgment : Rachaad White (28 snaps - 47%) led the backfield, followed by Ekeler (20 snaps - 33%) and Jeremy McNichols (12 snaps - 20%). Ekeler played seven snaps against San Francisco, so Quinn followed through on giving him more work . Ekeler’s 18-yard run took Washington to Philadelphia’s 8-yard line in the second quarter. Diggs caught the tying touchdown on the next snap. The backfield split could change again against the Rams. Quinn said Monday that Jeremy McNichols has a midfoot injury and added, “I'm concerned it's serious.” More scans are planned for Tuesday. With Jacory Croskey-Merritt still on injured reserve, Washington could need Ekeler to handle more work if McNichols can’t play.
One of the most interesting takeaways from glancing at the snap counts for Sunday night's Commanders vs. Eagles game was seeing Mike Sainristil's jersey number next to his total number of defensive snaps. That's right: Sainristil played 16 special teams snaps, but zero on defense, as Washington beat Philadelphia 27-10. Now the question becomes: where does he fit in the defensive rotation after a game in which Washington never used him there? Snap Judgment : Amik Robertson (68 snaps - 99%), Trey Amos (60 snaps - 87%), and Rasul Douglas (32 snaps - 46%) handled Washington’s cornerback snaps against Philadelphia. Quinn said Monday that Amos no longer needs the workload restriction he had against San Francisco. He also praised Nick Cross’ work at nickel, where Washington used him near the line of scrimmage and as a blitzer. One question for Daronte Jones at his next press conference is why Sainristil never entered on defense. The next game will tell us whether he gets back into the rotation, Williams continues to lead the receivers in opportunities, and Omenihu stays this involved up front. title: Commanders Report Card: Who Delivered in Eagles Win — and Who Still Fell Short?
full_text:
The first few minutes of the Washington Commanders' attempt at revenge over the rival Philadelphia Eagles seemed to hit every last beat of what Washington fans didn't want to see in the squad's humiliating return to the primetime slate.
They made plenty of mistakes on their first few drives, but look no further than their very first series for a who's-who of classic errors that have regularly peppered Commanders games all season. Jayden Daniels missing on makeable throws, back-to-back false starts, surrendered once-friendly field position on third-and-one, and a blown kick by increasingly inconvenienced kicker Drew Stevens ruled the drive moot, all while backup Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee moved the ball upfield on the defense.
But the second the Commanders, down multiple scores, heard the boos from inside their own house at Northwest Stadium, they erased yet another slow start. Unlike in their previous loss to the San Francisco 49ers, they never took their foot off the gas, scoring 27 straight and somehow climbing right back into the divisional standings at 2-4-1 behind a complicated, well-rounded win.
Daniels looked generally lethargic at first, specifically during one of the false-start calls he initiated with a strange pre-snap pump-fake , but he mostly made the right plays from then on once he exorcised that gaffe from his system. Fans can't quibble with a stat line of 217 yards on 16/29 passing with a touchdown thrown in if he can perform as surgically as he did past the first quarter.
Jayden Daniels ➡️ Stefon Diggs for the TD! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Okl6kfEkFL
That pass to Stefon Diggs was just the tip of the iceberg in Daniels' unflappable passing aggression. He stuck with Treylon Burks for a 53-yard gain after an early drop and kept finding Chig Okonkwo for bailout opportunities, using his receivers' varying strengths to interchange big plays with short-range reads.
This wasn't the cleanest overall outing he's completed in Washington, but Commanders fans have to feel relieved that one of the more subtly frustrating statistics surrounding the team can finally vanish; despite his best (if inconsistent) efforts, he'd yet to secure a win since Week 5 in 2025 , having had to watch backup Marcus Mariota secure this roster's lone previous victory over the Seattle Seahawks on the sidelines while the usual starter recovered from a dislocated elbow. This division win, the first of the Commanders' campaign in four tries, belongs to him as much as anyone.
Even if Jacory Croskey-Merritt were active enough to take his regular spot in the depth chart ahead of spot-starting back Rachaad White, the consensus around the Commanders' less-than-inspiring run game still likely wouldn't be very optimistic given their infrastructure. Whether it's a lack of high-end rushing talent, blockers struggling to create the necessary holes, or both excuses working in tandem, this element of the offense has yet to jump off the screen.
White ended the night with a team-high 55 yards on the ground, but just about all of that chunk yardage and the touchdown it resulted in arrived on Washington’s late, game-clinching drive. Older reserves Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols added 57 more rushing yards, barely enough to punch the spiraling Eagles defense where it hurt.
The new top-three receiving trio post-Terry McLaurin did not disappoint. Following Burks' early flubbed attempt at a simple catch-and-run, a blunder that once looked like an omen for another tough showing out on the field, he, Diggs, and Antonio Williams did well to convert on the chances that Daniels passed their way.
They settled into zones, caught in stride with their passes and held their own against a usually feared Philadelphia secondary. The Eagles, who have often held up against big plays over their contending years, still had 2025 Pro Bowler and All-Pro cornerback Quinyon Mitchell to disrupt the Commanders' wideouts, but even he arguably got the worst of it when Burks burnt him on a deep route.
Quinyon Mitchell is a decent CB at best and Eagles fans will act like he’s playing like 09’ Darrelle Revis pic.twitter.com/V7HlEB7hVP
The receiving room may yet survive and enjoy some thrills without McLaurin, who's slated to miss the remainder of the season following a torn patellar tendon against the 49ers, meaning that Washington will take whatever they can get out of its prospects and supplementary veterans. As it turns out, their scheme heading forward heavily involves Okonkwo, and he's ready for Daniels' heaves.
32 yards on two completions on four targets doesn't look like much, but the tight end always seemed to be available whenever Daniels needed a savior out deep. That's where Okonkwo's size came in handy, with few individual defenders able to deter someone with his agility and hands. Had he not coughed up a tough fumble on one of his receptions, this could have easily gone down as the big receiver's most impactful outing of the 2026 slate.
CHIG OKONKWO ALMOST HAD ONE pic.twitter.com/hp1UGVPaQr
His double-catch to help Washington escape its own end zone already seemed like a special grab in the moment, and that was before he came within a foot of collecting a play-of-the-year contender with a goal-line fade attempt for the ages. The tight end rotation has desperately needed anyone to aid Daniels' pass-catching corps, and Okonkwo finally seems at home in Washington's offense.
At the very least, Washington's offensive linemen allowed the quarterback to sit back and watch routes develop a few times, a luxury that fans have come to appreciate given his slight frame and their lack of reliable blocking.
Even if Philadelphia's pass-rushers still made life tough for the tackles, this grade is a procedural, pre-snap-related indictment of the position group's composure. This unit is far too handsy in drawing holding calls and much too jumpy with Daniels calling the shots, with the false starts repeatedly hurting the offense's chances of converting on their promising drives.
Still, only two sacks in Daniels' game recap have to be mentioned when discussing a blocking line that's not completely untalented- just undisciplined.
Everyone enjoyed moments to shine against an Eagles offense that seemed to disintegrate as the game trudged on. McKee went down five times to sacks from Commanders tacklers, largely because Washington emphasized rushing the quarterback's distribution process.
There were the usual suspects, like regular edge presences like Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson, but then there were breakouts like Charles Omenihu in his best Commanders appearance yet and Shy Tuttle, the impressive veteran who continues shining since barely sneaking onto the roster . The strength in numbers, particularly from versatile middle linebackers Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu, empowered plenty of niche defenders to get in on the action within the deceptive scheme and keep the Eagles' own stoppers guessing.
This unit didn't have as much to do as in Week 1, when Eagles receiver DeVonta Smith was active in Philadelphia, but they still made their collective presence known within the blitzing attack. Nick Cross was everywhere as the much-appreciated safety who can split defenders at scrimmage, as was Amik Robertson in his typically loud breakups on screen pass attempts.
Trey Amos , now that his return game against San Francisco is finally in the past, looked comfortable breaking up his rare targets in isolation, and fans will remember the pick he collected off of Dallas Goedert's hands that was wiped out following a roughing-the-passer penalty. No matter: Rasul Douglas stepped up a few minutes later with an interception that triggered no flags, thereby setting up the final, game-clinching scoring drive in the matchup's closing minutes.
Rasul Douglas with the INT for the Commanders! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/UYdodH2LDO
The one blooper that went down on the special…

Here are my immediate reactions in this week’s Game Pulse. *Game Pulse collects my instant takeaways after each quarter and at the final whistle.
The Eagles walk off the field, losers of 6 straight pic.twitter.com/0tT0qYOZAC

A season-high five sacks is the production Washington has needed from this group; Washington did it without Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, and Jer’Zhan Newton, while holding Saquon Barkley to 30 yards on 13 carries. - Antonio Williams’ 30-yard catch was excellent work finishing the play and keeping the ball off the ground. Washington needed somebody to make that catch, and the rookie delivered. Between his involvement on the touchdown drive and that fourth-quarter gain, Williams gave Jayden Daniels important completions at different stages of the game. - Drew Stevens followed his opening miss with four straight makes, including the 42-yarder that gave Washington a two-score lead. Philadelphia went the other direction, backing itself up with penalties before Jake Elliott hit the upright. Washington benefited from that miss, then made the next possession count. - K'Lavon Chaisson’s late sack helped put Philadelphia in a desperate situation, and Rasul Douglas took advantage when McKee floated a ball up for grabs. Chaisson’s penalties were costly, but he also helped Washington close this game. After having an earlier interception erased by a flag, the defense made this takeaway count. - Rachaad White put it away. His 33-yard run set up the one-yard touchdown, and Washington finished with 27 unanswered points after falling behind 10-0. The penalties still need fixing, but the Commanders turned their last takeaway into a touchdown and finished the job on the ground.
SUUUUUUUUUL pic.twitter.com/oKB3eTFhwW
- Nick Cross and the left side of the defense blew up a run in the backfield, and Sonny Styles later helped hurry McKee into releasing the ball before Omenihu could get there again. Washington is making Philadelphia work for its yards despite the missing pieces up front. - Charles Omenihu made his return count, beating two blockers for his first sack with Washington. Dorance Armstrong then forced a fumble that Omenihu recovered. Those are the kinds of disruptive plays Washington needed from its veteran defensive ends, and both delivered in the third quarter. - Chig Okonkwo practically caught that 22-yarder with three fingers. After his first-quarter fumble, that was a good response and another reminder of what he can give this passing game when Washington gets him involved. - The offensive line still found ways to make things harder. Another presnap flag, followed by Chris Paul getting beaten for a sack, brought back the same problems Washington spent the bye trying to fix. The offense has shown improvement tonight, but those mistakes keep limiting what it can do. - Daniels’ 54-yard connection with Treylon Burks gave Washington a much-needed explosive play, and Stevens finished the possession with a 25-yard field goal. Washington had scored 16 unanswered points. You’d like a touchdown after a gain like that, but the Commanders were finally making Philadelphia chase them. - Chaisson’s second personal foul was especially costly because it wiped out an interception at the end of the quarter. Washington had a chance to take the ball away again and instead gave Philadelphia another opportunity. The defense was doing enough to get off the field; that penalty kept it out there.
Tough break for the Commanders as they get flagged for roughing the passer. You hate to see a player going up to swat a pass and coming down and getting flagged but that's the Roger Goodell experience pic.twitter.com/SODurabvPq
- Antonio Williams caught three passes on the touchdown drive, and Austin Ekeler added an 18-yard run around the outside. That’s a better look at how Washington can keep this offense moving without McLaurin. Williams gave Daniels somewhere to go with the ball, and Ekeler showed why getting him more involved made sense. - The touchdown to Stefon Diggs was a well-designed use of traffic to create separation without drawing an offensive pass interference flag. That’s the pick/not-pick play you want down there. Blough helped free his receiver, Daniels delivered, and Washington finished the opportunity. - Even after scoring, Washington couldn’t get through the extra point without another pre-snap penalty. Then K’Lavon Chaisson created pressure and forced a hurried throw, only to get called for a personal foul afterward. The offense showed some life in the second quarter, but the discipline problems keep following this team. - Luke McCaffrey has helped Washington in the return game. Between his 44-yard kickoff return and 27-yard punt return, he’s giving the offense opportunities to work with a shorter field. - Diggs cutting back inside on his late 20-yard catch was smart with timeouts available. Take the extra yards when Washington still has a way to stop the clock. Daniels took a hard hit along the way, but the Commanders got into position for Stevens’ 38-yard field goal and came away with points before halftime. Daniels looked like he was in some pain after the hit, but he stayed in the game.
Washington is bringing the pressure with an 88% blitz rate. 👀 #NextGenStats powered by @awscloud . pic.twitter.com/rJz9xlHooa
- Two weeks to clean things up, and Washington still turned third-and-1 into third-and-11 with back-to-back false starts. Luke McCaffrey’s 44-yard opening return had set the offense up at midfield, but that opportunity ended with a missed field goal. The later ineligible receiver penalty and Chris Paul’s false start added to a quarter full of avoidable mistakes. - The defense gave Washington something to work with on Philadelphia’s opening possession, getting Tanner McKee off his spot and forcing a three-and-out. With the defensive front missing so many pieces, that was an encouraging start. The offense needed to do more with the opportunities it was getting. - Treylon Burks’ drop hurt, but Daniels had his own miss on the third-down throw to Stefon Diggs. Washington needs both its quarterback and receivers to finish those plays, especially with Terry McLaurin out. There were chances to keep possessions moving. - Chig Okonkwo’s fumble added another mistake from a player Washington needs to lean on. He has become an important part of this passing game, which makes ball security even more important when the offense is already struggling to sustain drives. - Drew Stevens answered his miss from 55 yards by hitting from 56. Good response from the rookie, but Washington keeps asking him to salvage possessions from a long way out. The offense has to give itself a chance to finish closer to the end zone.

title: Commanders Make Final Call on Treylon Burks, John Bates for Eagles Rematch
full_text:
The Washington Commanders will have Treylon Burks and John Bates available for Sunday Night Football against the Philadelphia Eagles. Both entered the weekend questionable, with Burks dealing with a foot injury and Bates a shoulder issue. That gives Jayden Daniels two receiving options in an offense already without Terry McLaurin, although Washington will still be missing both starting defensive tackles . Daron Payne (foot) and Javon Kinlaw (knee) are inactive for tonight’s Week 8 rematch. Here are the full inactive lists for both teams:
QB Athan Kaliakmanis (Emergency 3rd QB) CB Fabian Moreau CB Isaac Yiadom G Tanoa Togiai DT Daron Payne DT Javon Kinlaw
Marcus Mariota is available to back up Daniels after missing the San Francisco game with a knee injury. Charles Omenihu is also active after sitting out that game, giving Washington another option on the defensive line. Jer’Zhan Newton remains on injured reserve after being downgraded to out Saturday . Washington elevated Byron Cowart from the practice squad to help an interior rotation that includes Tim Settle Jr. and Shy Tuttle.
WR DeVonta Smith LB Jihaad Campbell WR Dontayvion Wicks CB Jonathan Jones C/G Jake Majors WR Britain Covey
Philadelphia gets edge rusher Nolan Smith back, although it will be without receivers DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks and Britain Covey. Saquon Barkley is active after dealing with hamstring and back injuries during the week.

title: Commanders Make Late Roster Move, Get Encouraging News Ahead of Eagles Game
full_text:
After returning to practice Wednesday, Washington Commanders defensive tackle Jer'Zhan Newton was downgraded Saturday from questionable to OUT for Sunday night's game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Newton will remain in his 21-day activation window while he continues his comeback from a torn pectoral muscle . Washington instead elevated defensive tackle Byron Cowart from the practice squad. The Commanders' interior defensive line is ultra-thin right now, with starters Daron Payne (foot) and Javon Kinlaw (knee) out with injuries . According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, Payne suffered a season-ending Jones fracture during Friday's practice. Cowart last appeared in a regular-season game in 2024. Tim Settle Jr. and Shy Tuttle are the remaining established defensive tackles available, with Cowart providing additional depth. That leaves Washington particularly thin in the middle against an Eagles offense that expects to have Saquon Barkley available despite his hamstring and back injuries. ESPN's Adam Schefter reported Sunday morning that Treylon Burks is expected to play against the Eagles after being listed as questionable with a foot injury, following limited practice Wednesday and Friday and missing Thursday's practice altogether . Burks has nine receptions for 152 yards and two touchdowns in five games this season, including four catches for 66 yards against San Francisco before the bye. Of course, expected to play isn't 100% a given; Washington's inactive list will have the final say. title: Commanders vs. Eagles Weather Forecast for Sunday Night Football
full_text:
The Washington Commanders return from their bye Sunday night to host the Philadelphia Eagles at Northwest Stadium, and fans planning to go should bring an extra layer. The forecast calls for very little wind and a low chance of rain, but temperatures are expected to fall into the 40s during the game. Kickoff is scheduled for 8:20 p.m. ET on Sunday, Nov. 1, in Landover, Maryland, with Washington looking for its second win of the season.
According to the National Weather Service’s hourly forecast for Landover , temperatures should be around 51 degrees at 8 p.m., just ahead of kickoff, with a southeast wind around 1 mph. Rain chances are listed at 0% throughout the expected game window. Forecast checked Saturday, Oct. 31. The following times are for Sunday, Nov. 1, in Eastern Standard Time.
The table accounts for Sunday morning’s clock change to Eastern Standard Time.
With so little wind in the forecast, Jayden Daniels shouldn't have to make big adjustments when Washington wants to throw downfield. David Blough will still have to find what works against Philadelphia's defense, but the current outlook gives him little reason to build the passing plan around the weather. Drew Stevens should also have a fairly calm evening from a weather standpoint. Washington will get a better feel for his range during warmups, but there isn't much wind in the forecast to add another complication to longer field-goal attempts.
The Commanders’ gameday guide lists parking lots opening at 4 p.m., Legends Plaza at 5 p.m. and stadium gates at 6 p.m. Anyone planning to tailgate could be spending several hours outside before the game even begins. Afternoon temperatures are expected to reach the 60s, so fans arriving early should bring something warmer to put on later. A jacket or sweatshirt over a lighter layer makes sense if you're planning to stay through the final whistle, with the forecast dropping into the upper 40s late in the game. title: How to Watch Commanders vs. Eagles: TV Channel, Start Time, Streaming, and Radio
full_text:
The Washington Commanders get another shot at the Philadelphia Eagles Sunday night, seven weeks after their season began with a two-point loss in Philadelphia. This time, the rematch comes at Northwest Stadium with Washington returning from its bye at 1-4-1 and the Eagles sitting at 2-5. A lot has changed since Philadelphia's 24-22 win in Week 1. The Commanders are now without Terry McLaurin for the season , while the Eagles have Jalen Hurts on injured reserve and will also be without DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks Sunday night. Washington's defensive line took another hit Friday when Daron Payne joined Javon Kinlaw among the players ruled out . Here is everything you need to know to watch, stream, and listen to the Commanders' Week 8 matchup against the Eagles.
Date: Sunday, Nov. 1 Kickoff: 8:20 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium, Landover, Maryland TV: NBC
threads of the week pic.twitter.com/dC0Wi8ZS73
NBC will carry Sunday's game nationally as part of Sunday Night Football. Play-by-play: Mike Tirico Analyst: Cris Collinsworth Sideline: Melissa Stark The game will also be available in Spanish on Universo.
Fans can stream Sunday Night Football with a Peacock subscription. Live TV streaming services that include a local NBC affiliate also provide access through eligible plans. NFL+ subscribers in the United States can watch the game live on supported phones and tablets through the NFL app. NFL Sunday Ticket does not include Sunday Night Football. That subscription covers out-of-market Sunday afternoon games. For fans watching in the United Kingdom, the game will air on Sky Sports NFL. NFL Game Pass International on DAZN also carries games outside the United States, subject to availability and local broadcast restrictions.
Washington's radio broadcast will be available on BIG 100 (WBIG-FM) and throughout the Commanders Radio Network. Play-by-play: Bram Weinstein Analyst: London Fletcher Sideline: Logan Paulsen
Fans can also listen through the iHeartRadio app . The Commanders' Spanish-language broadcast features Moises Linares and Juan Romero and is also available through iHeartRadio. The team's official pregame show begins two hours before kickoff and can be heard through the Commanders app. NFL+ subscribers also have access to live game audio across supported devices.
Payne was initially listed as questionable Friday before being ruled out. NFL.com reported Saturday that he suffered a season-ending Jones fracture in his foot during Friday's practice.
Newton was downgraded to out Saturday and will remain on injured reserve for Sunday's game. Washington also elevated defensive tackle Byron Cowart from the practice squad, adding depth with Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw already ruled out. Treylon Burks will reportedly play . Jayden Daniels , Marcus Mariota, Stefon Diggs and Charles Omenihu finished the week without game designations.
Running back Saquon Barkley was limited Friday after missing the first two practices of the week with hamstring and back injuries, but he carries no game designation and is cleared to play.
Sunday night's rematch gives Washington another chance against the team that handed it a two-point loss in the season opener. The Commanders will have the home-field advantage this time, but they'll also have to face Philadelphia without several key players on both sides of the ball.
